﴿And there was no nation but that a warner had passed among them.﴾ (Surah Fatir, 24)

His saying:

﴿That is because your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people were unaware.﴾ (Surah al-An'am, 131)

And His saying:

﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a messenger.﴾ (Surah al-Isra', 15)

Therefore we see that those who do not believe in the method of heaven set down for themselves laws that organize their lives. Do they not have a law that defines crimes and prescribes punishment for them? There is no punishment without criminalization, no criminalization without a text, and no text without promulgation.

Hence arises the importance of enacting laws and publishing them in the public newspapers and gazettes so that everyone may know them. It is not right to punish a person for a crime he does not know to be a crime. He must first be informed of it, so that he knows that this act carries such-and-such a penalty, and thereby the proof is established against him.

Here we also observe that two messengers may be contemporaries. Were not Abraham and Lot contemporaries? Were not Shu'ayb and Moses contemporaries? What is the reason for this?

We say: because the world was formerly in a state of isolation, each group isolated in its place from the others, for there were no means of transport. Each group was in a land that did not know of the others and had no knowledge of them.

Hence each group had its own environment, with its customs, traditions, and wrongs that suited it. These people worship idols, those give short measure in weight and measure, and those commit male-with-male acts instead of with women.

Therefore, every environment has its own suitable crime, and it is necessary to send messengers to address these crimes, each in its own land separately.

But the message of Muhammad (ﷺ) came at a time when distances had converged with the existence of means of transport, to the point that a sin committed, for example, in America is known about on the same day. Thus the environments and conditions became one, and so it was logical that he (ﷺ) be sent to all people and for all times.

The Noble Qur'an has expressed this universality in His saying:

﴿And We have not sent you except comprehensively to mankind as a bringer of good tidings and a warner.﴾ (Surah Saba', 28)

That is: to all, leaving no one out, just as the tailor says, "I gathered (kaffantu) the cloth," meaning I brought some of it upon some other, so that nothing of it is lost. Then the Almighty says:

﴿That worship Allah and avoid Taghut.﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 36)

This is the mission of the messengers: ﴿...that worship Allah...﴾ (36). Worship means commitment to a command that is carried out and a prohibition that is refrained from. Therefore, if someone comes claiming divinity without a method, we say to him: how shall we worship you? What is the method you have brought? What do you command us? From what do you forbid us?

Here there is a command to worship and a prohibition against Taghut (the tyrannical false power, or false deity), and this is what they call tahliyah wa takhliyah (adornment and clearing): adorning oneself by worshipping God, and clearing oneself by distancing oneself from Satan.

On these two elements the matter of faith is built. In "I bear witness that there is no god" there is negation, and in "except Allah" there is affirmation, as though the one who utters the testimony negates plurality and affirms the oneness of God, may He be exalted. In this way you have cleared yourself of polytheism and adorned yourself with divine oneness.

Accordingly, the reward for these in the Hereafter will be of the same kind as this adornment and clearing. This is why in the saying of the Blessed and Exalted Lord we find:

﴿Whoever is drawn away from the Fire...﴾ (Surah Al 'Imran, 185)

that is, cleared of punishment.

﴿...and admitted to Paradise...﴾ (Surah Al 'Imran, 185)

that is, adorned with bliss. And His saying:

﴿...and avoid Taghut...﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 36)

means: keep far from Taghut. The counterpart of this is: draw near to God. The word "Taghut" contains intensification, indicating one who has reached the peak of tyranny and increased in it. There is a difference between the bare act, such as taghā (to transgress), and its intensification, such as taghut. It is one who, when people submit to his falsehood, increases in tyranny over a greater falsehood.

An example of this: a youth rebels against his society and begins to commit small and trivial wrongs. He finds that people draw near to him and flatter him to avert his evil. So he advances further in his falsehood, buying for himself a weapon with which to attack lives, stealing precious wealth, and reaching the peak of injustice and aggression. Had people held his hand from the very first incident, he would not have reached this state.

From here we find that blood money (diyat) is borne by the 'aqilah (the close kin group) and paid on behalf of the guilty perpetrator, because of the responsibility that falls upon them for leaving this offender, and on the others to take hold of his hand and restrain him from harm.

We note in this word, Taghut, that because it combines every intensification of the act, it resists being made to conform, as though it were a tyrant in its form and meaning. We find it applies to the singular, the dual, and the plural, and to the masculine and the feminine. We say: rajul taghut (a tyrannical man), imra'ah taghut (a tyrannical woman), rajulan taghut (two tyrannical men), imra'atan taghut (two tyrannical women), rijal taghut (tyrannical men), nisa' taghut (tyrannical women). It is as though it has tyrannized over all forms by its wording.

Thus: Taghut is the one who, when people submit to his injustice, grows in injustice. From this is His saying:

﴿So he made his people feeble-minded, and they obeyed him.﴾ (Surah al-Zukhruf, 54)

His condition reached the point where he claimed divinity and said:

﴿I know of no god for you other than me.﴾ (Surah al-Qasas, 38)

It is related in the stories of false prophets that when news reached one of the caliphs of a man claiming prophethood, he ordered his men not to concern themselves with his affair, to leave him alone, and not to give his matter any attention, perhaps he would end. Then after a time another appeared claiming prophethood. They brought the first one to see his opinion of the new prophet. He said: "What is your opinion of this one who claims prophethood? Which of you is the prophet?" The first said: "He is a liar, for I did not send anyone!" He had thought they believed his claim to prophethood, so he went beyond this to claim divinity. Such is Taghut.

This word, Taghut, occurs eight times in the Qur'an. Six of these are suitable for both masculine and feminine usage, and once it occurs in the feminine in His saying:

﴿And those who avoid Taghut, not worshipping it...﴾ (Surah al-Zumar, 17)

And once it occurs in the masculine in His saying:

﴿They wish to seek judgment before Taghut, though they were commanded to reject it.﴾ (Surah al-Nisa', 60)

In the language there are words in which masculine and feminine are equal, such as the saying of the Truthful Lord, may He be blessed and exalted:

﴿And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it; and if they see the way of right guidance, they will not adopt it as a way.﴾ (Surah al-A'raf, 146)

and His saying:

﴿Say: This is my way...﴾ (Surah Yusuf, 108)

So the word "sabil" (way) came once in the masculine and once in the feminine.

Then He says:

﴿So among them are those whom God guided, and among them are those upon whom error was justly decreed.﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 36)

Some have taken this verse as proof, saying through it that guidance is in God's hand and we have no part in whether we are guided or not, and so on with such sayings. We say: come, let us read the Qur'an. He, may He be exalted, says:

﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance.﴾ (Surah Fussilat, 17)

Had guidance meant what you intend, they would not have preferred blindness and chosen it. But "hadaynahum" (We guided them) here means only: We pointed them out and directed them, and they have the right of choice, and they are fit for this and for that. Indication comes to both the believer and the disbeliever. God indicated to all, so the one who turns to God in faith, God increases him in guidance and gives him his piety, as He said:

﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and gives them their piety.﴾ (Surah Muhammad, 17)

From this is what some consider a contradiction between His saying:

﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love.﴾ (Surah al-Qasas, 56)

and His saying:

﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path.﴾ (Surah al-Shura, 52)

where the Almighty negates guidance from the Messenger (ﷺ) in the first and affirms it for him in the second. We observe that the act here is one, which is guidance, and the one spoken of is one, the Messenger (ﷺ). How can one act be affirmed of one agent once and negated of him another time?

The aspect must be distinct. In "Indeed, you do not guide..." (56), that is: you cannot place faith into the heart of whomever you love. Rather, you indicate and direct only. As for the guidance of faith, it is in the hand of God, may He be exalted; He guides to it whoever has readiness for faith, and turns away from it whoever turns from it and rejects it. It is as though God is in the service of His servants: whoever loves something, He gives it to him and makes it easy for him. Thus He guided the believer to faith, and He sealed the heart of the disbeliever with disbelief.

Thus guidance comes in two senses: in the sense of indication and direction, as in the previous verse, and in the sense of assistance and expanding the breast to faith, as in His saying:

﴿But God guides whom He wills.﴾ (Surah al-Qasas, 56)

and His saying:

﴿And He increased them in guidance.﴾ (Surah Muhammad, 17)

So His saying, ﴿So among them are those whom God guided...﴾ (36), means guidance of faith and assistance: that He enabled the method within him, made it easy for him, and expanded his breast by it.

﴿And among them are those upon whom error was justly decreed...﴾ (36).

"Haqqat" (was justly decreed): that is, it became a due right for him and was incumbent upon him because of the deeds he had committed, for which he deserves nothing but error. They were not made to deserve it, and it was not incumbent upon them, except by what they did. This is like His saying:

﴿Indeed, God does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ (Surah al-An'am, 144)

Which came first: God's not guiding them, or their wrongdoing? It is clear that the wrongdoing came from them first, so God named them wrongdoers, and then the result was that they were deprived of guidance. Here I mention an example that we have often repeated so that it may be fixed in minds, and to God belongs the highest likeness: suppose you are traveling on a road heading to a certain town, and you come to a junction of many roads with signs pointing in different directions. At that point you turn to a traffic policeman and say: "Please, I want the town of such-and-such." He says to you: "This way." You say: "Praise be to God, I was nearly lost. May God reward you with good."

When he finds that you received his words with contentment and love, and thanked him for his kindness, he wishes to increase his giving to you. He says to you: "But on this road there is a difficult obstacle, and I will accompany you until you pass through it safely."

Thus the first from him was merely indication, whereas the second is the m

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah 16, verse 37:

God, blessed and exalted is He, consoles His Messenger (ﷺ), affirms his eagerness for his community, and shows that he bears himself in the cause of their guidance beyond what God has laid upon him, as He said to him in another verse:

﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not become believers.﴾ (Surah al-Shu'ara', 26:3)

And He, exalted is He, says:

﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves; grievous to him is what you suffer; [he is] concerned over you and to the believers, kind and merciful.﴾ (Surah al-Tawbah, 9:128)

Then, after this, God, glorified is He, cuts off hope before the obstinate deniers, and He says, exalted is He:

﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who misleads.…﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 16:37). That is: He does not lead astray except one who does not accept faith in Him, so He leaves him to his disbelief; indeed, He seals up his heart, without any regret over him. This is His will, and God has granted him what he wills.

﴿And for them there will be no helpers.﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 16:37)

So then: the matter is not merely the absence of guidance; rather, there is a battle in which they find no helper or supporter to deliver them from it, as He, exalted is He, says:

﴿So we have no intercessors, and no devoted friend.﴾ (Surah al-Shu'ara', 26:100–101)

So then: God does not guide whoever has chosen misguidance for himself, and indeed He will punish him with a punishment in which he finds no one to help him.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 16, verse 38:

{And they swear by Allah with their most emphatic oaths...} "38" {(Surah An-Nahl).}

Glory be to Allah! How do you swear by Allah while you do not believe in Him? And what is the meaning of the word "Allah" for you? This is a sign of stupidity among the disbelievers, and proof that the matter of faith is not clear in their minds. For the word "Allah" itself is evidence of belief in Him, glory be to Him, and a word does not exist in the language except after what it signifies has first existed. Television, for example, before it existed had no name; then, after it came into being, they gave it a name.

So: meanings exist first, and then names are assigned to the meanings. If you see a name, does its meaning come before it or after it? It comes before it. So if they say, "Allah does not exist," we say to them: "You have lied, for the word 'Allah' is a term existing in the language, and it must have a meaning that preceded its existence."

So: faith precedes disbelief. Disbelief came logically, because the meaning of disbelief (kufr) is concealment (sitr). The question then is: what did it conceal? It concealed faith, and one only conceals something that exists. Thus we say: disbelief is evidence of faith.

{And they swear by Allah with their most emphatic oaths...} "38" {(Surah An-Nahl)}, meaning: exaggerating in the oath and making it emphatic. How close their stupidity is here to what they said in another verse: {O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment} "32" {(Surah Al-Anfal)}.

This is not the speech of sensible people. What they swore by Allah was that {Allah does not raise up one who dies...} "38" {(Surah An-Nahl)}, and this is a denial of resurrection, just as they had said earlier:

{They said: "When we are dead and have become dust and bones, shall we truly be resurrected?"} "82" {(Surah Al-Mu'minun)}

Allah, the Truthful, answers them with {Balaa} "Yes," which is a particle that negates what precedes it. The people of the language say: the negation of a negation is an affirmation. So {balaa} negates the negation preceding it, which is their saying: {Allah does not raise up one who dies...} "38" {(Surah An-Nahl)}.

So the meaning is: "Rather, Allah does raise up one who dies."

{A promise binding upon Him, a true one...} "38" {(Surah An-Nahl)}. A promise (wa'd) is the announcement of something whose time has not yet come. When a promise is made of an event that will happen later, we look at the one who promised: is he able to bring about what he promised, or not?

If he is not able to carry out what he promised, because he does not secure all the causes that enable him to fulfil his promise, we say to him: "Say: if Allah wills." So that when the time of execution comes and you do not fulfil your promise, we may find an excuse for you, and so that you are not then described as a liar, for the matter has been attributed to the will of Allah.

Blessed and exalted Allah does not prevent us from planning for the future, working towards this and building that. Plan as you wish and prepare for the future its preparation, but attach to this your saying: "If Allah wills," for you do not possess all the causes that would enable you to do what you want in the future. Blessed and exalted Allah has said: {And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow," except [with the qualification], "If Allah wills."} "23-24" {(Surah Al-Kahf)}.

For example, suppose you wish to go tomorrow to a certain person to speak with him about some matter. Have you guaranteed for yourself that you will live until tomorrow? Have you guaranteed that this person will be present tomorrow? Have you guaranteed that the motive you have will not change? Perhaps all these conditions are available to you, yet when you set out, something prevents you from going. So: we must attach to any future action our saying: "If Allah wills."

As for a promise from Allah, Exalted is He, He is able to carry out what He promises, because no power can stand against His will, and nothing in the earth or the heavens can frustrate Him. Therefore His promise is {haqq} (binding truth) that He will fulfil.

Then Allah, the Truthful, says: {But most of the people do not know} "38" {(Surah An-Nahl)}, meaning: they do not know that Allah is able to resurrect, as He, Exalted, has said:

{And they say, "When we are lost in the earth, shall we indeed be [re]created anew?"} "10" {(Surah As-Sajdah)}

And He said: {And they say, "When we are bones and crumbled remains, shall we indeed be resurrected as a new creation?"} "49" {(Surah Al-Isra')}

The disbelievers thought the resurrection far-fetched, because they could not imagine how Allah would resurrect creation from the time of Adam, peace be upon him, until the Hour arrives. But why do you consider it far-fetched? Allah, the Exalted, has said: {Your creation and your resurrection are not but as a single soul} "28" {(Surah Luqman)}. So the matter is not a process by which Allah, glory be to Him, gathers the individual parts of mankind each separately... no. There is in the matter no working or treatment that takes time.

{His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is} "82" {(Surah Ya-Sin)}.

For this we give an example, and to Allah belongs the highest example. We see such commands in the world of people: when a teacher or trainer who drills soldiers comes, he teaches and trains first, then when he wishes to put these commands into effect, he stands before all the soldiers and with a single word he utters, all of them obey and stand in the required formation. Did the trainer seize each soldier and position him as he wished? No. Rather, with one word his desire is accomplished.

It is as if the obedience of the one commanded to the command is the original state; likewise, every particle in the universe is disciplined to His command, Exalted and Blessed is He. It is one word by which everything is accomplished. There is no treatment in the command, for treatment would mean that the agent directly applies the particles of his power to the particles of the being; but resurrection is not like this. Rather, it is by the command of discipline: "Be."

Therefore He, Exalted, says: {But most of the people do not know} "38" {(Surah An-Nahl)}.

We say: Praise be to Allah that there are a few people who know the matter of resurrection and believe in it.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 16, verse 39:

The meaning of His, exalted is He, words ﴿That He may make clear to them that about which they differ﴾ (Surah An-Nahl), i.e., of the matter of resurrection, because the affair does not stand upright without resurrection and recompense. That is why, in my debate with the Communists, I used to say to them: "You have encountered ferocious and slanderous capitalists, who drank the blood of people and did such-and-such and such-and-such. So what have you done to them?" They say: "We did to them such-and-such and such-and-such." So I said: "And before the existence of Communism in the year 1917, was there not oppression like that of these people?"

They said: "Yes."

I said: "Then it is in your interest that there be a resurrection, a reckoning, and a punishment from which those who preceded you will not escape, and whom you were unable to punish."

Then comes the decisive word in His, exalted is He, words ﴿And that those who disbelieved may know that they were liars﴾ (Surah An-Nahl), i.e., liars in their saying ﴿Allah will not resurrect those who die﴾ (Surah An-Nahl, 38).

This is knowledge of certainty and direct witnessing, but after the time has passed. The time is a time of reckoning and recompense, in which confession does not benefit and affirmation does not avail. So now they confess that they were liars in their oath that Allah would not resurrect those who die, though they had exaggerated in their oaths and affirmed them. That is why He, exalted is He, says about them in another verse:

﴿And they used to persist in the great violation﴾ (Surah Al-Waqi'ah, 46).

Therefore: the matter of resurrection is not a process of treating the particulars of each person, gathering their parts and arranging them from Adam until the Hour arrives. Rather, the matter is precisely governed by the Divine command (Kun, "Be").

Once it is issued, and without any need for time or practice, everything is present and obedient, each one waiting for its turn, waiting for the signal. For this reason a report says: "Matters that He initiates and does not begin (anew)..." [the hadith as it stands in the text: "أمور يبديها ولا يبتديها"].

So the matter depends on the permission: "Appear," and it appears.

An example of this, and to God belongs the highest likeness, is a man who prepares a time bomb and sets it to a specific time. The bomb remains until the moment of detonation set within it, then it explodes without any intervention from its makers. Merely granting it permission to explode, and it explodes.

Even the word (Kun) itself requires time, but there is nothing closer to it in terms of permission. Yet with regard to Him, exalted is He, the matter does not require "Kun" or anything else.

The emigrants (al-Muhajirun) are a people who believed in Allah with a faith that reached one of the levels of certainty (yaqin), which made them endure harm, injustice and persecution for the sake of their faith. A person will not sacrifice his wealth, his family and his own self unless he acts on a matter of certainty.

This verse comes after the verse affirming the Resurrection, which the disbelievers denied, insisted on denying, and exaggerated in denying, even swearing oaths about it: ﴿And they swore by Allah their most emphatic oaths that Allah will not resurrect those who die﴾ (Surah an-Nahl 16:38).

They know that among creation there are those who do evil and those who do good. Would they believe, by the standard of reason, that Allah would leave the one who did evil to run riot among the creatures of Allah without calling him to account?

This means that they fear the Resurrection. Had they been good-doers, they would have longed for it. But since they have committed excess against themselves, to the point that they dread reckoning and requital, it is natural that they deny the Resurrection and seek to soothe themselves with false wishes, so that they may feel secure that what they took of people's wrongful gains, their blood, their honour and their security is a matter for which they will not be held accountable.

Since they denied the Resurrection, and there was a Messenger with believers who believed in the Resurrection and requital with a faith that reached the degree of certainty, which impelled them to sacrifice for this faith, then it follows that there must be a fierce struggle between the people of faith and the people of disbelief, a battle between truth and falsehood.

Part of Allah's wisdom is that Islam spread at its beginning among the weak, so that no one would suppose that the believers imposed their faith by force. No: these were the weak who could not defend themselves, while the disbelievers were the lords. Thus Islam came to confront the great, the chiefs and the stubborn tyrants.

Allah could have given victory to these weak people and raised the word of the religion from the very beginning. But the Truth, blessed and exalted, willed that the call of faith should first be in Makkah, because Makkah was the centre of sovereignty in the Arabian Peninsula. The Quraysh were the people of prestige, influence and authority, and no tribe in the Peninsula could oppose them. It is well known that they had gained this standing through their care for the Sacred House of Allah and their service to those who came to it.

Had Islam chosen a place other than Makkah, they would have said: Islam preyed upon a group of weak people and enticed them with words until they believed in it. No. The Islamic call came into the ears of the lords of Quraysh and the lords of the Peninsula, whom Allah had secured in the journey of winter and summer, and they were the people of power and wealth.

If this is so, why did Allah not give victory to His religion in the land of the lords? We say: No. The call to falsehood is heard in the land of the lords, in Makkah, but the victory of the religion does not come through these lords. It comes in Madinah.

This is from Allah's wisdom, so that no one would say later: the partisanship (asabiyyah) for Muhammad in Makkah imposed faith in Muhammad. Rather, He willed that faith in Muhammad (ﷺ) should create the partisanship for Muhammad (ﷺ). So He brought him a partisan support far from the Quraysh, and after that the Quraysh themselves submitted to it.

As long as there is a battle, who is ground down in it? The one ground down is the weak who cannot protect himself, and these are the ones who were wronged. They were wronged in the very place where they lived. Therefore it was necessary that Allah lift this injustice from them.

The lifting of injustice from these weak people came in stages. The first stage was that the oppressed departed from Makkah, not to a land of faith that would protect them and help them spread their religion, but to a land of security only, where they would be safe in their religion, merely a security that allowed them the opportunity to perform the commands of the religion.

For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) surveyed all the lands to see which places would be suitable as a land of security to which the believers of his call could emigrate without anyone opposing them. He found none but Abyssinia. Therefore he said of it: "Indeed in the land of Abyssinia there is a king under whom no one is wronged, so join his land until Allah grants you relief and a way out from what you are in."

This description of the king of Abyssinia suffices for the believers to emigrate to him. At this stage of supporting the religion, we do not want more than that. Thus the first emigration (hijrah) to Abyssinia took place.

Then Allah facilitated for His religion followers and helpers who met the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and pledged to him support and assistance. These are the Ansar (Helpers) from the people of Madinah who pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at al-Aqabah, and who prepared the way for the second emigration to Madinah. This emigration was to a land of security and faith, where the Muslims would be secure in their religion and would find the opportunity to spread it throughout the earth.

Here we pause at His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And those who emigrated﴾ (Surah an-Nahl 16:41).

The root of this verb is h-j-r. There is a difference between hajara and haajara. Hajara: a person dislikes living in a place, so he leaves it for another place that he sees as better than it; the place itself did not compel him to emigrate. The meaning is: he left the place by choice.

As for haajara, it indicates mutual action (mufa'alah) from both sides. The doer here is not averse to the place, but the mutual action that occurred from the people compelled him to emigrate. This is what happened in the emigration of the believers from Makkah, for they did not leave it for another place except after they had been exposed to persecution and injustice. Thus they became, in effect, participants in the action; had the people not confronted them and wronged them, they would not have emigrated.

For this reason the Truth, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿after they had been wronged﴾ (Surah an-Nahl 16:41).

This meaning applies to the verse of al-Mutanabbi: "When you depart from a people while they were able to offer you what would ease your staying among them, yet they did not, and let you leave though they could have prevented it, then the ones who departed are in truth them."

Its meaning: if you are in a group and wish to leave them, and they are able to provide you with the help that would make your residence among them easy, but they do not do so and let you go although they could have, then in reality it is they who have departed, because they did not help you to remain.

So it was when the believers emigrated from Makkah, for it is not sensible that these people would dislike Makkah, which contains the Sacred House, in whose neighbourhood every Muslim wishes to dwell.

Therefore the emigrants did not leave Makkah; rather they were compelled to leave it and were forced to do so. It is natural, then, that they should seek another land until their strength grows, and then return to dwell in Makkah again in a natural and sound residence. Then the Truth, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Emigrate in the cause of Allah﴾ (Surah an-Nahl 16:41).

We note in the noble hadith that clarifies the meaning of this verse: "Whoever's emigration was to Allah and His Messenger, his emigration is to Allah and His Messenger; and whoever's emigration was for a worldly gain he might obtain, or for a woman he might marry, his emigration is to what he emigrated for."

What, then, is the difference here between "hajara fi Allah" (emigrated in Allah) and "hajara ila Allah" (emigrated to Allah)?

Hajara ila (to) indicates that the place to which he emigrated is better than the one he left, as if the place he left was not suitable for him.

As for hajara fi (in), it indicates that the earlier residence was also in Allah: their very residence in Makkah, and their bearing harm, injustice and persecution, were also in Allah.

Had the verse said "hajaru ila Allah", that would indicate that their earlier residence was not for Allah. So the meaning of the verse is: ﴿Emigrate in Allah﴾ (Surah an-Nahl 16:41), that is, their residence was for Allah, and their emigration was for Allah.

A similar example is His saying: ﴿And hasten toward forgiveness from your Lord﴾ (Surah Al 'Imran 3:133), meaning: if you are not in forgiveness, then hasten to forgiveness. In another verse: ﴿They hasten to the good deeds﴾ (Surah al-Mu'minun 23:61), because they were already in a previous good, and would hasten to another good. That is: you are in good, but hasten to a good greater than it.

There is another point in His saying: ﴿And those who emigrated﴾ (Surah an-Nahl 16:41).

We note that the word "alladhina" (those who) is plural. But is it specific to those whom the verse was revealed about, or is it general to everyone who was wronged in any place for the sake of Allah and then emigrated from it?

The truth is that the consideration here is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion of revelation. It is general to everyone to whom these circumstances apply. Even if this verse was revealed concerning a group of the Companions, among them Suhayb, Ammar, Khabbab and Bilal, it includes others who were compelled to emigrate to flee with their religion.

We know the story of Suhayb (may Allah be pleased with him), who was a smith. When he wished to emigrate with his religion, he presented the matter to the Quraysh: "By Allah, I am an old man. If I am with you, I will be of no benefit to you, and if I am with the Muslims, I will not trouble you. I have wealth; take it and let me emigrate." They agreed to that, took Suhayb's wealth and left him to emigrate.

Therefore the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Profitable was the sale, O Suhayb," meaning: a profitable transaction. And 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "What a fine servant Suhayb is; had he not feared Allah, he would not have disobeyed Him."

It seems that his not disobeying was not out of fear of punishment, but out of love for Allah, exalted be He, for He does not deserve to be disobeyed.

Then the Truth, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿We will surely settle them in this world in a good place﴾ (Surah an-Nahl 16:41). "Nubawwi'annahum" is like His saying: ﴿And when We settled for Abraham the place of the House﴾ (Surah al-Hajj 22:26), meaning: We showed him its place. We say: "baa'a al-insan ila baytihi" when a person returns to his house. A person goes out to strive in the earth's expanses, in farming or trade, then he returns (ya'wi) and goes back (yabu') to his house. So "baa'a" means "returned", or it means the dwelling of a person and what Allah has prepared for him.

If the believers were now going out of Makkah defeated and persecuted, We would give them, grant them and lodge them in a position better than the one they were in. They had been persecuted in Makkah, and they became secure in Madinah. If they had left their homeland, We would prepare for them the whole world, in which they would spread with the method of Allah and reap all the good of the world. Then afterwards We would return them to their homeland as lords and honoured ones, after Makkah had become a land purely for Allah, free of the worship of idols and images. This is the good in this world.

Then He, exalted be He, said: ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is greater﴾ (Surah an-Nahl 16:41). What we have mentioned of the good of this world and its benefit for the believers is among the things that hasten the reward for action. But the goods of this world, however great they are, will end in cessation: either you leave them or they leave you. Allah has fulfilled His promise to the believers in this world: they returned victorious to Makkah, and the whole Arabian Peninsula, and indeed the whole world, submitted to them. They spread eastward into Persia and westward among the Romans, and within half a century they were the masters of the entire world.

If this is the immediate good of this world, there is also the deferred good of the Hereafter: ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is greater﴾ (Surah an-Nahl 16:41), meaning: what is prepared for them of the bliss of the Hereafter is greater than what they found in this world. For this reason, when our master 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) gave one of the Companions the share of the emigrants from the stipend, he would say to him: "May Allah bless it for you. This is what Allah promised you in this world, and what is stored up for you in the Hereafter is greater than this." This is the good of this world.

﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is greater﴾ (Surah an-Nahl 16:41). When you hear the word "akbar" (greater), know that its opposite is not "asghar" or "saghir" (smaller), but its opposite is "kabir" (great). So the good of this world with which Allah settled them is "great" (kabirah), but what awaits them in the Hereafter is "greater" (akbar).

Likewise, the form of the superlative (af'al al-tafdil) may be less laudatory than other forms. Among Allah's beautiful names is "al-Kabir" (the Great), whereas "al-Akbar" is one of His attributes, not one of His names. In the formula of our call to Allah we say "Allahu akbar", not "Allah kabir", because whatever is other than the "kabir" is "saghir", whereas whatever is other than the "akbar" is "kabir". So we say in the adhan "Allahu akbar", because the affairs of this world are, for the believer, great in so far as they are a means to the Hereafter.

So beware lest you suppose that the worldly activity you leave for the sake of prayer is small. Rather, it is great in what it contains of means that help you obey Allah: by it you eat, drink and gain strength, by it you gather wealth to meet your needs, you pay zakat, and so on. For this reason the activity of this world is great, and the prayer was

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah an-Nahl (16), verse 42:

The Exalted Lord, blessed and high, wishes to give us a description of the state of the emigrants (muhajirun). They were wronged, persecuted, and harmed in the way of Allah. This trial did not turn them away from their religion; rather, they endured and bore it patiently. Moreover, they left their wealth and children, and abandoned their homeland and land, for the sake of their religion and their creed. This happened from them relying upon the fact that Allah, the Exalted, would never abandon them.

For this reason the Qur'anic expression came in this way: ﴿صبروا﴾ ("they endured"), in the past tense, because patience actually took place from them. It is as if the harm they endured patiently was a period of the past that has ended, and what remains for them is honour, protection, and strength, so that no one can persecute them after that. This is among the good tidings in the Qur'anic style.

As for reliance (tawakkul), Allah the Exalted said concerning them:

﴿وعلى ربهم يتوكلون﴾ ("and upon their Lord they rely") (Surah an-Nahl), in the present tense, because reliance upon Allah took place from them in the past, and they continue in it in the present and the future. This is the condition of the believer. After that, the Noble Qur'an spoke about a matter which the disbelievers also took a stance of stubbornness, arrogance, and denial towards, namely the matter of the sending of messengers.

The disbelieving obstinates objected to the Messenger being a human being. They said: "If God wished to send a messenger, he should have been an angel," and so they said: ﴿Had God willed, He would have sent down angels﴾ (Surah al-Mu'minun 23:24). It is as though they considered the message unworthy when it comes through a human being. This too is from the stupidity of disbelief and the folly of the disbelievers, because when the Messenger conveys the message of God, two responsibilities fall upon him: the responsibility of conveying the knowledge, and the responsibility of applying it through action and exemplary conduct. He commands the prayer and prays, commands the zakat and gives it, commands patience and is patient. Conveying is not by speech alone, but by practical, exemplary conduct.

For this reason, Sayyida 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "His character was the Qur'an."

He was a Qur'an walking on the earth; that is, he was a complete application of the method that he brought from the Truth, blessed and exalted is He. And the Exalted says concerning him (ﷺ): ﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of God you have a good example﴾ (Surah al-Ahzab 33:21).

So how can we imagine that the Messenger would be an angel? And how would he carry out this mission among humans? An angel may perform the task of conveying, but how can he perform the task of being an example and of exemplary practical application? How, when we know that the angels are a creation disposed to obey God: ﴿They do not disobey God in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded﴾ (Surah al-Tahrim 66:6). And from where would the avenues of human influence reach him when he does not eat, drink, or reproduce? If an angel came with the message of heaven and wished to forbid his people from one of the sins, what would we expect? We would expect one of them to say: "No, I cannot do that. You are an angel of a heavenly nature who can abandon this act, but I cannot."

Therefore, the nature of exemplary conduct requires that the Messenger be a human being, so that when he commands, he is the first to comply, and when he forbids, he is the first to refrain. From here it was among the favours of God upon the Arabs, and among His bounty to them, that He sent among them a messenger from themselves: ﴿There has certainly come to you a messenger from among yourselves﴾ (Surah al-Tawbah 9:128). He is first "from yourselves," and this gives him immediacy; then he is a human being, and an Arab, not from a foreign nation, but from your own environment, from your own land, Makkah, and from Quraysh. This is so that you would have complete knowledge of his history, his character, and his conduct; you know his movements and stillnesses. You used to acknowledge his truthfulness and trustworthiness, and you would entrust him with every precious and valuable thing you had, because of your knowledge of his trustworthiness. So how do you now disbelieve in him and accuse him of lying?!

Therefore the Truth, blessed and exalted, responded to them in another verse, saying:

﴿Nothing prevented the people from believing when guidance came to them except that they said, "Has God sent a human as a messenger?"﴾ (Surah al-Isra' 17:94). So what kept you from believing in him was that he is a human being! Then we take another point against these people: because they retreated from their claim that the Messenger should come from among the angels, and they said: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man from the two cities, great?﴾ (Surah al-Zukhruf 43:31). This is an astonishing vacillation by the disbelievers, and a lack of consistency in their opinion; it is mere obstinacy and denial. And it was said long ago: "If you are a liar, then be a good memorizer." The Qur'an answers them:

﴿Say: If there were angels walking calmly on the earth, We would have sent down upon them from the heaven an angel as a messenger﴾ (Surah al-Isra' 17:95). So if there were angels on the earth, We would have sent them an angel, so that the exemplary conduct would be realized. Therefore, exemplary conduct necessarily requires unity of kind. Let us illustrate this with an example: suppose you saw a lion roaming and prowling in the forest, devouring everything before it, and no one could confront it. Would you then think of becoming a lion? No. But if you saw a horseman holding his sword, cutting down the necks of the enemies, would you not love to be a horseman? Yes, you would love it.

This is the true, beneficial exemplar; if the kind differs, the exemplar is not suitable. Here the Truth, blessed and exalted, responds to the fabrications of the disbelievers with His saying:

﴿And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed﴾ (Surah al-Nahl 16:43). That is: you, O Muhammad, are not an innovation among the messengers; those who preceded you were men throughout the past centuries, and in the procession of all the messages.

The word "men" (rijalan) came here to inform humanity first as a kind, and then to specify the type mentioned secondly; this is because the nature of the Messenger is based on mixing and association with his people; he appears to all and speaks to all. As for woman, she is built upon concealment, and she cannot perform the role of an example for people. If we look at the nature of woman, we find in her nature many matters that do not suit the role of prophethood nor accord with the mission of the Prophet, such as her cessation from prayer and worship because she is menstruating or in postnatal bleeding.

Likewise the word "men" is qualified by His saying:

﴿To whom We revealed﴾ (Surah al-Nahl 16:43). So the Messenger is a man, but beware of saying: "He is a man like me and a human like me." No, there is another distinction: that revelation is sent to him, and this is a lofty station that we must preserve for the Prophets, may the blessings and peace of God be upon them all. Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿So ask the people of the reminder if you do not know﴾ (Surah al-Nahl 16:43). That is: if this matter escapes you, the matter of the sending of messengers from among humans, and I do not think it escapes you because it is common to all the messages. It would not have been hidden from you, especially since you have among you people of knowledge of the previous religions, such as Waraqa ibn Nawfal and others, and you have the people of biography and history, and you have the Jews and Christians. So ask all of these about the humanity of the messengers.

This is a clear matter that cannot be denied, and no one can oppose it. And what would the Jews and Christians say? Moses and Jesus... so they are human.

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿If you do not know﴾ (Surah al-Nahl 16:43) suggests that they do know, and that they have no doubt about this matter. It is like if you say to your interlocutor: "Ask about such-and-such if you do not know it." This means that he knows it. But if there were doubt about the matter, we would say: "Ask about such-and-such" without the conditional particle. So they do know, but it is argument, obstinacy, and arrogance against accepting the truth.

Al-Sha'rawi opens the verse with the words of the Most High:

﴿With the clear proofs and the scriptures…﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 16:44).

The scholars of language say: the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa'l-majrur) must have something it depends on (muta'alliq). So on what does the prepositional phrase here depend? They said: it may depend on the verb (nuhi, "We reveal"), and the sense would be: "And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed, with the clear proofs and the scriptures."

It may also depend on (ahl al-dhikr, "the people of the Reminder"), so the meaning would be: "Ask the people of the Reminder with the clear proofs and the scriptures." These are two possibilities for what the prepositional phrase refers back to.

Al-bayyinat (the clear proofs) are the plain and evident matter about which no one has doubt. It is either a sign establishing the truth of the message, such as the miracle that challenges the deniers to produce its like; or it is the cosmic signs that draw creation's attention to the existence of the Creator, the Most High, such as the signs of the night and day, the sun, the moon and the stars.

As for al-zubur (the scriptures), their meaning is written books. Ordinarily only a precious thing is written down, lest it be lost, and there is nothing more precious here than what comes to us from God's method that organizes the movement of our lives.

We know that the Arabs in former times used to ask about everything, however trivial. They had knowledge of the arrow, of who first made it, and of the bow and the saddle, and similar simple things. Would they not ask about the signs of God in the cosmos, and the secrets and wonders in its creation that point to the Creator, the Most High?

Then the Blessed and Most High says:

﴿And We have sent down to you the Reminder, that you may make clear to people what has been sent down to them…﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 16:44).

The word al-dhikr (the Reminder) occurs often in the Noble Qur'an with various meanings. The root sense of dhikr is that a thing remains in mind so that it does not vanish; its opposite is forgetting. So we have remembrance and forgetting. The word "dhikr" here means the existence of something we must not forget. What is it?

When God the Most High created Adam, peace be upon him, He took a covenant from every particle of him, and He said, exalted is He:

﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes, we testify." Lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection: "Indeed we were unaware of this"﴾ (Surah al-A'raf, 7:172).

The covenant taken from Adam is a covenant upon all his descendants, because in each of the children of Adam there is a particle of their father Adam, and a living part of him, as a result of begetting and procreation from Adam until the Hour. And since this is so, we witnessed the taking of the covenant: "Am I not your Lord?"

It is as though the word (dhikr) came to remind us of the covenant buried in our constitution, which we should never have forgotten. When forgetting occurred, it became necessary to send messengers and reveal books to remind us of God's covenant with us.

﴿Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes…﴾ (Surah al-A'raf, 7:172).

From here we call the revealed books a dhikr. But the reminder comes gradually and in stages: each messenger came to remind his people according to the heedlessness they had. As for the Final Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, who came to all people until the Hour, he brought the true Reminder after which there is no other, which is the Noble Qur'an. The word (dhikr) may also come in the sense of honour and eminence, as in God's words to the Arabs:

﴿We have indeed sent down to you a Book in which is your dhikr…﴾ (Surah al-Anbiya', 21:10).

The Arabs gained standing through the Qur'an; their language lived through the Qur'an, and they took the forefront among the nations through the Qur'an. Remembrance may come from God to the servant, and it may come from the servant to God, as in His words, exalted is He:

﴿So remember Me, and I will remember you…﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 2:152). The meaning: remember Me through obedience and faith, and I will remember you with overflowing gifts, blessing, goodness, support and My reward. When the word dhikr is used without qualification, it refers to what was sent down upon the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, because it is the comprehensive Book containing all that was sent down to the earlier messengers and all that mankind needs until the Hour comes.

Likewise, the word kitab (book) applies to any book, but when it comes with the definite article (al-kitab), it refers to the Noble Qur'an. This is what we call "knowledge by dominance" ('ilm bi'l-ghalabah). The dhikr is the Qur'an that was sent down upon Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, and at the same time it is his everlasting miracle. It is both method and miracle. The earlier messengers came with miracles of their own and books of their own, so the book was separate from the miracle.

Moses had the Torah as his book and the staff as his miracle; Jesus had the Gospel as his book and method, and his miracle was healing the blind and the leper and raising the dead by God's leave. As for Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, his miracle is the very book of his method; neither is separated from the other, so that the miracle remains a support for the method until the Hour.

This is the secret of why the Blessed and Most High undertook to preserve and guard the Qur'an, as He said:

﴿Indeed, We have sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardians﴾ (Surah al-Hijr, 15:9).

As for the earlier books, the custody of each messenger's book was entrusted to his followers, as He said:

﴿Indeed, We revealed the Torah, in which is guidance and light, by which the prophets who submitted judged for those who were Jews, and the rabbis and the scholars, by what they were entrusted with of the Book of God…﴾ (Surah al-Ma'idah, 5:44).

The meaning of "istuhfizu" (they were entrusted): God asked them to preserve the Torah. This is a command of obligation that may be obeyed or disobeyed. What happened was that the Jews disobeyed, altered and distorted the Torah. As for the Qur'an, God the Most High undertook its preservation Himself and left it to no one, because it is the final Book that will accompany humanity until the Hour.

Also part of the Reminder is what the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, brought along with the Qur'an, namely the noble hadith. The Messenger had another task: his spoken method and his noble sayings, which came from the niche of the Qur'an, explaining and clarifying it.

As he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Verily I have been given the Qur'an and its like with it. Soon a full man reclining on his couch will say: 'Between us and you is the Book of God; whatever we find in it of lawful we make lawful, and whatever we find in it of unlawful we make unlawful.' Indeed, what the Messenger of God made unlawful is like what God made unlawful."

The Blessed and Most High says:

﴿…that you may make clear to people what has been sent down to them…﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 16:44).

So: the Qur'an came as a book of miracle and a book of method, but it mentioned only the foundations of this method, and did not mention the methodological definitions and the explanations necessary to clarify it; otherwise the matter would have been prolonged, the Qur'an would have swollen, and it might have strayed from its intended meaning.

So the Qur'an came with the fixed foundations and left to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, the task of explaining it to people, elucidating it and clarifying what it contains.

Some may think that everything the Sunnah brought is not binding upon us to perform, because it is a sunnah: one who does it is rewarded and one who omits it is not punished. We say: no. We must distinguish here between the sunnah of the evidence (sunniyyat al-dalil) and the sunnah of the ruling (sunniyyat al-hukm), so that the matter is not confused for people.

The sunnah of the evidence means that there is an obligation (fard), but its proof is established from the Sunnah, such as the explanation of the number of units (rak'at) of the obligatory prayers: Subh, Zuhr, 'Asr, Maghrib and 'Isha'. These are established by the Sunnah and they are obligatory.

As for the sunnah of the ruling, these are matters and legal rulings (ahkam fiqhiyyah) that came from the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, for which the doer is rewarded and the one who omits them is not punished. So when the Messenger makes a ruling clear to us by his conduct and example, we look: is it the sunnah of the evidence, in which case it is an obligation, or the sunnah of the ruling, in which case it is a sunnah? This also appears to us from the Messenger's constancy in the matter: if he persisted in it and adhered to it, it is obligatory; if he did not persist in it, it is a sunnah.

So: the Messenger's task is not merely to hand over the Qur'an and convey it to people, but also to explain the divine method it contains. Conveying cannot be upright here without explanation. We must distinguish between the two gifts: the Qur'anic gift and the Prophetic gift.

We must know here that among the distinctions by which the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was singled out over his fellow messengers is that he was the only messenger whom God entrusted with legislation. The earlier messengers conveyed only the commands of heaven, and the matter ended there. But Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, was addressed by the Blessed and Most High concerning him:

﴿Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it…﴾ (Surah al-Hashr, 59:7).

So he received the distinction of legislation, and his Sunnah became the second legislation after the Noble Qur'an.

Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿…that they may reflect.﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 16:44). Reflect upon what? They are to reflect upon the state of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, before his mission, when nothing was transmitted of him that he was an orator, a man of letters or a poet, and nothing was transmitted that he was a writer or a learned man. This was never known of him throughout the forty years of his blessed life. Therefore He commanded them to contemplate and ponder this matter. What Muhammad brought was not a genius that burst forth all at once at the age of forty; the natural age for genius comes in the late twenties and early thirties.

It is not conceivable that genius would be postponed in the case of God's Messenger until this age, while he saw his people fall around him: his father died while he was in his mother's womb; then his mother died while he was still a small child; then his grandfather died. Who guarantees him life until the age of forty, when this genius burst forth in him?

So reflect: this is not a genius from Muhammad; it is a matter from heaven. For this reason his Lord, the Blessed and Most High, commanded him to say to them:

﴿Say: "If God had willed, I would not have recited it to you, nor would He have made it known to you. Indeed I dwelt among you a lifetime before it. Will you not then reason?"﴾ (Surah Yunus, 10:16). So it was incumbent upon you to reflect on this matter. Had you reflected, you ought to have rushed to Islam, for you are the people most knowledgeable about Muhammad. You tested him and found him neither a liar nor a traitor, nor occupied with poetry or oratory. He would not have been trusted among you and then lie about God.

We must distinguish between intellect ('aql) and reflection (fikr). Intellect is the faculty that receives sensory data and distinguishes them, and from them draws general propositions which become the principles a person lives by, and which become stored information. Reflection is that you think about these things in order to derive a ruling from them.

God the Most High left us freedom of thought and freedom of intellect in the affairs of our worldly life, but He bound us with compulsory matters without which the world would be corrupted. What corrupts the world is that we abandon what God has legislated for us. As for the remaining matters which entail no harm, He leaves us room for thought and experiment, since failure in them does no damage.

So what God wills as a binding ruling He imposes by an explicit text about which there is no disagreement; and what He wills in several ways He leaves to ijtihad (independent legal reasoning), where the act may admit several aspects and an error does not lead to corruption.

The matter is thus an intellectual balance that governs sensory data and orders propositions, so that we first see what God wills definitively and what He wills by ijtihad. Since it is ijtihad, what the mujtahid arrives at may be a valid way to worship God. But the affliction of people in matters of ijtihad is that some of them accuse those who differ, and the situation may reach the point of charging their opponents with unbelief, God forbid.

To such a person we say: fear God. This is an ijtihad in which whoever is correct has two rewards, and whoever errs has one reward. Therefore we find among the scholars one who knows the nature of ijtihadi matters, and so he says: "My opinion is correct and may be wrong; the opinion of others is wrong and may be correct." Thus everyone coexists and opinions are respected.

Among God's mercy to His servants is that He commands them to reflect, contemplate and consider; for they are His creation, and they are too honoured by Him to be left to error and unbelief, after He has honoured them with creation and intellect. So He, exalted is He, wished to honour them with another honour: obedience and faith.

It is as though He, exalted is He, says to them: Restrain your minds and souls from the pride of disputation and the depths of contention. And even if you do not believe in the Resurrection in the Hereafter, and in the punishment prepared there for the wrongdoers, then look at what happened to them and the torment hastened upon them in this world.

Look at the deniers of the nations who went before you and what their end came to. Or are you secure from punishment, far from it?

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 16, verse 45:

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Do they then feel secure...? (45)﴾ (Surat an-Nahl). The hamza here is the interrogative particle (hamzat al-istifham), which asks about the content of the sentence that follows it. As for the fa' after it, it is a conjunctive particle (harf 'atf) that links one sentence to another. So there is a sentence before the fa' that is to be understood as: "Are they ignorant of what befell the opponents of the earlier prophets of punishment, so that they feel secure from the plotting of God?" That is, their sense of security from the plotting of God arises from their ignorance of what befell the deniers among the earlier nations. Then He, Exalted is He, says:

﴿...who plot evil deeds...(45)﴾ (Surat an-Nahl). Al-makr (plotting, scheming) is the hidden scheming to harm someone whom one cannot confront with the truth and face openly. You do not scheme against anyone except when your power is too weak to confront him directly. So your scheming against him and plotting with him is a proof of your weakness. For this reason they made makr the first of the degrees of cowardice, because the schemer schemes only because he is unable to confront. And to the extent that the scheming is great, the weakness is likewise great. This is what we observe in His saying concerning women:

﴿Indeed, your plotting is great (28)﴾ (Surat Yusuf).

And He said concerning Satan: ﴿Indeed, the plotting of Satan is ever weak (76)﴾ (Surat an-Nisa'). So scheming is a proof of weakness, and since the plotting of women is great, their weakness too is great, and likewise the plotting of Satan.

Of old they said: "Beware lest the weak man take possession of you, for when he gains power over you and the opportunity presents itself to him, he will not let you escape from him, because he knows his weakness and cannot guarantee that the opportunity will come to him again. Therefore he does not waste it, unlike the strong, who is not eager to take revenge when the opportunity comes to him, and may let it pass because of his strength and his ability to overcome his adversary, and his power over him at whatever time he wishes." In the same meaning came the saying of the poet:

"A weak one, when it hits an opportunity, kills; likewise is the power of the weak."

So the power of the weak may kill, whereas the power of the strong is not so.

Then there is another pause with makr: insofar as makr may give you victory over your equals and over those like you among the sons of Adam, if you encounter one who is stronger than you, more cautious than you, and firmer than you in scheming, your scheming may then avail you nothing, and he may even overcome you with his scheming and his precaution. How then is the situation when the one who schemes against you is the Lord of the worlds, blessed and exalted?

And the Mighty God spoke truly when He said:

﴿And they scheme, and God schemes, and God is the best of schemers (30)﴾ (Surat al-Anfal).

And He said: ﴿And the evil scheme does not encompass anyone except its own people (43)﴾ (Surat Fatir).

So the scheming of the servants is exposed before God, whereas His scheming, glorified is He, no one can withstand, and no one can guard against it; therefore the Truth, glorified is He, is the best of schemers.

The evil scheming (al-makr al-sayyi') is the futile scheming that occurs only in evil, such as the scheming of the deniers of the messengers throughout the ages, namely that you plot against another in a way that nullifies a truth.

Every messenger was confronted by his people who denied him with scheming and deception, which is proof that they cannot confront him directly. The Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, was subjected to several stages of plotting, scheming, and deception, for a wisdom that the Truth, blessed and exalted, intended: that the disbelievers should despair of victory over him, may God bless him and grant him peace. They plotted against him, planned to kill him, and devised plans toward that end, and their plan failed on the night of the Hijra.

In another stratagem they tried to bewitch him, may God bless him and grant him peace, but God exposed their affair and frustrated their effort. So, whatever means of refuting this call you have not succeeded in, God has granted him victory over you, as He said:

﴿God has decreed: "I shall surely prevail, I and My messengers" (21)﴾ (Surat al-Mujadila).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿...that God should cause the earth to swallow them up...(45)﴾ (Surat an-Nahl).

Al-khasf (swallowing up by the earth) is the earth's engulfing of what is on its surface, so that a thing "sank" (infakhasa) means it disappeared into the inside of the earth; from it comes khusuf al-qamar, the eclipse of the moon, meaning the disappearance of its light. And from this also is His saying concerning Qarun:

﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home (81)﴾ (Surat al-Qasas).

This is one kind of punishment, which came in several forms as the Noble Qur'an mentioned:

﴿So each We seized for his sin: among them were those upon whom We sent a storm of pebbles, and among them were those seized by the Blast, and among them were those whom We caused the earth to swallow, and among them were those whom We drowned... (40)﴾ (Surat an-Nahl).

These are kinds of punishment that befell the deniers, and it was incumbent upon these people to take warning and admonition from their predecessors, and to guard against befalling the same fate as their predecessors. Then the Truth, blessed and exalted, says:

﴿Or that the punishment should come upon them from where they do not perceive (45)﴾ (Surat an-Nahl).

The meaning is that if they guard against the scheming of God and the punishment that falls upon them, God will come upon them from a direction they do not perceive, one that never occurred to them. And since it never occurred to them, they did not guard against it, so their seizure will be easy, as He said:

﴿Then God came upon them from where they had not reckoned (2)﴾ (Surat al-Hashr).

Al-Taqallub (fluctuation, movement): moving from one state to another, or from one place to another. Moving from one's place of residence to another place is a sign of strength and capability, for a person moves from his place carrying his goods, his equipment and everything he owns, so as to establish a new life of activity in his new place.

Therefore: fluctuation in life is a manifestation of strength, such that one is able to establish a new life and to safeguard his wealth during his journey of movement. There is no doubt that this is a manifestation of honour, status and prosperity, which only the strong can undertake.

Hence we see in the words of the Blessed and Exalted Truth concerning the people of Sheba:

﴿And We placed between them and the towns which We had blessed other visible towns, and We determined therein the travel: "Travel therein by night and day in safety."﴾ (Surah Saba') "18" "But they said, 'Our Lord, make the distances of our journeys farther apart.'" (Surah Saba') "19"

These are a people for whom Allah gathered various kinds of luxury, secured their lands and their journeys, and made for them stations of rest during their travel. Yet, strangely, they asked Allah to make the distances between their journeys farther apart, as if they wished to distinguish themselves from the weak who are unable to bear the hardship of travel and wandering. They said:

﴿Make the distances of our journeys farther apart﴾ (Surah Saba') "19" — so that the weak among them could not cross these distances.

Therefore: one who moves about the earth is evidence that he has both a state of residence and a state of travel, and the ability to transport what he has in order to settle in another place. For this reason they said: "Wealth in exile is a homeland." And whoever is able does what he wills.

The Blessed and Exalted says to His Messenger ﷺ: ﴿Let not the fluctuation of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you﴾ (Surah Al 'Imran) "196" — so let not their movement between the winter and summer journeys frighten you, for Allah the Exalted is able to seize them in their fluctuation. Their fluctuation may also refer to their fluctuation in thoughts and evil scheming against the Messenger ﷺ and his Companions, as in the Exalted's words:

﴿Indeed they had sought discord before, and turned matters over for you﴾ (Surah al-Tawbah) "48"

They sat plotting, scheming and planning to eliminate the call in its infancy. He, the Exalted, says:

﴿And they will not escape [Allah]﴾ (Surah al-Nahl) "46"

Mu'jiz (one who cannot be overcome, the incapacitator): it is the one who does not allow you to overcome him. These people will never overcome Allah the Exalted, nor will they be able to escape His punishment; for however they plan by night, their scheming and deception are with Allah. As for Allah's plotting, if He wills to plot against them, they will not perceive it:

﴿And they plot, and Allah plots; and Allah is the best of plotters﴾ (Surah al-Anfal) "30"

And He said: ﴿Indeed, they are plotting a plot, and I am plotting a plot. So give time to the disbelievers; give them respite for a little while﴾ (Surah al-Tariq) "15-17"

Whoever cannot overcome you submits to you, and as long as he submits to you, the method you brought prevails over him. Inability before strength may itself be a sign of strength, just as the Arabs' inability before the challenge of the Qur'an was a sign of their strength in the field in which the Qur'an challenged them; for when Allah challenges and engages, He does not engage the weak, but rather engages the strong in the field of this challenge.

Al-Takhawwuf: it is fear of something that has not yet happened, whereby the imagination goes off in various directions, and a person anticipates many kinds of evil, whereas reality occurs in one single way.

Suppose you are waiting for a beloved who is late for his appointed arrival time; your imagination and speculation carry you off to many matters: "I wonder, has such-and-such happened, or such-and-such?" Each of these imaginings leaves an impression and a sting in the soul, and thus fears multiply. But if you wait until you know the reality, then if there is any alarm, it comes only once.

For this reason they say in proverbs: "The descent of calamity is better than awaiting it" (نزول البلا ولا انتظاره). That is because if it descends, it will descend in one form, whereas awaiting it spreads through the soul many kinds of alarm and fear. So, the anticipation (al-takhawwuf) is more severe and greater than the occurrence of the event itself.

This alarm used to afflict the disbelievers whenever they learned that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had dispatched one of the expeditions (sariyya). Each group among them would expect that it was targeting them, and thus Allah spread fear into all their souls, even though the expedition had set out toward a specific direction.

Some exegetes said: al-takhawwuf means al-tanaqqus (diminution), that Allah diminishes the territory of disbelief by the entry of tribes into Islam, one tribe after another, so that each of them reduces the territory of disbelief. This is as found in His, the Exalted's, saying:

﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits.﴾ (Surat al-Baqarah) Then the Truthful, Blessed and Exalted, says in concluding this verse:

﴿Indeed, your Lord is Kind and Merciful.﴾ (Surat al-Nahl, 47) Is this concluding phrase suitable for the verse and what precedes it of threat and warning? Reason says: the suitable conclusion for it would be, for example, "Indeed, your Lord is severe in punishment."

But here we must know that this is the bounty of lordship (ʿaṭāʾ al-rubūbiyya), which encompasses all servants, believer and disbeliever alike. Allah, the Exalted, has summoned everyone to this world and has guaranteed for all what preserves their lives: sun, air, earth and sky. These things were not created for one to the exclusion of another. And Allah, the Exalted, has said:

﴿Whoever desires the harvest of the Hereafter, We increase for him in his harvest; and whoever desires the harvest of this world, We give him from it, but he has no share in the Hereafter.﴾ (Surat al-Shura, 20)

It is as if in the verse there is a form of His, the Glorified's, mercy toward His creation and His eagerness for their salvation; for He alerts them to what may befall them if they persist in their disbelief, and makes them see the consequence of their disbelief. Insight is an admonition, and admonition is compassion toward them and mercy, so that this threat and warning does not overtake them.

Examples of this kind of conclusion are abundant in Surat al-Rahman. The Truthful, Blessed and Exalted, says:

﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests.﴾ (17) ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ (18) (Surat al-Rahman)

This is a blessing that suits His saying:

﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ (18) (Surat al-Rahman)

And likewise in His saying:

﴿He let loose the two seas, meeting side by side. Between them is a barrier they do not transgress.﴾ (19–20) (Surat al-Rahman)

This is one of Allah's blessings that suits the concluding phrase:

﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ (21) (Surat al-Rahman).

As for His saying:

﴿Everyone upon it will perish. And there remains the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor.﴾ (26–27) ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ (28)

(Surat al-Rahman).

What is the blessing in "Everyone upon it will perish"? Is death a blessing?

Yes, death is a blessing from Allah upon His servants; for it tells the doer of good: death will come so that you receive the reward of your goodness and the recompense of your deeds. And it also tells the disbeliever: beware, be cautious, death is coming. It is as if He, the Glorified, awakens the disbelievers and admonishes them so that they desist from what they are engaged in. Is this not a blessing from Allah and a mercy from Him, the Glorified, toward His servants?

And likewise consider the saying of the Truthful, Blessed and Exalted:

﴿There will be sent upon you both a flame of fire and smoke, and you will not be victorious.﴾ (35) ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ (36) (Surat al-Rahman).

What blessing is in: ﴿There will be sent upon you both a flame of fire and smoke...﴾ (35) (Surat al-Rahman)? What blessing is in this punishment?

Indeed, whoever reflects upon this verse finds in it a great blessing; for in it is a threat and warning of punishment if they persist in the disbelief they are in. Within it is a warning and eagerness for their salvation, just as you threaten your son: "If you neglect your lessons, you will fail, and I will do such-and-such to you." You say this only out of your eagerness for his success and well-being. Therefore, the concluding of the verse with His saying:

﴿Indeed, your Lord is Kind and Merciful.﴾ (Surat al-Nahl, 47)

is a conclusion suitable to what precedes it of threat and warning, and in it is a clarification of the mercy of Allah to which He calls each of the believer and the disbeliever.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 16, verse 48:

The words of the Exalted:

﴿Have they not looked at what Allah has created..? (16:48)﴾ (Surat al-Nahl). The meaning: Are they blind, that they have not looked, and have not reflected upon what Allah has created?

﴿...of anything...? (16:48)﴾ (Surat al-Nahl). The word "shay'" (thing), which they call the genus of genera (jins al-ajnas), and "min" (from/of) indicates the beginning of what is called a thing, i.e., the most trivial thing that exists; and this they call the lowest of the genera. It also indicates generality, so that it means:

﴿...of anything...? (16:48)﴾ (Surat al-Nahl), i.e., every thing. So look at any thing in existence, however trivial it may be, and you will find that it has a shadow:

﴿...whose shadows turn around... (16:48)﴾ (Surat al-Nahl). "Yatafayya'" (turn around): from "fa'a," meaning "returned." The intended meaning is the return of the shadow to the sun again, or the return of the sun to the shadow.

If we look at the shadow, we find two kinds: a fixed, continuous shadow, and a changing shadow. The fixed shadow is always in places that the rays of the sun do not reach, such as the bottoms of seas and the interior of the earth; this is a fixed shadow that the rays of the sun never reach at any time.

The moving shadow, which is called "fay'" because it returns from shadow to sun, or from sun to shadow. Thus, a shadow is not called "fay'" unless it returns to what it was. But... how is a shadow formed? A shadow is formed when a dense body stands in the path of the sun and blocks its rays, so it casts a shadow on the side opposite the sun. This shadow has two lengths and one state of equilibrium.

It is long at sunrise until it reaches sunset; then it begins to shorten as the sun rises, and when the sun is at its zenith, the shadow of the thing becomes equal to the thing itself; this is the state of equilibrium. Then the sun inclines toward setting, and the first length of the shadow is reversed from the west toward the east.

The Truth, blessed and exalted, draws our attention to this cosmic sign in His saying:

﴿Have you not considered your Lord, how He extends the shade? And if He willed, He would have made it stationary. Then We made the sun for it an indicator. Then We take it in towards Us, a gentle taking. (25:45–46)﴾ (Surat al-Furqan).

This is because if you look at the shadow, and how it extends, and how it contracts and recedes, you will find something truly wondrous. You observe the shadow in both states moving in a smooth, continuous flow.

What is meant by "insiyabi" (smooth, continuous)? It is a type of motion: motion is either a smooth motion, or motion arising from successive stillnesses between movements.

The latter we observe in the movement of a clock's hands; it is clearest in the second hand, less so in the minute hand, and barely perceptible in the hour hand. If you observe the second hand, you will find it moves through regular jumps, so that it is motion, then stillness, then motion, and so on.

This means that it gathers motion while stationary, then releases it, and thus there passes over it a moment in which it was not moving. This is what we call jerky motion (al-harakah al-qafziyyah). This motion cannot be detected in the hour hand, because its jump is so minute that the naked eye cannot perceive or observe it. This is jerky motion.

As for smooth motion, it means that every portion of time contains a portion of motion; that is, a continuous motion distributed evenly over time.

We illustrate this with the growth of a child. A newborn child grows continuously, but his mother, being constantly with him, does not notice this growth, because her gaze is always upon him. So how is the motion of growth in the child? Is it a jerky motion in which the child's growth accumulates each week or each month, for example, and then grows in a single burst?

If his growth were like that, we would notice the child's growth; but it is not so. Rather, he grows by smooth motion, distributing the single millimeter of growth over the length of time, so that we scarcely perceive his growth.

Likewise, the motion of the sun is smooth motion, such that it distributes the parts of motion over the parts of time. The sun is not fixed to a mechanism that moves by gears like a clock, for example; no. Rather, it is bound to the command of Allah, connected to the perpetual "Be."
