Let us clarify this by saying: suppose you have a mountain of gold, or a mountain of silver, and hunger has seized you on some day. Could you eat gold or silver?

You now need a loaf of bread, not a mountain of gold or silver. The loaf of bread that preserves your life in this situation is better than all of that. This is the direct provision which God has provided for His servants, whereas wealth is indirect provision, which you cannot eat or live upon.

As for the word (anything), that is, the least thing that can be called a thing: the idols and images do not possess for them any provision, however small, because someone might say: they do not possess a provision sufficient for them. No, rather they do not possess anything at all. Then the Truth, glorified is He, gives us another hint in His saying: ﴿and they are not able﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 73). That is, they do not possess for them any provision in the present, and will not possess it in the future. This cuts off hope from them: they do not possess today, and will not possess tomorrow. This is because some matters are decided for a time, and other matters are suspended and may be resumed later. This phrase ﴿and they are not able﴾ is a decisive judgment with no appeal afterwards. Therefore, we find those who love to find a handle in the Qur'an dispute over His saying:

﴿Say: O you disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship, nor do you worship what I worship, nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped, nor are you worshippers of what I worship, to you your religion and to me my religion﴾ (Surah al-Kafirun). These people see in the surah a repetition that is contrary to the eloquence of the noble Qur'an. We say: there is no repetition in the surah if you reflect. In the surah there is the severing of relations on the basis of permanence and continuity, for the Truth, glorified is He, says: ﴿to you your religion and to me my religion﴾ (Surah al-Kafirun, 6), in the present, in the future, and until the Day of Resurrection. So His saying: ﴿I do not worship what you worship, nor do you worship what I worship﴾ (Surah al-Kafirun, 2-3) is the severing of relations in the present. But who knows whether we may resume other relations later? So there came His saying: ﴿nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped, nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾ (Surah al-Kafirun, 4-5), not for repetition, but to cut off hope of restoring relations in the future. So the matter is then settled from now on by way of finality. Likewise the meaning in His saying: ﴿and they are not able﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 73): that is, they are not able now, nor in the future.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (*Tafsir al-Sha'rawi*, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 16, verse 74:

Al-amthal (the parables, similitudes): plural of *mithl*, which means a peer, an equal. The verse forbids us to liken God, glory be to Him, to anything else, because the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, is one in His essence, one in His attributes, and one in His acts. Beware of saying about any essence that it resembles His essence, glory be to Him, or about any attribute that it resembles His attributes. If you find an attribute of God Most High that has a counterpart among humans, know that it is by way of comparison.

﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ (42:11). God, glory be to Him, forbids us to strike parables for Him. Rather, it is He, glory be to Him, who strikes parables, because He is wise and strikes the parable in its proper place, in order to clarify an obscure matter through a matter that is observed. That is why He, Exalted, says: ﴿And to God belongs the highest similitude﴾ (16:60), that is, the highest attribute in everything. So when you find attributes shared between you and the Truth, glory be to Him, then declare God free of the like, the equal, the peer and the counterpart, and say: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾. You exist and God exists, but your existence is preceded by non-existence and is subject to non-existence, whereas His existence is not preceded by non-existence nor subject to non-existence.

God has struck for us a parable of Himself, glory be to Him, in order to clarify for us His illumination of the cosmos, and it is not a parable of His light as we may suppose. Rather, it is a parable of His illumination, not of His light. He, Exalted, says in Surah al-Nur:

﴿God is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The parable of His light is as a niche in which is a lamp, the lamp in a glass, the glass as if it were a glittering star, kindled from a blessed tree, an olive that is neither of the east nor of the west, whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it. Light upon light. God guides to His light whom He wills. And God strikes parables for people, and God is Knower of all things﴾ (24:35).

"The light of the heavens and the earth": because guidance comes through light, whether sensory or spiritual. Sensory light is like the light of the sun, the moon and other sources of illumination. This sensory light is what makes things clear to us, so that we may walk through the cosmos with insight and guidance. If you try to walk at night without a light to guide you, you will collide with things around you: either something stronger than you which will crush and harm you, or you will be stronger than it and crush it. What guides your steps is sensory light.

Light may also be spiritual, namely the light of values and morals. This light too makes you walk through life with insight and guidance, and protects you from stumbling in the wilderness of ideas and theories. This is the light of values which God has sent down to us in His noble Book, and of which He said:

﴿There has come to you from God a light and a clear Book, by which God guides whoever follows His pleasure to the ways of peace, and brings them out of darkness into light by His permission, and guides them to a straight path﴾ (5:15–16).

So it is light, but spiritual: by values, morals and virtues. Do not say of this parable that it is a parable of God's light; rather it is a parable of the authority of His illumination of the cosmos. Had we reflected on the rest of the verse, we would have realised this.

﴿The parable of His light is as a niche﴾ (24:35). Some people say: the *mishkah* (niche) is the lamp. No. The *mishkah* is the recess or sealed opening in the wall, which the people of the countryside know in their old buildings. It is a non-piercing hollow in the wall in which the lamp is placed.

﴿The lamp in a glass﴾ (24:35): that is, it is not an ordinary lamp but one in a glass, which protects the light of the lamp from being scattered by the air on every side, while at the same time allowing it enough air to keep burning. Thus the light is steady and clear, and no smoke issues from it to cloud the clarity of the glass.

The people of the countryside know the kerosene (*jaz*) flame that has no glass, and the dark, harmful smoke that issues from it. So the lamp here is at the utmost purity and strength, because the glass too is not an ordinary glass but "as if it were a glittering star". That it is like a glittering star means that it shines by itself.

﴿The glass as if it were a glittering star, kindled from a blessed tree﴾ (24:35): this lamp is fuelled with oil that is not ordinary, but oil from an olive tree, an olive tree of moderate climate.

﴿Neither of the east nor of the west﴾ (24:35): this oil has reached such purity and clarity that it glows even if no fire touches it. Therefore it gives the utmost strength: ﴿whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it﴾ (24:35).

For this reason God, Exalted, describes this lamp: ﴿Light upon light﴾ (24:35).

Now that you have considered the attributes of this lamp, that it is placed in a small recess, tell me by God: is it possible for there to be a dark spot in this recess?

So this is a parable not of His light, glory be to Him, for His light cannot be perceived; it is rather a parable of His illumination of the cosmos, which is like the recess and the opening in this parable. Thus the meaning of His words ﴿God is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾ (24:35) is: that is, the one who illuminates them. Just as it is not conceivable that there is a dark spot in this recess, so too is His light, glory be to Him, and His illumination of the cosmos. This is the sensory light with which God has sustained the cosmos.

Then the Qur'an speaks of the spiritual light that descends upon the righteous servants of God as luminous manifestations and divine effusions, which we receive in the houses of God: ﴿In houses which God has permitted to be raised and in which His name is mentioned; therein glorify Him in the mornings and the evenings, men﴾ (24:36–37).

Thus we combine sensory light and spiritual light, (peace be upon him). For this reason, when Abu Tammam wished to praise the caliph, he likened him to the famous Arabs in courage, generosity, forbearance and intelligence, and said:

*The boldness of Umar with the generosity of Hatim,*
*the forbearance of al-Ahnaf with the intelligence of Iyas.*

One of Abu Tammam's rivals objected to this comparison and said to him: How do you liken the caliph to the rough Arabs? In his army there is a thousand like Amr, and in his treasury a thousand like Hatim.

But Abu Tammam extricated himself from this predicament and escaped the trap his rival had set for him. He improvised immediately:

*Do not deny my striking for him, apart from him,*
*a parable far-reaching in generosity and courage.*
*God has struck the lesser for His light*
*a parable from the niche and the lamp.*

God, though He has forbidden us to strike parables for Him because of our lack of knowledge, is able to strike parables, even with the smallest and most insignificant of creatures in our eyes. He, Exalted, says: ﴿Indeed God is not ashamed to strike a parable of a gnat or what is above it﴾ (2:26). So do not belittle this gnat, and do not consider it too small for God to make it a parable, for He, glory be to Him, is not ashamed to strike a parable with it. In this gnat are all the mechanisms of the formation of life that are in you, and in the largest animals such as the elephant and the camel. And this gnat, which you despise, may be stronger than you, and may overpower you despite your strength, cunning and might.

He, Exalted, says: ﴿And if the fly should snatch away from them a thing, they could not retrieve it from it. Weak are the seeker and the sought﴾ (22:73).

By God, can you, with your strength and capabilities, retrieve from a fly what it has taken from your food? Are you able to do this?

So when God strikes a parable for you, you must respect God's striking of the parable, and seek the wisdom behind the parable: that He, glory be to Him, brought this parable with this creature which is insignificant in your eyes, in order to clarify for you an obscure matter to which He draws your attention.

Because of the importance of striking parables in clarifying the obscure, poets resort to them in order to bring the meaning closer to understanding. A poet may face a complex matter that only the intelligent comprehend, and he wishes to bring it to the understanding of the common people. Such is the matter of the envious person who, through his envy, reveals the merits and noble qualities of the one he envies. He may falsely accuse an innocent person, and thereby become the cause of that person's elevation among his people.

The Arab poet took up this meaning, shaped it into verse, and struck an explanatory parable for it, saying:

*When God wishes to spread a virtue, it is folded up; were it not for the fire blazing around it,*
*a jealous tongue would make it known to the world, one who would not know the fragrance of the oud wood.*

See how he moved from the spiritual matter to a general matter that the ordinary man knows. You may have a hidden virtue, unknown to anyone, until you are subjected to an envious person who accuses you and disfigures your image. Then the truth is revealed to all, and what you possess of talents and virtues appears. This is like the fragrant oud wood, whose scent we only smell when we burn it.

The cause of this poetic parable was that a man of goodness used to visit from time to time one of the houses of the town, in which lived an old paralysed woman in need of help. He would help her with what he could. Next to her house lived one of the beautiful women who might be an object of desire. One of the envious people exploited this closeness and accused the righteous man of going to this beautiful woman. Indeed people followed him, and he was seen going to the house of the paralysed old woman. From this, people came to know of a virtue of his that no one had known.

Throughout history we have seen people who were falsely accused, and things were said about them that would make the forehead sweat; then a just judiciary vindicated them and showed that they were heroes deserving of honour. Had it not been for the accusation they suffered, we would not have known their merits and noble qualities.

As for His words, ﴿Indeed God knows, and you do not know﴾ (16:74), this is the reason for the prohibition of striking parables: we do not know, whereas the Truth, glory be to Him, strikes parables for us because He knows, and He brings the parable in its proper place.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 16, verse 75:

After our Lord, glorified is He, had prepared us to receive parables and readied our minds to accept the parables from Him, the True One, glorified and exalted, brought this parable, presenting for us a likeness with two sides:

The first side: a slave (ʿabd), that is, a possession (mawlā), described as one whose disposal is owned by another, who is unable to do anything of work. This is because a slave may be a slave and yet work, such as when his master permits him to trade, for example, while he remains a slave. There is also the mukātab slave, who agrees with his master on a sum of money he will pay to him in order to attain his freedom, so his master lets him work in freedom until he gathers the agreed sum. This one is still a slave and owned, and is unable to do anything of striving or work.

The second side: a free master, whom God provided for and gave a good provision (rizq ḥasan), that is, lawful and pure. Then God enabled him to spend from it in various kinds of spending: secretly and openly. This is a high station: a provision from God described as lawful and pure, with no doubt in it; after that, God enabled him to spend from it, each according to what suits him. Some spending is suited to secrecy, and some is suited to openness: ﴿If you disclose your charities, they are good; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you...﴾ [2:271]

(Surat al-Baqarah): These are the two sides of the parable presented to us, and the Qur'anic context leaves us to judge between them, as if the True One, glorified, says: I am content with your judgment: are they equal?

The True One, glorified, does not leave us without an answer except when the answer will come in accordance with what He wills. And there is no reasonable answer to this question except that we say: They are not equal. It is as if the True One, glorified, made us utter this judgment ourselves.

This parable was given for the worshippers of idols, who ate of God's provision and worshipped other than Him. So the True One likened the idols to the owned slave who is unable to do anything, and gave the other parable for the master whom God provided with a good provision, so he spends from it secretly and openly. Do you not see His saying in another verse: ﴿And He has poured upon you His favours, apparent and hidden﴾ [31:20], to show them their error in turning away from the worship of God despite what He had given them of provision, toward the worship of idols which give them nothing?

From here the wisdom becomes clear in that God, exalted, left the judgment to them in this parable, and brought it in the form of a question, so that they would take the judgment from their own mouths and bear witness against themselves, to cut off from them the path of denial and dispute.

Here we pause at His saying: ﴿Are they equal?﴾ [16:75]. The discourse concerns a dual (muthannā), and the analogy would have been to say: هل يستويان (hal yastawiyān)? So why did He shift from the dual to the plural? We say: because the parable, although it is struck with a singular against a singular, applies to many. The singular is common across many enslaved persons, and across many masters who possess good provision. This is so that the parable is generalized.

Thus: there is nothing in the change of pronoun here that conflicts with the eloquence of the Noble Qur'an; rather, it is precision of expression, because the speaker is the True One, glorified and exalted. Likewise in His saying: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight, then make peace between them...﴾ [49:9], some see in the verse an objection, since it speaks of the dual, then uses the plural pronoun in (iqtatalū), then returns to the dual in (baynahumā). We say to them: if you reflect on the meaning, you will know that what you take as an objection, and regard as a difference in style, is the utmost precision in Qur'anic expression. The discourse concerns two groups: a dual... yes. For if they fought, would each group take up one sword to fight the other? No. Rather, each soldier in them would take up a sword. The fighting is thus collective: the whole of each group against the whole of the other group, so it was fitting to say (iqtatalū), because fighting is an act originating from each individual in the two groups. But when the time for reconciliation comes, do we reconcile every soldier of this with every soldier of that? No. Rather, reconciliation is the affair of the masters, leaders and commanders of each group, so in reconciliation we return to the dual, where these stand in for one group and those for another, and the peace is made between them. Thus: the difference of pronoun here is a sign of the miraculous eloquence (iʿjāz bayānī), because the speaker is the True One, glorified and exalted. And His saying: ﴿Praise be to God...﴾ [16:75 segment], as if the True One, glorified, says: Praise be to God that your judgment has matched what I willed, for you have spoken and judged yourselves.

﴿Nay, but most of them do not know﴾ [16:75]. His saying ﴿most of them do not know﴾ indicates that a minority do know. This is what they call "preserving the possibility" (ṣiyānat al-iḥtimāl), because when the Qur'an was revealed, there were groups of disbelievers and People of the Book who were thinking about faith and embracing this religion. Had the Qur'an denied knowledge to all of them, it would have shocked these people and perhaps turned them from what they were contemplating regarding faith. So the Qur'an preserves the possibility that some among them have knowledge and desire faith.

This is another example of two men: one of them is dumb (abkam), and the dumb one is the one who cannot speak. Deafness (summ) must necessarily precede dumbness, because speech is the offspring of hearing. If we take an Arab infant and raise him in an English environment, we find that he speaks English, and the reverse is also true. That is because speech is not a racial trait, nor blood or flesh; rather, it is the product of the environment, and what the ear hears, the tongue utters. So if he hears nothing, how can he speak?

Therefore, our Lord, glory be to Him, says of the disbelievers: ﴿Deaf, dumb.﴾ [2:18] This dumb man is unable to do anything of work or benefit for you. Almighty God says: ﴿And he is a burden upon his master﴾ [16:76], meaning: a dependent upon his master, who does not benefit even himself. Yet even so, he may have some wisdom by which he could accomplish something for his master, but even this he does not have.

﴿Wherever he directs him, he brings no good.﴾ [16:76] So, there is no good in him, and no benefit at all, neither for himself nor for others. These are the attributes of the first man. What then of his counterpart? ﴿Is he equal to one who enjoins justice?﴾ [16:76] This is the first attribute of the other man: that he enjoins justice. The attribute of enjoining justice implies that he has heard a method, his ear has retained it, and his tongue has spoken forth, commanding justice. This attribute stands in contrast to the dumb man who is unable to do anything.

﴿And he is upon a straight path﴾ [16:76], meaning: he proceeds directly toward the goal, by the shortest of routes. This stands in contrast to: "Wherever he directs him, he brings no good." The question here too is: are the two equal? The answer that reason gives is: No.

This is another example concerning the idols. They do not hear, they do not speak, and they do not express anything; they are unable to do anything, neither for themselves nor for their worshippers. Rather, they are a burden upon them: it is they who bring them from the stones of the mountains, carve them, set them up, and repair their breakage. Thus it is they who serve them, and they gain nothing from them.

If you do not equate the first man with the other who enjoins justice while being upon a straight path, then how can you equate a God who possesses absolute perfection with idols that possess no power to benefit or harm you?! Or we may say: this is an example of the believer and the disbeliever, as evidenced by the fact that in the preceding example the Truth, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Allah presents an example: a slave owned [by another]﴾ [16:75],

and in its counterpart He said: ﴿And one whom We have provided with good provision from Us﴾ [16:75], and He did not say "a slave" or "a man." Rather, here He said: ﴿two men﴾ [16:76]. So it may be understood from this that it is an example of the disbelieving man, represented by the dumb one, and the believing man, represented by the one who enjoins justice while upon a straight path.

Almighty God willed to teach us from it the world of dominion (ʿalam al-mulk) and the world of the unseen dominion (ʿalam al-malakut). ʿAlam al-mulk is the world, the visible world, and ʿalam al-malakut is the hidden world that is concealed from us so that we do not see it.

For this reason, when our Lord, glorified and exalted, honoured our master Ibrahim, peace be upon him, He said: ﴿And thus did We show Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth, that he might be among the certain [in faith]﴾ (Surat al-Anʿam). 

So then: God, exalted, has in His creation the manifest and the unseen. The manifest has cosmic laws (nawamis kawniyya) that all people see, and He has unseen matters that no one sees and no one perceives. Even within yourself there are unseen matters that no one among people knows, and likewise among people there are unseen matters that you do not know. This unseen we call the unseen of the human being.

So: I am absent from myself in some things, and others are absent from themselves in some things. This unseen that we do not know, some people consider it a deficiency in us, but in reality it is a kind of perfection in the human soul; for if you wish to know the unseen of people, then allow them to know your unseen.

If I were given the choice in this matter, I would choose that each one of you keep his unseen to himself, that no one perceive it. I do not know the unseen of people, and they do not know my unseen; for this reason they say: "What is covered is beautiful." The concealment of the unseen is a perfection in the universe, because it nurtures and enriches the benefit within it. How?

Suppose you know a man who is upright and has many good deeds, then you come to know of one single misdeed of his while it was hidden. You will find that this one misdeed is enough to make you lose interest in all his good deeds, to make you hate him, and to call you to aversion from him, so that you benefit from him in nothing. Whereas if this misdeed had been hidden from you, you would have been able to benefit from his good deeds. And thus the unseen increases the benefit in the universe.

In some of the transmitted reports, the Lord, glorified be He, says: "O son of Adam, I have concealed from you and concealed from you [your faults]; so if you wish, We will expose you and expose you, and if you wish, We will let the veil of concealment hang over you until the Day of Resurrection." So make yourself now the one addressed by this hadith; what will you choose?

I believe everyone will choose concealment. As long as you love concealment and hate that people should know your unseen, then beware of presuming to know the unseen of others.

The unseen is what is absent from the sensible perceptions, of hearing, sight, smell and taste, and what is absent from the intellects of the mental perceptions.

There is also an unseen which God has placed in His creation as antecedents that lead to it and causes so that it does not remain unseen, like electricity and gravity and others. They were unseen before they were discovered. Thus all discoveries and secrets that science reveals to us were unseen to us at one time, then became observed at another time. That is because God, glorified be He, does not scatter all the secrets of His creation at once, but sends them down in measure and reveals them to us with reckoning. He, glorified be He, says: ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasures, and We do not send it down except in a known measure﴾ (Surat al-Hijr). So what was unseen in the past has become manifest and observed today, because God has revealed to us its causes and we reached it. This is an unseen for which God has made antecedents that the one who searches the universe arrives at; then when God permits it and the time of its birth arrives, God guides one of the researchers to discovering it, either through research, or even through error in attempt, or by coincidence.

For this reason, if you examine all inventions and discoveries, you would find 90% of them came by coincidence, while they had not been intent on searching for them or reaching them; and this is what we call "the unseen of the cosmos." An example of this unseen: if you assign your son to solve a geometry exercise... and the meaning of solving the exercise is that the son reaches a point you want him to reach. What does the son do? He takes the data you give him, then uses the theories he has and the intelligence he possesses, and extracts the required result from them.

So the son here has not brought anything new; rather he used the data. Likewise the things present in the universe are the data; whoever searches in them reaches the unseen matters and secrets of the universe. This kind of unseen is what God, exalted be He, speaks of: ﴿God—there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of [all] existence. Neither drowsiness overtakes Him nor sleep. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission? He knows what is before them and what will be after them, and they encompass not a thing of His knowledge except for what He wills﴾ (Surat al-Baqarah). So when God permits them, secrets are unveiled to them: either by research, or by error, or even by coincidence. So as long as the time of this unseen's birth and its discovery has arrived, then if it meets human research, the two meet; otherwise God reveals it to us without research and without effort on our part.

There is another kind of unseen, which is the absolute unseen, the unseen that God has kept exclusively to Himself, and which has no antecedents or causes that lead to it, as in the first kind. Concerning this unseen, God, exalted be He, says: ﴿[He is] Knower of the unseen, and He does not disclose His unseen to anyone, except to a messenger whom He has approved﴾ (Surat al-Jinn). So when the Messenger informs us of some unseen matter, we do not say that he knows the unseen, for he knows only what God has informed him of the unseen. So then: this is an unseen that no one perceives by his own essence, ever.

From this absolute unseen is an unseen that God has kept to Himself, and He does not disclose it to anyone, not even the messengers.

In the Night Journey and the Ascension, the Prophet (ﷺ) tells us that God gave him three vessels: a vessel he was commanded to convey, which is the vessel of the message; a vessel He gave him a choice in, so he gives it only to those who have spiritual readiness, who accept God's secrets and whose intellects do not reject them; and a vessel He withheld, which is a particularity of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

For this reason the narrator of the hadith says: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) gave me two vessels; as for one of them, I have spread it, that is, I have related it and spoken it to the people; and as for the other, if I were to disclose it, my throat would be cut. This is among the secrets that the Messenger (ﷺ) chooses someone to guard.

As for the words of God, exalted be He: ﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth...﴾ (Surat al-Nahl). This is what they call a restrictive construction by fronting the prepositional phrase (qasr bi-taqdim al-jar wa'l-majrur), meaning the unseen of the heavens and the earth is restricted to Him, glorified be He. For if we said, for example, "The unseen of the heavens and the earth is for God," it would be possible for someone to say: "and for other than God." But: ﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth...﴾ (Surat al-Nahl):

That is: to Him alone, without partner. "The heavens and the earth" means: and what is between them and what is beyond them; but the well-known of God's creatures are the heaven and the earth. Then He, exalted, says: ﴿And the matter of the Hour is not but as a glance of the eye or even nearer...﴾ (Surat al-Nahl). The verse brought this unseen as the sole unseen, because it is the unseen that God has kept exclusively to Himself, and none reveals it at its time except Him. So it was fitting that, in speaking of the unseen, it should bring this absolute unseen that no one knows but God. And what is "a glance of the eye"?

We have several verbs that all denote general seeing, though each has its own particular meaning: we say ra'a (saw), naẓara (looked), ramaqa (glanced), laḥaẓa (looked sidelong) and lamaḥa (glanced quickly). So ra'a, for example, means with the gathering of the eye; ramaqa with the upper part; laḥaẓa with the side; all of them are linked to the movement of the pupil, and this movement is what we call the lamḥ (glance).

So: lamḥ al-baṣar is the movement of the pupil of the eye toward the direction of the seen object. If you wish to see what is above you, the pupil moves upward; if you wish to see what is below, the pupil moves downward, and so on. This movement is the glance of the eye: the transfer of the pupil from one position to another.

So: God, blessed and exalted, likened the matter of the Hour with Him, glorified be He, to a glance of the eye; but a glance is an event, and events need times, and times may be long in themselves, yet they are short to the observer.

Modern science has brought this matter closer to us through what it has reached in replaying recorded scenes in slow motion, to give you the opportunity to follow them precisely; so they replay for you, for example, a football scene to see all its details, and you find the scene that passed like a glance of the eye presented before you slowly over a longer time, whereas the time in its speed gathers into a gathering that you cannot perceive by any measure, neither by the minute nor by the second.

So: these are particulars of movement within particulars of time. The glance of the eye, which is the movement of the pupil, needs time and an interwoven duration; but this is not the case with the matter of the Hour; rather this is the closest thing a human knows and the closest comparison for understanding the matter of the Hour in relation to Him, glorified be He.

If you are asked: "What is the matter of so-and-so? What is his affair?" you begin to narrate events: such and such happened... But if we say: "What is the matter of the Hour? What is its affair?" — the Hour when the living die first, then all are brought to life from the time of Adam, peace be upon him, then gathering, reckoning, reward and punishment.

Many great events for numerous creatures of men and jinn... all this happens like a glance of the eye relative to us; but beware of imagining that this needs time with respect to God, glorified be He.

Things with respect to Him, glorified be He, are not processed; rather they are: "Be, and it is." Even "Be, and it is" consists of two letters: the kaf is an utterance that has a duration, and the nun is an utterance that has a duration; the matter of the Hour is closer than the kaf and the nun, but there is nothing less than this in our understanding.

When God, exalted and glorified, spoke of the people of the graves, He said: ﴿As if they, on the day they see it, had not remained but an evening or its morning﴾ (Surat al-Nazi'at), whereas we see that they were absent for a long time in their graves. So how is time measured? It is measured by your following of events; when there is no event, there is no time. This is what we see in the state of the sleeper who cannot determine how long he slept, except as is generally the case among people.

For this reason, in the story of the People of the Cave who slept for three hundred and nine years, they said: ﴿We have remained a day or part of a day﴾ (Surat al-Mu'minun). This is the general custom among people; for when they awoke they found nothing around them indicating a long time; the state was as it was, nothing in them had changed. Had they awoken and found themselves old men after having been youths, they would have known the passage of time. So then: time, relative to the non-occurrence of events, is annulled time.

Or we may say: the matter of the Hour, in that God makes it gather people except as a glance of the eye, so whatever happens in it you cannot measure by time; for what is measured by time is only the events arising from an agent who has ability and power, which are distributed over time.

If you wanted to move this thing from here to there, it would require time and effort from you; but if you assigned a child to move it, it would take more time and require more effort. So: time varies inversely with the capacity of the agent.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Able over all things﴾ (Surat al-Nahl): that is, the matter of the Hour is so; because God is capable of all things, and since events differ according to capacities, the power of God is the supreme power that needs no time for the occurrence of events.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 16, verse 78:

(من بطون أمهاتكم) The intended meaning is "the wombs," because they are within the bellies, and the contained is considered as contained within the container, just as if you say: "In my pocket there is such-and-such money," or "In my wallet there is such-and-such money." Both expressions have the same meaning.

"Ummahatikum" is the plural of "umm" (mother). Analogically, the plural of umm should be "ummat," but He said: ﴿And Allah brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers﴾ (Surah An-Nahl), with the addition of the "ha'" (هاء). When the fetus is in its mother's belly, its life is a dependent life; all its organs are subordinate to its mother. So when Allah wills for it to be born, He gives it an independent, self-standing life. At birth, we see obstetricians saying: "The fetus is in the normal position, or in an abnormal position." So what is meant by the normal position of the fetus at birth?

The normal position is that the head of the fetus is downward at birth; this is the normal position, because the Truth, glory be to Him, wished to bring it forth as another creation: ﴿Then We produced it as another creation﴾ (Surah Al-Mu'minun). It was, as it were, a creation, but it was dependent on its mother, so Allah brings it forth as another creation, independent in its own being. Thus the head comes downward, and it is the first thing to descend from the newborn, and as soon as it descends, the process of breathing begins.

From this moment the fetus separates from its mother, and with breathing it gains its own selfhood. If the emergence of the rest of its body is difficult, it has the opportunity to breathe, and this is from the kindness of Allah, the Exalted; because the fetus in this case does not suffocate while the rest of its body is being dealt with.

But if the opposite happens, with the head upward and the fetus descending by its feet, then as soon as the legs descend it separates from its mother, and it needs an independent life and needs to breathe. If the birth is difficult, suffocation occurs, which may lead to the death of the fetus.

Science has taken up one of the matters of the universe that is established, and for which there is evidence. And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿You know nothing﴾ (Surah An-Nahl), is because the means of knowledge and perception have not yet begun to function. When Allah wills for it to know, He creates for it the means of knowledge, which are the five senses: hearing, sight, smell, touch, and taste. These are the outward senses by which a person acquires knowledge and learning, and by which he perceives what is around him.

Although modern science has revealed to us some other senses, in the science of physiology they say: if you hold two pieces of iron, for example, by which sense do you distinguish between them in terms of weight?

It is not known by touch, hearing, sight, taste, or smell. So there is a new sense that distinguishes weight, which is the muscular sense (haasat al-'adal).

Likewise there is the sense of "bayn" (haasat al-bayn), by which you can know the thickness of cloth, for example, when you are in a cloth shop, rubbing the cloth between your fingers, and you can distinguish between the thin and the thick. So the newborn child knows nothing; this is natural, because its means of knowledge and perception have not yet performed their task. And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He made for you hearing and sight and hearts﴾ (Surah An-Nahl).

The scholars of physiology have explained to us that this Qur'anic order of the organs is the natural order: the child, after birth, hears first, then after about ten days it sees. You can test this: you will see the child startle at a loud sound a few days after birth, but if you place your finger before its eyes it does not blink, because it has not yet seen. From hearing and sight, which are the masters of all the senses, the information that is in the hearts is formed. This is the Qur'anic existential order, and it is the natural order that agrees with modern science.

We note in the verse that "hearing" is singular, while "sight" and "hearts" are plural: ﴿And He made for you hearing and sight and hearts﴾ (Surah An-Nahl). Why did hearing not come in the plural? The speaker here is the Truth, glory be to Him; therefore the words come precise and miraculous. Let us consider why hearing is singular here. Hearing differs from the other senses: when a sound occurs in a place, everyone hears it; there is nothing in the ear that prevents hearing, and there is no lock on it that we can close if we wish not to hear. So hearing is one for everyone. But the visible differs, because we do not all look at one thing; rather, what each of us sees differs: this one looks at the ceiling, and that one looks at the pillars, and so on. Thus our objects of sight are different. Likewise the eye has a natural lid that can be lowered over it so that it does not see; so our sights are different and many.

The same applies to the hearts: they came in the plural because they are many and different: one comprehends and perceives, another does not comprehend or perceive, and one may comprehend more than others.

So the singular of "hearing" here is a sign of the precision of the miraculous Qur'anic expression, because the speaker is the Lord of Might, glory be to Him.

We also note the placing of hearing before the other senses, because it is the first of perceptions; it accompanies a person from the time he is born until he departs this life, and it is not absent from him even if he is asleep, because by hearing one is awakened from sleep.

We have said in the story of the People of the Cave that they could not have slept a deep sleep for three hundred and nine years unless Allah had withdrawn this sense from them, so that sounds would not disturb them. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿So We struck upon their ears in the cave for a number of years﴾ (Surah Al-Kahf). That is: We told the ear to be inactive for this period, so that the sounds of the desert would not disturb them and unsettle their resting place, while Allah, the Exalted, wanted for them slumber and deep sleep.

As for His saying: ﴿And He made for you hearing...﴾ (Surah An-Nahl), do these perceptions exist after the emergence (birth), or do they exist before it? One must distinguish between hearing and its instrument. Before emergence, the instruments of sight, hearing, taste and others are formed for the fetus, but they are instruments that do not function; the fetus in its mother's belly is dependent on her and has no independent life. When it descends into the world and becomes independent in its life, Allah makes these instruments perform their function.

So the meaning of ﴿And He made for you hearing﴾ is: He made for you the faculty of listening, not merely the instrument of hearing. As for His saying: ﴿so that you may give thanks﴾ (Surah An-Nahl), the verse suggests that hearing, sight and hearts will provide us with much new information and perceptions that benefit us in our lives and in the foundations of our existence, and by which we benefit others; and these blessings deserve gratitude from us. So whenever you hear a sound or a wise saying, praise Allah that He made for you an ear that hears; whenever you see a wondrous sight, praise Allah that He made for you an eye that sees; whenever you smell a fragrant scent, praise Allah that He made for you a nose that smells. Thus blessings call for thanking the Bestower, Exalted is He.

And so that you may stand over the blessings of Allah upon you, look at those who have been deprived of them, reflect on your condition and theirs, and on what you have of the blessings and pleasures of life, and what they suffer of deprivation.

Thus Allah, glory be to Him, here moves us to another image of the cosmos, after having spoken to us about man and what surrounds him. Before Allah created man in this existence, He prepared for him the means of his life: the sun, the moon, the stars, the earth, the sky, the waters and the air. All of these are things that came into being before man, in order to prepare existence for him in this universe.

Having ensured for us the preservation of life through sustenance, and the preservation of the species through marriage and procreation, Allah, glory be to Him, wants us to enrich our belief by contemplating the dominion of Allah (malakut) and the wonders within it, so that we may infer that He, glory be to Him, fashioned His cosmos with a wondrous, interlocking craftsmanship, and made it firm with a perfection in which there is no collision.

﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outstrip the day; each is in an orbit, swimming along.﴾ (Surah Ya-Sin, 40). Consider Allah's vast cosmos: how many planets, stars and celestial bodies it contains, how full it is of motion, rest and rotation. Yet no collision has occurred within it, and no harm has ever come from it at any time. The whole cosmos proceeds by a precise order and a wondrous harmony. And so that this truth may become manifest to you, look at the handiwork of man: how many collisions and accidents there are in it, whose victims number in the thousands.

This is an example visible to all: the bird in the sky. What holds it from falling to the earth? It is as though Allah, glory be to Him, wishes to draw our attention to a greater matter: ﴿Surely Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they should cease; and if they were to cease, none could hold them after Him.﴾ (Surah Fatir, 41). So we must affirm this matter. We do not perceive with our eyes the mass of the earth, nor the mass of the sun, the stars and the planets. We are not able to know everything in the cosmos. Therefore, we must accept our Lord's word and not dispute it.

And here is this example which you witness every day: ﴿Have they not seen the birds, subjected in the atmosphere of the sky? None holds them up except Allah.﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 79). Beware of saying that it is the flapping of wings. We see the bird hold its wings steady in the air, and yet it does not fall to the earth. There is therefore something that holds it from falling. For this reason the Exalted said in another verse: ﴿Have they not seen the birds above them, spreading and folding their wings?﴾ (Surah al-Mulk, 19), meaning that they are in a state of spreading their wings, and in a state of folding them, and they remain suspended and do not fall. Likewise we find among birds some that have long wings but do not fly, such as the ostrich and other birds.

Therefore, the matter is not a matter of wings; rather, it is a sign of Allah's signs that holds this bird in the atmosphere of the sky. You see it free and unfettered, not drawn to the earth by anything, nor drawn to the sky by anything; rather, it is free: it rises if it wishes to rise, and descends if it wishes to descend.

This is a sensible sign by which we may infer the power of Allah, which is not perceptible except through Allah's own report of it. So when He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Surely Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they should cease; and if they were to cease, none could hold them after Him.﴾ (Surah Fatir, 41), we believe and affirm. His saying, exalted be He: ﴿in the atmosphere of the sky﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 79) means in the air surrounding the earth. The one who reflects on the cosmos finds that air is the principal factor in the stability of things in the universe. As for mountains, buildings and other things, what holds them from falling? Beware of thinking it is cement, iron and architectural engineering. No, rather what holds them is the air that surrounds them on every side, as evidenced by the fact that if you were to empty one side of them of air, they would immediately collapse toward that side, because air has pressure; when you empty one side of it, the pressure there diminishes and it collapses. Air, then, is the regulator of this matter, and by air the bird balances in the sky, moves as it desires, and travels as it loves.

Then He, exalted be He, says: ﴿Surely in that are signs for a people who believe﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 79), meaning: the bird that flies in the sky contains signs, that is, wonders—wonders of craftsmanship and wonders of creation—which you must contemplate and take lessons from.

In order to dwell upon this sign in the bird, let us see what happened to the first man who tried to fly. He was the Arab ʿAbbas ibn Firnas, the first to attempt flight in al-Andalus. He made two wings for himself and threw himself from a high place. What happened to the first human bird?

He flew a short distance, then landed on his rear, which broke, because he forgot that the matter is not merely flying: there is also landing, for which he neglected to prepare, and he failed to make for himself a (zamki), which is the tail that preserves balance upon landing.

Likewise, those who make aircraft: how much do they expend? How many instruments, measuring devices and controls are in them? And after that they need a pilot who flies them or a director who directs them. When they wished to make the airplane, they made it in the shape of the bird in the sky, having two wings, a front and a tail. Yet despite that, what happens if its engine fails, or its balance is disturbed?

Thus the bird in the sky is a sign deserving of observation and reflection, so that through it we may know the power of the Creator, glory be to Him. And He, exalted be He, says: ﴿for a people who believe﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 79), who believe in the existence of the Necessarily Existent, who believe in His wisdom and the precision of His making, and that there is no likeness to it in human craftsmanship, however precise and firm it may become.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 16, verse 80:

His saying: ﴿And Allah has made for you from your houses a dwelling place...﴾ (Surat an-Nahl: 80).

The word sakan (dwelling, repose) is derived from sukun (stillness), and sukun is the opposite of movement. We call the house sakan because a person takes refuge in it to rest from the movement of life outside the house. So outside there is movement, and inside the house there is sakan. Sakan may be material, like the house, which is the sakan of the body (qalib), and it may be immaterial, as Allah the Exalted said concerning spouses:

﴿And He created for you from yourselves spouses that you may find tranquility in them...﴾ (Surat ar-Rum: 21). Thus the wife is an immaterial sakan for her husband, and this is what they call the sakan of the heart. If someone says: "﴿From your houses﴾ (Surat an-Nahl: 80) means: we are the ones who made and erected them. How then did Allah make them for us?" We say: And how did you make them? And of what did you build them? You made them from reeds or wood, or you built them from clay or brick... All these materials are from the substance of the earth, a gift of Allah to you, and likewise the mind that thinks and designs, and the strength that builds and erects, are all from Allah.

So: "(He made for you)" is either a direct making or an indirect making. Allah the Glorified made these materials for us; this is direct making. He helped us and empowered us to build; this is indirect making. But in which places are houses built?

Houses are only built in places of settlement, where the means of life are available. Before we organize a residential city, we first look for its foundations of stability: food, drink, utilities, services, water, drainage... and so on.

If these foundations are available, there is no objection to building here. But if utilities are not available in the desert and the areas of the Bedouins, then permanent houses and building are not suited to them; rather what suits them is: ﴿And He made for you from the hides of cattle houses that you find light [to carry] on the day of your travelling and the day of your settling﴾ (Surat an-Nahl: 80). We see the people of the desert taking tents and pavilions from hides, for we see them moving often, seeking pasture and grass, and migrating in search of grazing and water. Thus their life is in constant movement from one place to another, so a house of hide or wool or fine hair, light to carry, suits them; they set it up wherever they halt their baggage and lift it wherever they travel. Al-Zu'n (ظعن) means moving from one place to another.

So: the word (sakan) implies settlement and provides all the means of life. Therefore the Truth, glorified and exalted, says to Adam: ﴿Dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden...﴾ (Surat al-Baqarah: 35), meaning the place in which is your comfort and your bliss, and He specified for him a place of residence and dwelling. This place of residence may be general or specific. For example, if you say: "Dwell in Alexandria", this is a general dwelling. But if you want your true private dwelling, you say: "Dwell in such-and-such street, in such-and-such building, in apartment number such-and-such", and perhaps you have a private room within this apartment.

So this is your own private dwelling, your true sakan in which you feel calm, comfort and privacy. Sakan requires a personal stability that no one shares with you. Therefore we see some residents of apartment buildings complaining of disturbance and noise, and wishing to live in independent houses that give them the sufficient comfort in which no one troubles them.

So: when we look at sukun, at sakan, we need a narrow place that achieves for us complete privacy, reaching to a room that is not merely a room, but means my true private dwelling. Privacy may even reach the point that we give each child a separate bed of his own in the same room.

When we look at movement in life, we find that man, on the contrary, seeks spaciousness, because movement requires spaciousness in place. Whoever has a farm seeks an estate, and whoever has an estate wishes for a second and a third, and so on, because the movement of life requires a wide, vast field.

This is concerning the first type, which is material sakan, the sakan of the body, and it is among the greatest of Allah's blessings upon His servants that they have a dwelling to which they retreat and in which they rest from the toil and movement of life. Therefore, when the Truth, glorified be He, wished to punish the Children of Israel, He scattered their dwelling throughout the whole earth and deprived them of the blessing of a true private dwelling, and He said:

﴿And We said after him to the Children of Israel: Dwell in the land...﴾ (Surat al-Isra': 104). The earth is the general place in which all people dwell. They have no country that gathers them; rather Allah dispersed them in the earth and did not make a homeland for them, as He said in another verse: ﴿And We divided them in the earth into nations﴾ (Surat al-A'raf: 168). Even in the countries in which they live, you find them isolated from people in places specific to them, not melting into others. Thus they dwelt in the earth and no country was determined for them.

As for the second type of sakan, which is immaterial sakan or the sakan of the heart, it is the husband's sakan in his righteous wife, who lightens for him the toil of life and its worries, who smiles in his face when he is joyful and calms his anger when he is angry, enveloping him with the love, tenderness and sincerity she has. This is the immaterial sakan, the sakan of the heart.

His saying: ﴿And from their wool, their fleece and their hair, furnishings and provision for a time﴾ (Surat an-Nahl: 80). Ash-sha'r (wool) for sheep, awbar (fleece) for camels, and sha'r (hair) for goats. What is the difference between these three in use?

People use both the wool and the fleece, because their fibres are very fine, so they can be carded and spun and benefited from in rugs, carpets, quilts, clothing and other things people need. As for goat hair, its fibres are thick and cannot be carded or spun, so it cannot be benefited from in these woven goods.

His saying: ﴿furnishings and provision for a time﴾ (Surat an-Nahl: 80). Ath-ath (furnishings): what is found in the house of what the movement of life requires, such as carpets, mattresses, clothing and curtains.

Al-mata' (provision): what one enjoys and benefits from. The difference between them is that furnishings may be fixed and not change much, whereas provision may change according to need.

For example, you may need to change the old television to bring a new one, colour perhaps, but you rarely change the refrigerator or the washing machine.

His saying: ﴿for a time﴾ (Surat an-Nahl: 80). For a person may be deceived when he fulfils the requirements of his life, and these blessings may distract him from what the Bestower, glorified be He, requires, so he occupies himself with the blessing he is in rather than with the Bestower who bestowed it upon him. So this verse comes as a warning: beware of being deceived by provision and furnishings, for they are provision for a time, a provision limited in time that does not last. However much you take your share of them in this world, they are heading to one of two things: either you will lose them by death, or they will lose you through poverty and need. So they are passing, passing away. Therefore remember always His saying: ﴿for a time﴾ (Surat an-Nahl: 80). The provision of blessings is limited, but the provision of the Bestower, glorified be He, is eternal.

After Allah, glorified is He, spoke of the people of settled homes, who find the necessities of life, and spoke of nomadic and travelling people and the light tents suited to them, which they carry on their journeys, He turned here to those who own nothing, not even the hides of livestock. What do such people do?

Allah, glorified is He, made shade for them to shelter under from the blaze of the sun, and made caves and tunnels in the mountains for them to take refuge in and dwell in. In this way the verses cover every condition a human being may be in. Allah scatters His blessings among people so that each one takes what suits him of Allah's favours.

As for one who has no house to shelter him, and no livestock from whose hides he can make a tent, Allah has made trees for him to shade himself with from the heat of the sun, and made mountain caves for him to shelter and dwell in.

We note here that the verse mentions shade that protects us from the heat of the sun, and does not mention cold, for example. That is because the Noble Qur'an was revealed in the Arabian Peninsula, a hot land, whose need for shade is greater than its need for warmth. His saying ﴿ظلالاً﴾ ("shade") (Surah al-Nahl, 16:81): *zilal* is the plural of *zill*, which is that which protects from the sun and its rays. Shade may be described as *zill zalil*, meaning the shade itself is shaded. We see this in the making of tents, for example, where they make a roof of a single layer that receives the heat of the sun. Even if it blocks the sun's rays, it does not block the heat. So here they make the roof of two layers with a gap between them to reduce the sun's heat.

Here we say: the shade itself is shaded. The same holds for the shade of trees, where the leaves shade one another, so that under the shade of trees you feel a pleasant, cool atmosphere, for a dense shade covers you, blocking the sunlight while allowing the air to pass, so you do not feel oppressed.

Therefore the poet, describing a garden, says:

"It shielded us from the scorching of the sand, and a shade that turns the sun away wherever it faces us,
watered by abundant, generous rain, which veils it and gives leave to the breeze."

His saying ﴿أكناناً﴾ ("shelters") (Surah al-Nahl, 16:81): it is the plural of *kinn*, which is a cave or grotto in the mountain that serves as a dwelling and a cover for one who seeks refuge in it and is sheltered by it. *Kinn* derives from concealment, because it hides people. We say, for example, to a child, "*unkun*" (meaning: settle down and hide yourself), i.e., "*uskun*" and "*unstur*."

Allah, exalted is He, says ﴿وجعل لكم سرابيل تقيكم الحر﴾ ("and made for you garments that protect you from the heat") (Surah al-Nahl, 16:81). *Sarabil* means what is worn of clothing or armour. ﴿تقيكم الحر﴾ means: it protects you from the heat. Here it mentions heat too, so some scholars have tried to find a way out of this verse. They said: the meaning is "that protects you from the heat and protects you from the cold," and the verse suffices with mentioning heat instead of cold, because when one thing is mentioned its opposite is understood, so it is not necessary to mention both states, since one implies the other.

This is a commendable defence from them and an acceptable meaning regarding this verse. But if we reflect on the other verses that speak on this subject, we find: one speaks of heat, which is this verse, and another speaks of cold, in His saying ﴿والأنعام خلقها لكم فيها دفء﴾ ("And the cattle He created for you; in them is warmth") (Surah al-Nahl, 16:5), meaning that from the hides and wool of livestock we make what protects us from cold and what we warm ourselves with. Thus the verses complement one another and the meaning harmonizes.

One who reflects on human warming will find that the clothes a person wears do not give him heat to warm him; rather, they preserve the body's own heat. A person's heat is inherent, from within him, and by this heat the Creator, glorified is He, preserves the human being.

Physicians say: the healthy body has a temperature of 37 degrees, which does not differ whether a person lives at the equator or lives among the Eskimos at the North Pole. This is the general temperature of the body. However, the body's various organs may differ in temperature, each according to what suits it. The liver, for example, has a temperature of 40 degrees, and its function is disturbed if it falls below this degree. The temperature of the eyelid, for example, is 9 degrees, and if its temperature rises the eyeball would melt and a person would lose sight. Glory be to Allah, who preserves the temperature of these organs in the body so that none of them overpowers another.

For this reason, when we travelled to America, and in one of the regions of extreme cold, the first advice given to us was not to hold our ears with our hands. Why? They said: because the temperature of the hand is lower than the temperature of the ear, and placing a cold hand on the ear may cause much harm.

So: all the clothes and coverings we use to protect us from winter's cold do not give us heat; rather, they preserve our natural heat so that it does not escape, and in this way warming is achieved. You can place your hand on your bed before sleeping and find it cold, while in the morning you find it warm. The bed has acquired heat from the heat of your body, not the reverse.

His saying ﴿وسرابيل تقيكم بأسكم﴾ ("and garments that protect you from your violence") (Surah al-Nahl, 16:81). Here *ba's* means war. The *sarabil* that protect from *ba's* are the armour that soldiers wear in war to protect them from blows. But this verse is in the context of speaking of some of Allah's blessings upon us in settlement and dwelling, and what He has made for us of houses and shade, a life of ease, peace and blessing. So what is the purpose of mentioning war here?

That is because life has a logic of safety for everyone. If the logic of safety is disturbed, people must stand against whoever disrupts the safety of society, and be prepared for that at all times. In times of peace we must prepare for war. Therefore He speaks of war and its preparations while He speaks of tranquillity, stability and blessing.

When the Almighty, exalted is He, sends down the clear verses that carry to us the method of heaven, He says: ﴿لقد أرسلنا رسلنا بالبينات وأنزلنا معهم الكتاب والميزان ليقوم الناس بالقسط﴾ ("We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs and sent down with them the Book and the balance, that people may uphold justice") (Surah al-Hadid, 57:25). This is the method that relies on argument and persuasion. If this method does not suit some people and they rebel against it, then comes the role of force and subjugation. He, exalted is He, says: ﴿وأنزلنا الحديد فيه بأس شديد ومنافع للناس﴾ ("And We sent down iron, wherein is great might and benefits for people") (Surah al-Hadid, 57:25).

His saying ﴿كذلك يتم نعمته عليكم﴾ ("Thus does He complete His favour upon you") (Surah al-Nahl, 16:81).

It is as if the completion of Allah's favour is that we protect it from those who would corrupt it for us, and stand ready for them and strike their hand, for if we leave these corrupters in our society they will corrupt these blessings for us, and we will remain threatened, not feeling the pleasure of life and its enjoyments.

So: the favour is not complete except by preserving the general safety of society. His saying ﴿لعلكم تُسْلِمُونَ﴾ ("that you may submit") (Surah al-Nahl, 16:81). *Tuslimun* means: that you hand over the reins of submission to Allah, to whom you have submitted, and you hand over your reins only to one you trust. A person may hand over his reins in a matter he does not excel at to a human being like himself who excels at that matter. If you, in matters of your own needs, hand over your reins to someone like you, who shares your lack of knowledge and your lack of wisdom, yet you submit your affairs to him merely because he excels at something you do not, then will you not hand over your reins and submit your affairs to your Lord and Creator, the Creator of all these blessings for your sake?

So: the mention of these blessings came, then the command to submit one's face to Allah and surrender to Him, glorified is He, so that we submit with certainty and conviction. Allah, blessed and exalted is He, has no interest in our obedience, and our disobedience does not harm Him. If we obey Him, we add nothing to His dominion, and if we disobey Him, we subtract nothing from His dominion.

So: our surrender of the matter and the reins to Allah is for our own benefit. When a person hands his reins to another, the other may have an interest that bends his opinion in the matter. But our Lord, when He directs a ruling to us, has no interest in it, so He does not bend it; it can only be for your benefit.

After enumerating these blessings in the self, the surroundings, the dwelling and the impressions, He says: beware, after this, of handing your reins over to other than Me, even if I impose upon you what takes you out of the benefit of safety, for I do not impose on you what takes you out of the essence of safety except for a purpose that is safer than it.

Therefore we say: there is no worship like submission, for submission to wisdom is submission to the Wise, submission to one who does not benefit from it. As long as you have handed over your reins to your Lord, mighty and majestic, who will make clear to you the wisdom in what befalls you of events, so that you know His approval of a wisdom in His wisdom, you say: "I am content with Your judgement, O Lord."

That is why we say in supplication: "I praise You for all Your decree and all Your measure, with the praise of one content with Your judgement, certain of Your wisdom." That is: "You have wisdom, O Lord, in what You have brought upon me of events, but I do not see it."

One who knows the station of submission to Allah in what befalls him of events and what afflictions strike him does not become impatient or resentful, for by that he lengthens for himself the term of the decree, because Allah does not lift His decree from His servant until he is content with it. Allah has no compulsion over him.

If you wish the decree to be lifted, be content with it first. If the decree is not lifted from you, know that the place of contentment in your self was not accepted. You may be content with your tongue, but your heart is still resentful and impatient.

So one who hands his reins to Allah, and refers every event that occurs or affliction that befalls him back to Allah and to the wisdom of the One who sends it, Allah says to him: "You have understood Me," and lifts the affliction from him.

In the station of submission to Allah always, we mention the story of our master Ibrahim, when his Lord commanded him to sacrifice his son Isma'il, peace be upon them both. Is there any affliction greater than a man being tested by slaughtering the son whom he was granted in old age, and slaughtering him with his own hand?

It is a trial of many degrees and from various aspects. Would that the matter had come by manifest revelation, but it came by a dream, in which one could have interpreted; yet the dreams of the prophets are true.

We see Ibrahim, peace be upon him, relate the matter to his son, out of concern that his heart not turn away from his father at the moment he takes him to slaughter him, and also so that his son might share with him in contentment with the decree of Allah, and not be deprived of the reward of this trial. So he said to him:

﴿إني أرى في المنام أني أذبحك﴾ ("Indeed, I see in a dream that I slaughter you") (Surah al-Saffat, 37:102). The purpose here is not to alarm or frighten him, but to tell him: this is a matter of worship that the Creator, glorified is He, has commanded us, so that he too may be informed and his heart not change toward his father. That is why the son was wise in his reply, and said: ﴿يا أبت افعل ما تؤمر﴾ ("O my father, do what you are commanded") (Surah al-Saffat, 37:102), meaning: since the command is from Allah, do it. Thus Isma'il submitted as Ibrahim submitted. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿فلما أسلما وتله للجبين﴾ ("So when they had both submitted, and he put him down upon his forehead") (Surah al-Saffat, 37:103).

*Aslama*: meaning the father and the son, and they were both content with Allah's decree. Relief came and the decree was lifted, for each of them understood the matter from Allah. Not only was the decree lifted, but We ransomed him with a great sacrifice. And that is not all: We bestowed on him another son by granting him good tidings: ﴿وبشرناه بإسحاق﴾ ("And We gave him good tidings of Isaac") (Surah al-Saffat, 37:112).

So: that you may hand your reins over to Allah, and know that He created the universe for you before He brought you into it, and supplied you with all the requirements of life, as a guarantee for the continuation of your life and the continuation of your kind, and these enjoyments. The One who has bestowed all this upon you, without any need of yours, deserves that you hand over to Him the reins of your affairs and submit to Him.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 16, verse 82:

Meaning: Do not grieve, O Muhammad, if your people turn away. You are commanded only to convey (al-balagh). Allah, glory be to Him, addresses him in another verse: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself [with grief] that they will not become believers﴾ (Surah ash-Shu'ara', 26:3), i.e., destroy it. And He, exalted is He, says: ﴿If We willed, We could send down to them from the sky a sign, and their necks would remain bowed to it in humility﴾ (Surah ash-Shu'ara', 26:4).

But religion does not stand on control over the outward form (al-qalib), and there is a difference between control over the outward form and control over the heart (al-qalb). With a pistol in your hand you can compel me to do what you want, but you can never compel my heart to believe in something it does not believe in. Allah wants from us hearts, not outward forms. Had He wanted from us outward forms, He would have made them compelled and submissive, with not one of them deviating from His will, glory be to Him.

Therefore, when Allah sent Sulayman (peace be upon him) and made him a king and a messenger, no one could stand against him or oppose him, because of the authority and power that accompanied the prophethood. As for the matter of his call (ﷺ), however, it rests on conveyance alone, without compulsion. His saying: ﴿the clear conveyance﴾ (82), (Surah an-Nahl), means: the complete, perfect conveyance that encompasses every detail and movement of life. The divine method came comprehensive of life, beginning with the saying "There is no god but Allah" down to removing harm from the road. He left nothing without informing us of it. This is a clear conveyance, encompassing the interests of people. So let no one now come and quibble, saying: "Our Lord left out such-and-such." The method of Allah is complete. If you do not take it as a religion, you must take it as a system.

We now see nations that oppose Islam encountering problems in the movement of life for which they find no solution in their laws, so they are forced to other solutions that correspond fully or nearly to the solution of the Qur'an and the method of the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted.

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on surah 16, verse 83:

The Qur'an has related their words in other verses:

﴿And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say, "Allah." So how are they deluded?﴾ (Surah al-Zukhruf, 87)

And it says of them: ﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance.﴾ (Surah al-Naml, 14)

That is because they know full well that Allah created them, and that He created the heavens and the earth. They know all the blessings of Allah upon them, yet they deny and reject them. Why? Because belief in Allah and acknowledging His blessings is a burdensome matter for them. Had it been merely a word to be spoken, they would have said it. How easy it would be for them to say, "There is no god but Allah." But they know that "There is no god but Allah" carries obligations. For as long as there is no god but Allah, only Allah legislates, only Allah commands, only Allah forbids, only Allah makes lawful, and only Allah makes unlawful.

Thus, the obligations of "There is no god but Allah" have put them in a mold of iron, bound by a method that destroys their dominion and prevents tyranny and arrogance, a method that makes masters and slaves equal.

So the true religion restricts their movement, and they do not want that. Hence you find them recognising Allah but not believing in Him, because they know the obligations of "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah" (ﷺ). Otherwise, had it been merely a word, they would have said it.

As for His saying: ﴿And most of them are disbelievers.﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 83)

Some scholars say: "Most of them" means "all of them." No, rather this is a Qur'anic style for preserving possibility (ṣiyānat al-iḥtimāl), and as a precaution for the small minority among these disbelievers who think about Islam and are troubled by the matter of this new religion. We must take account of this minority and leave the door open for them, so the possibility remains.

Had the Qur'an said, "All of them are disbelievers," this would have conflicted with those who are considering embracing Islam. It is also out of consideration for the children of the disbelievers who have not yet reached the age of legal responsibility. So His saying "most of them" (wa-aktharuhum) is a precise expression, containing what we call ṣiyānat al-iḥtimāl.

The Exalted, may He be blessed, is alerting us here that the matter is not merely a religion, where the affair ends with "whoever believes believes, and whoever disbelieves disbelieves." Rather, a resurrection, reckoning, reward and punishment await us, a return to Allah the Exalted and a standing before Him. So if you did not remember Allah for the blessings He bestowed upon you earlier, then take precautions for your meeting with Him later.

Al-Shahid (the witness): he is the Prophet of the community, who bears witness against them concerning what was conveyed to them of the methodology of Allah. The Exalted said in another verse: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation that you may be witnesses over mankind and the Messenger may be a witness over you...﴾ [143] (Surat al-Baqarah). It is as if the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) was given by Allah the trust of testimony over creation, because it conveyed to them. Thus everyone who believes in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is required to convey what the Messenger conveyed, so that he may be a witness over those to whom he conveyed that he conveyed: ﴿Then they will not be permitted to make excuse...﴾ [84] (Surat an-Nahl).

So when the witness testifies against them, they are not permitted to offer excuses, as the Exalted said in another verse: ﴿And they will not be permitted, so they will not make excuse﴾ [36] (Surat al-Mursalat), or when one of them says: ﴿My Lord, return me, [99] that I might do righteousness in what I have left behind [100]﴾ (Surat al-Mu'minun). He is not answered in that, because if he were returned to the world he would do as he did before. The Exalted says: ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾ [28] (Surat al-An'am). And His saying: ﴿nor will they be allowed to seek to make amends﴾ [84] (Surat an-Nahl).

Yastaʿtibun (they seek to make amends): the root is istaʿtaba, from al-ʿitab (rebuke/reproach). Al-ʿitab is derived from al-ʿatb, whose origin is anger and resentment that you feel toward a person who has done something toward you that was not expected of him. So you feel resentment and anger toward the one who wronged you.

If the ʿatb, which is anger and resentment, settles in the soul, then you either rebuke the one who wronged you and make clear to him what angered you, perhaps he had an excuse, or he erred unintentionally. If he clarifies the matter to you, satisfies you and removes your anger, then he has made amends (aʿtabaho). So we say: "So-and-so was resentful toward so-and-so, so he made amends to him," meaning he removed his resentment.

A person only reproaches someone dear to him, whom he is eager to keep his bond with, and whom he places in a position from which wrongdoing is not expected. It is his right upon you that you reproach him and do not let this wrong destroy what is between you.

Thus the meaning of ﴿nor will they be allowed to seek to make amends﴾ [84] (Surat an-Nahl) is: no one among them will ask to return from what necessitated the rebuke, which is their disbelief. There is no longer any time for reproach, because the Hereafter is an abode of reckoning, not an abode of action or repentance. It is no longer an abode of obligation.

The punishment would be set up before them, so they would see it before they experienced it. In this way, Allah gathers upon them various kinds of punishment, because the perceptions of the soul are harmed by witnessing it before the senses are pained by the punishment itself. Therefore He said:

﴿So the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be given respite.﴾ [16:85]

And His saying ﴿nor will they be given respite﴾ [16:85] means: they will not be given time, nor will they be granted a delay.

That is when Allah gathers the polytheists together with their partners: the devils of mankind and jinn, the idols, and everyone they associated with Allah, face to face on the Day of Resurrection, and this confrontation will take place between them. When the polytheists see their partners who misled them, made disobedience attractive to them, and made polytheism and disbelief in Allah attractive to them, they will say: "These are the cause of our misguidance and our disbelief." As Allah the Exalted said about them in another verse: ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed, and they see the punishment, and their ties are cut off﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:166], and He the Exalted says: ﴿Those who were deemed weak will say to those who were arrogant: "Had it not been for you, we would have been believers"﴾ [Saba' 34:31], and His saying: ﴿Then they will cast the word at them...﴾ [Al-Nahl 16:86], meaning: they will answer them in kind and debate them with proof, as Allah the Exalted said concerning the Devil: ﴿I had no authority over you except that I invited you, and you responded to me. So do not blame me; blame yourselves. I cannot help you, nor can you help me...﴾ [Ibrahim 14:22].

So they will reply to them: "You had no authority over us. We invited you, and you responded to us; we had no power to compel you to act, nor any proof to persuade you to disbelieve." This is why they will accuse them of lying: ﴿Indeed, you are liars﴾ [Al-Nahl 16:86], meaning: you are liars in this claim.

The Peace (al-salam): that is, submission (al-istislam). The time of choice has passed and the period of respite has ended; you either act or you do not. Now, indeed, (﴿To whom belongs the dominion today?﴾).
