So the fortress that protects us from the plot of Satan is faith in Allah and reliance upon Him, glory be to Him. Upon whom, then, does Satan dominate? The Truth, blessed and exalted, makes clear the opposite side.

Meaning of "yatawallawnahu": that is, they take him as a patron (waliyy) whose command they obey, submit to his whispering, and follow his footsteps: ﴿Those who take him as a patron and those who associate others with Him﴾ (Surah An-Nahl 16:100). That is, they associate partners with Allah. Or the meaning may be: "and they, through him" — that is, because of him they associated others with Allah, since he has become one who issues commands and prohibitions and they obey him. This is worship itself; it is as if they worshipped him besides Allah through their obedience to him in his command and prohibition.

Allah has named the method of Satan in misguidance and deception "waswasa" (whispering). In reality, whispering is the sound of the jewelry when it moves on women's hands, producing a delicate sound with an attraction and enticement that stirs the soul. Likewise, Satan enters upon you through enticement and beautification. When your soul is aroused and speaks to you of disobedience, and you abandon it, at that point his task ends.

But does the soul commit disobedience only through the whispering of Satan?

They say: No. The soul here meant is the soul that commands to evil (al-nafs al-ammara bi'l-su'), and it may commit disobedience of its own accord without whispering from Satan. Satan may also whisper to it, incite it, stir it up, and beautify for it a disobedience that had not been on its mind.

How then can one distinguish between these two kinds of disobedience?

When the soul desires a disobedience or a lust, you find it fixed upon one specific disobedience and does not budge from it. When you resist your soul and try to divert it from this desire, it presses you insistently and seeks that very thing. The desire of the soul is thus fixed, because it craves one particular thing and insists upon it.

But when Satan whispers to you a lust and finds from you resistance and the ability to confront it, he turns your attention to another, because he wants you to be disobedient in any form whatsoever. So you find him beautifying for you one disobedience after another, until he attains from you what he wants.

An example of this is what we see in bribery, for instance, God forbid. If you refuse a bribe of money, he beautifies for you the bribe of a gift; if you refuse the bribe of a gift, he beautifies for you the bribe of a exchange for arranging a benefit in return.

Thus this accursed one remains behind you until he reaches a point of weakness in you. So he is not like the soul, which stops you at one lust; rather he wants to bring you down in any form whatsoever.

So that we may be aware of the entrances of Satan and be on guard against him, we must know that Satan has great knowledge, by which he reached the ranks of the angels; indeed they called him "the peacock of the angels." We can observe something of Satan's knowledge in the precision of his oath, when he swore to the Truth, blessed and exalted, that he would mislead the children of Adam, saying: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all, except Your sincere servants among them﴾ (Surah Sad 38:82–83).

Thus Satan knew how to swear the appropriate oath. He did not say, "By my strength or by my argument I will mislead creation," but rather he recognized for God, exalted be He, the attribute of might ('izza), for He is Mighty and cannot be overcome. Therefore He left His creatures free to believe in Him, saying: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:29).

The meaning is: "By Your might, concerning Your creation: whoever believes, believes, and whoever disbelieves, disbelieves. I will enter by this door to lead mankind astray, but I dare not approach those whom You have chosen and selected. I will not come near Your sincere servants; I have no concern with them and no authority over them."

Likewise we must know that Satan is precise in his planning, and this is among his entrances and deceptions, which calls us to be wary of this accursed one. Satan has no need to go to the taverns, for example, since their people have spared him the burden of whispering and saved him the effort. These are his allies and beloved, and they bring him rest by their disobedience of God. But he is in need of being in the mosques, to corrupt the obedience of the people of obedience.

This matter was clarified and perceived by the great imam Abu Hanifa al-Nu'man, who was renowned for his acuteness and was knowledgeable about the entrances of Satan and his deceptions, and all of this gave him a long reach in issuing legal opinions (ifta'). One of them presented this question to him:

He said: "O Imam, I had money that I buried in such-and-such a place, and I made a sign on it. Then a flood came and obliterated that sign, so I could not find it. What should I do?"

Abu Hanifa smiled and said: "My son, there is no knowledge in this. In which chapter of the chapters of jurisprudence would you find this case?! But I will devise a stratagem for you."

Indeed, the imam's mind brought forth this stratagem, which shows his knowledge and jurisprudence. He said to him: "When you come at night, perform ablution and stand before your Lord in night prayer. In the morning, inform me of your news."

At the dawn prayer the man met him smiling, saying: "I have found the money." He said: "How?" The man said: "When I stood before my Lord in prayer, I remembered the place, so I went and found my money." The imam laughed and said: "By God, I knew that Satan would not let you complete your night with your Lord."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 16, verse 101:

The words "wa-idha baddalna" (﴿And when We substitute﴾). Among its meanings: abdalta and istabdalta, i.e., raised up a verse and discarded it, and brought another in its place. The preposition bi- may be attached to the thing that is abandoned, as in His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Would you exchange that which is lower for that which is better?﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 61), i.e., you abandon what is better and take in its place what is lower.

What is the meaning of the verse? The word āyah (sign, verse) has several meanings, among them:

A wondrous thing that attracts attention and dazzles the intellect, as we say: "This is an āyah in beauty, or in courage, or in intelligence," meaning that it has reached a degree that calls for wonder and amazement.

Another is the cosmic signs. When you contemplate the creation of God around you, you find signs that point to the originality of the Creator, may He be glorified, and the wondrous workmanship, and you find harmony and coherence among these cosmic signs. He, Exalted, says of this kind of sign:

﴿And among His signs are the night and the day, and the sun and the moon﴾ (Surah Fussilat, 37).

﴿And among His signs are the ships running in the sea like mountains﴾ (Surah al-Shura, 32).

We note that these cosmic signs are fixed and constant, not changing, as the Truth, blessed and exalted, said:

﴿And you will not find any change in the way of Allah﴾ (Surah al-Fath, 23).

Among the meanings of the verse is the miracle (mu'jizah), which is the wondrous matter that breaks the normal custom. Miracles come at the hands of the prophets to serve as proof for them and as evidence of the truth of what they brought from Allah.

We note that in this kind of sign, it changes and varies from one prophet to another, because a miracle has its effect only if it is in a matter in which the people excelled, for that is the field of inimitability (i'jaz). If We had brought them a miracle in a field they had no knowledge of, they would have said: "If we had knowledge of this, we would have brought the like of it." Therefore the miracle comes in that in which they excelled and mastered well, until they became known for it.

When the people of Moses, peace be upon him, excelled in sorcery, his miracle was of the kind of sorcery that challenged their sorcery. When Jesus, peace be upon him, came and his people excelled in medicine and wisdom, his miracle was of the same kind, so he, peace be upon him, healed the blind and the leper and brought the dead to life by the permission of Allah.

When Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was sent, and his people excelled in eloquence, rhetoric and expression, and they used to hold markets for it and hang their poems on the curtains of the Ka'bah in pride of it, it was necessary that he challenge them with a miracle of the kind in which they excelled, namely the Noble Qur'an. Thus miracles change to suit the condition of each people, and challenge them with what they became known for, so that it is more compelling for belief and more firm as proof.

Among the meanings of the word āyah is the verses of the Noble Qur'an, which we call those carrying rulings. If āyah is a wondrous matter, what is the wonder in the verses of the Qur'an?

The wonder in the verses of the Qur'an is that you find these verses among an unlettered nation, revealed to an unlettered prophet among a people of nomadic Bedouins who are skilled at nothing but the craft of speech and eloquent discourse. Then you find these verses carrying laws, rulings and manners that overawe the two strongest contemporary civilizations, the civilization of Persia in the East and the civilization of the Romans in the West, so that you see them longing for Islam and seeking in its rulings what will save them. Is this not wondrous?

As for this last kind of signs, which are the signs of the Noble Book, which we call those carrying rulings, do they change like their predecessors?

We say: the verses of the Book do not change, because the rulings of Allah required of those who lived in the time of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, are like the rulings required of those upon whom the Hour will arise.

Islam was preceded by Judaism and Christianity. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was commanded to change the qiblah from Bayt al-Maqdis to the honoured Ka'bah. The Jews objected to this and said: "What is wrong with Muhammad that he does not stand by one state, commanding a thing today and its opposite tomorrow? If the true house is the Ka'bah, then your prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis is void, and if Bayt al-Maqdis is the true one, then your prayer toward the Ka'bah is void." Therefore the Truth, blessed and exalted, said:

﴿And when We substitute a verse in place of a verse—and Allah knows best what He sends down—they say, "You are but a fabricator."﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 101).

So what is meant by His saying, the Truth, Exalted is He: ﴿a verse in place of a verse﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 101): We brought a verse indicating a ruling that differs from what came in the Torah, for facing the Ka'bah in the Qur'an replaced facing Bayt al-Maqdis in the Torah. His saying: ﴿And Allah knows best what He sends down﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 101), i.e., He sends down every verse according to its circumstances: its community, environment, place and time. His saying: ﴿They say, "You are but a fabricator"﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 101), i.e., they accused the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, of deliberate lying, and that this change was from himself and not a revelation from Allah, Exalted is He, because the rulings of Allah do not contradict. We say: yes, the rulings of Allah, glorified and exalted, do not contradict within one religion; but when religions differ, there is no objection to the rulings differing.

So then: the verses of the Noble Qur'an do not change, but abrogation (naskh) occurs in them, as the Truth, blessed and exalted, said:

﴿Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or similar to it﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 106).

Here are examples of abrogation (naskh) in the Noble Qur'an: when the Truth, Exalted is He, said:

﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ (Surah al-Taghabun, 16).

He made capacity (istita'ah) the measure of action. So the Legislator, Exalted is He, when He sees that capacity is not sufficient, lightens the ruling for us, so that He does not burden us beyond our capacity, as in the fasting of the sick and the traveller, for example. He, Exalted, said:

﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 286), and He said: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul except with what He has given it﴾ (Surah al-Talaq, 7). So it is not for us after that to twist the verses and say: such-and-such a ruling the soul no longer bears, and it is no longer within our capacity. Rather, the Truth, Exalted is He, knows the capacity and imposes according to its measure; if He has imposed, then He has known the capacity, as evidenced by the fact that when He, Exalted, finds hardship, He lightens it for you of His own accord, as He said:

﴿Now Allah has lightened for you, and He knows that there is weakness in you﴾ (Surah al-Anfal, 66).

At the beginning of Islam, when the Muslims had courage and strength, He said: ﴿If there are among you twenty steadfast, they will overcome two hundred﴾ (Surah al-Anfal, 65), i.e., a ratio of one to ten. When Allah, the Exalted, knew weakness in them, He said: ﴿Now Allah has lightened for you, and He knows that there is weakness in you. So if there are among you a hundred steadfast, they will overcome two hundred﴾ (Surah al-Anfal, 66), i.e., a ratio of one to two. Allah, Exalted is He, is the One who knows the reality of our capacity, imposes on us what we are able to bear, and lightens for us when lightening is needed; so it is not proper for us to thrust ourselves into this matter and estimate capacity by our own desires.

Among examples of abrogation: the Arabs in ancient times did not give fathers any share of wealth, on the basis that the father is departing and passing away, and they made the whole portion for the children, on the basis that they are the ones facing life. When the Truth, Exalted is He, wanted to give a share to the parents, He made it a bequest, saying: ﴿It is prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves wealth, that he make a bequest to the parents﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 180). Then, when faith became firmly settled in souls, He made it a fixed inheritance and changed the ruling from bequest to something better, which is inheritance, saying: ﴿And for his parents, to each one of them is a sixth﴾ (Surah al-Nisa', 11).

So then: when the Truth, blessed and exalted, changes a verse, He abrogates it with something better than it. This is evident in the prohibition of wine, for example, where you see this wisely ordered gradualness that takes into account the nature of human souls, and that this matter is one of the habits that had taken hold of souls, and so gradualness was necessary for it; this is not a matter of creed requiring a decisive ruling admitting no dispute.

Look at this gradualness in the prohibition of wine. He, Exalted, said: ﴿And from the fruits of the palm and the grapes you take intoxicant and good provision﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 67).

When the people of taste and understanding of Allah heard this verse, they said: "Indeed Allah has made an implicit matter concerning wine in this verse, for He described provision as good and was silent about intoxication, not describing it as good, which indicates that there will be a discussion about wine later."

When he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about wine, the Qur'an answered them:

﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and benefit for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 219).

This came by way of counsel and guidance, not by way of ruling and legislation, so every believer who trusts the words of his Lord should see for himself a way out of the captivity of this evil habit. Then it was observed that some people prayed while intoxicated, to the point that one of them said in his prayer: "I worship what you worship," so the ruling came: ﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you say﴾ (Surah al-Nisa', 43). The requirement of this ruling was that it turn them away from wine for most of the time, so that prayer could not be performed in intoxication unless they abstained from it a sufficient time before prayer; and thus He trained them to abandon it for most of the time, just as a physician treating his patient for smoking, for example, advises him to reduce the amount gradually until he can overcome this habit.

Thus the Wise Legislator, Exalted is He, brought souls to a stage in which they became accustomed to abandoning wine and began to turn away from it, and souls became prepared to accept the absolute prohibition, so He, Exalted, said:

﴿O you who have believed, wine, gambling, stone altars and divining arrows are but an abomination of Satan's work, so avoid it﴾ (Surah al-Ma'idah, 90).

So then: Allah, Exalted and glorified, abrogated a verse and its ruling with what is better than it. What is strange is that we see some of our scholars who are zealous for the Qur'an and do not accept the claim of abrogation in it, though the Qur'an itself says: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or similar to it﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 106).

They say: because there is something called al-bada' (a change of mind by God). In abrogation it is as if Allah, Exalted, gave a ruling and then it became clear to Him that it was mistaken, so He turned from it to another ruling.

We say to them: you have strayed from the truth in this statement. The meaning of naskh is the announcement of the end of a previous ruling by a new ruling better than it, and in this sense abrogation occurs in the Noble Qur'an. Some stop at the words of the Truth, blessed and exalted: ﴿We bring one better than it or similar to it﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 106).

They say: "Better than it" contains a cause for the substitution and a necessity that requires abrogation, namely excellence; so what is the cause of substitution in His saying "or similar to it"?

First, regarding His saying, "We bring one better than it": someone may say, "Why did He not bring the excellence from the beginning?" We say: because the Truth, blessed and exalted, when He said: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah with the fear due to Him﴾ (Surah Al 'Imran, 102)—

This is a high rank in piety, which none but the elite of Allah's servants can fulfil. This verse was hard on the Companions, and they said: "And who can do that, O Messenger of Allah?" So it was revealed: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ (Surah al-Taghabun, 16).

Allah made piety according to capacity. Thus the first verse was abrogated as a requirement, but it remained as an elevation: whoever wishes to rise in his piety to "fear with the fear due to Him," then so be it, and may Allah increase the like of him and reward him well; and whoever is unable takes the second.

If we look at these two verses from another perspective, we find the first, ﴿Fear Allah with the fear due to Him﴾ (Surah Al 'Imran, 102), though it calls to much piety, the ones acting upon it are few; whereas the second:

﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ (Surah al-Taghabun, 16),

though it made piety according to capacity, the ones acting upon it are many. Hence the second is better than the first, as we say: a little constant is better than much interrupted.

As for His saying, "or similar to it," meaning that the first is like the second, what is the aspect of change here, and what is the cause of the substitution?

We say: its cause here is ikht—

Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 16, verse 102:

In this verse, the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, refutes the disbelievers' fabrication against the Messenger of Allah, and their accusation against him of deliberate lying, and that he brought these verses from himself. So He said to him: "O Muhammad, say to these people: 'Rather, it has been sent down by the Holy Spirit (Ruh al-Qudus).'"

Al-Quds means the purifier (al-Mutahhir), in the form of an attributed noun modified by its adjective, just as we say: Hatim al-Jud (Hatim the generous), for example. What is meant by "Ruh al-Qudus" is the emissary of revelation, Jibril (peace be upon him). Allah said of him in another verse:

﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ (Surah al-Shu'ara', 26:193)

And He said of him:

﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger, [who is] possessed of power, with esteem near the Owner of the Throne, obeyed there [and] trustworthy﴾ (Surah al-Takwir, 81:19-21)

As for His saying, glorified is He: ﴿from your Lord in truth﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 16:102), it means that Jibril did not bring this Qur'an from himself, but from Allah, in truth. So Muhammad (ﷺ) did not bring the Qur'an from himself, and likewise Jibril; the Qur'an is from Allah, not a fabrication against Allah, neither from Muhammad nor from Jibril, peace be upon them both. As for His exalted saying:

﴿to strengthen those who believe, and as guidance and good tidings for the Muslims﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 16:102), it means: to strengthen those who believe in their affirmation of what the Messenger brought of the verses, [and the knowledge] that Allah, exalted is He, knows best what He sends down of verses, and that each verse among them is suited to its time, its place and its circumstances. In this is evidence that the believers are obedient and submissive to Allah, exalted is He, and affirm the Messenger (ﷺ) in everything he conveyed from his Lord, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 16, verse 103:

In this verse there is another accusation against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and a new fabrication against him, one that the Qur'an does not disdain to broadcast. Whoever hears the accusation and the fabrication must hear the answer, for the Qur'an wants to expose the affair of these people and to show the bankruptcy of their arguments and the confusion they are in.

Allah, blessed and exalted, says:

﴿And We certainly know that they say, "It is only a human being who teaches him."﴾ (Surah An-Nahl 16:103)

They had earlier said of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he was "possessed (majnun)", and Allah cleared him by saying:

﴿And indeed, you are of a great moral character.﴾ (Surah Al-Qalam 68:4). A great moral character cannot be found in a madman, because a noble character is placed only in its proper place, as is evident from His saying:

﴿You are not, by the favour of your Lord, a madman.﴾ (Surah Al-Qalam 68:2)

They had also said that he was a "sorcerer (sahir)", and this is evidence that they are fools who stumble about in their misguidance. For if Muhammad were a sorcerer, why did he not bewitch you as he bewitched the believers in him, and the matter would have ended?

They had also said that he was a "poet (sha'ir)", even though they are the people most knowledgeable of the arts of speech, in verse and in prose and in oratory, and they never tested Muhammad (ﷺ) with anything of that kind. But falsehood, when it persists in its obstinacy and disdains to accept the truth, will say anything.

Here they came up with something new by which they lie against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they said:

﴿It is only a human being who teaches him.﴾ (Surah An-Nahl 16:103). That is, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would visit one of the people of learning in order that he might teach him the Qur'an. They said: he is a slave boy belonging to the Banu 'Amir ibn Lu'ayy, named (Ya'ish), who knew reading and writing, and used to bring books from the markets and read the stories of earlier peoples, such as 'Antarah and Dhat al-Himmah, and other books of history.

Their statements conflicted in identifying this person whom they claim the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) learned from. Some said his name was "'Addas". Others said: Salman al-Farisi. Others said: Bal'am, a Roman Christian blacksmith who knew much about the People of the Book, and so on.

Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, answers these people and exposes their intellectual bankruptcy and their insistence on denying the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), saying:

﴿The tongue of the one they refer to is foreign, while this is clear Arabic speech.﴾ (Surah An-Nahl 16:103)

"Lisan" (tongue) here means the language spoken. "Yulhidun ilayhi" means they incline towards him and attribute to him that he teaches the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). "A'jami" means: his language is obscure, not eloquent, and does not express speech clearly, as we see foreigners speaking Arabic, for example.

We note here that the Qur'an did not say ("'ajami") (a non-Arab), because "'ajam" (non-Arabs) is a category opposed to "'arab" (Arabs), and among the non-Arabs there may be someone who masters eloquent Arabic, as we have seen in Sibawayh, author of (al-Kitab), the greatest reference in grammar until now, who was a non-Arab.

As for "a'jami" it refers to the one who is not eloquent and does not express himself clearly, even if he is of Arab origin. There was in the tribe of Lu'ayy a man named Ziyad who was called "Ziyad al-A'jami", because he was not eloquent and did not express himself clearly, although he was of Arab origin.

So then: how could these non-Arabs, who are not eloquent and can hardly speak the Arabic language, how could they teach the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he came with a miracle in eloquence, rhetoric and clarity of expression?

How could he learn from these people, when it is not established that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) met any of them except 'Addas, who is said to have met him once, and it is not established that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) frequented any teacher, neither from these nor from others?

Moreover, what the Qur'an contains of verses, rulings, miracles and information requires a long time to learn, during which Muhammad would have to be a disciple at the hands of these people, and you have not tested Muhammad with any of this at all.

And is it reasonable that what is in the Qur'an could be contained in the breast of one of these people? If it had happened, he would have had among his people the standing and rank that the Prophet (ﷺ) had, they would have pointed at him with fingers, his fame would have spread, and his affair would have become known. None of that has happened.

As for His saying:

﴿And this is clear Arabic speech.﴾ (Surah An-Nahl 16:103), that is, the language of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is the language of the Qur'an, a clear and explicit Arabic, with no ambiguity or obscurity in it.

Al-Haqq tabaraka wa ta'ala says: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the signs of Allah...﴾ [16:104]. He negates from these people the attribute of faith. How then does He say after it: ﴿Allah will not guide them...﴾ [16:104]? Are they not non-believers and non-guided?

We say: guidance is of two kinds.

The first is the guidance of indication and direction (hidayat dalalah wa irshad, guidance in the sense of showing the way). In this, believer and disbeliever are equal, for Allah has indicated to all of them and made the path clear to all of them. Among its examples is His saying: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance...﴾ [41:17], meaning: We directed them and showed them the way.

The second is the guidance of assistance and success (hidayat al-ma'unah wa al-tawfiq), and this is granted only to the believer. Among its examples is His saying: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and gives them their piety﴾ [47:17].

So the meaning of ﴿Allah will not guide them﴾ [16:104] is: the guidance of assistance and success. It is also correct to say that the direction here is turned toward something else, so the meaning becomes: He will not guide them to the path of Paradise, but to the path of Hell, as He said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and do wrong, Allah will not forgive them, nor will He guide them to a path, except the path of Hell...﴾ [4:168-169]. The evidence for this is His saying after it: ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾ [16:104]. Also, because when He spoke of the believers in contrast, He said: ﴿And He will admit them to Paradise, which He has made known to them﴾ [47:6], meaning: He guided them to it and made its path known to them.

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah 16, verse 105:

It is as if the Exalted Lord is saying: "And if you fabricate against the Messenger of Allah, and accuse him of the true lie, [it is] that you deny the signs of Allah and do not believe in them."

We note, in the concluding phrase of this verse, that the Exalted Lord did not say: "And those are the disbelievers." Rather, He said: "the liars" (al-kadhibun), to indicate the abhorrence of lying, and that it is a quality that is not fitting for a believer.

For this reason, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked: "Does a believer steal?" he said: "Yes." That is because Allah said: ﴿And the thief, male and female, cut off their hands﴾ (Surah al-Ma'idah, 38).

Since He has legislated a ruling and attached a punishment to it, the matter has become something that occurs and is a possibility. He was asked: "Does a believer commit adultery?" He said: "Yes," because Allah said: ﴿The adulterer and the adulteress, flog each one of them﴾ (Surah al-Nur, 2). He was asked: "Does a believer lie?" He said: "No."

The hadith clarifies for us the monstrousness and abhorrence of lying, and how it is greater than all these wrongdoings. Allah has prescribed a known punishment for each of them, whereas He left the punishment for lying unspecified, to show that it is a crime greater than any punishment and more grievous.

So: lying is a quality that is not fitting for the believer, and it cannot be conceived in his case. That is because if someone becomes known as a liar, due to the people's familiarity with his lying, we would fear that when he says once, "I testify that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah," someone would say, "He is a liar, and this is one of his lies."

The Exalted Lord has already spoken of the ruling concerning believers and the ruling concerning disbelievers. Then He spoke of those who break their covenant and do not fulfil it, and then of those who slandered the Messenger of God and of those who denied the signs of God. All of these are matters of faith that had to be raised.

In this noble verse, the Exalted Lord makes clear to us that faith is not merely saying, "There is no god but God, Muhammad is the Messenger of God." Speech alone is not sufficient. One must bear witness to it, and bearing witness means that the heart and the tongue agree with each other in this statement.

Whoever reflects on this matter finds that logical division requires that we have four states:

The first: the heart agrees with the tongue affirmatively in faith. For this reason we say that the believer is consistent in his faith, because he says what his heart harbours.

The second: the heart agrees with the tongue negatively, that is, in disbelief. Likewise, the disbeliever is consistent in his disbelief in the sense mentioned earlier.

The third: he believes with his tongue while concealing disbelief in his heart. This is the state of the hypocrite (munafiq), and he is inconsistent in his faith, since he displays the opposite of what he conceals in order to benefit from the privileges of faith.

The fourth: he believes in his heart and utters the word of disbelief with his tongue.

This fourth state is the one intended in this verse. The Blessed and Exalted Lord here gives us a detailed account of the one who disbelieves after having believed: what is the cause of this disbelief, and what is his recompense?

His saying: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in God after his belief...﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 16:106).

This is a conditional clause whose answer is delayed until the end of the noble verse, so that you may pause first at the detail of this disbelief. It may be that it occurs under compulsion, over which the person has no control, so that he is forced to utter the word of disbelief while his heart is at rest in faith.

﴿Whoever disbelieves in God after his belief, except one who has been compelled while his heart remains firm in faith...﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 16:106).

Then the Qur'an falls silent about him, to show us that nothing is upon him, and there is no harm in a believer resorting to taqiyya (dissimulation under duress), which is a concession (rukhsa) that protects a person from the sources of destruction in such circumstances. In the history of Islam there are many examples of those who availed themselves of this concession, uttering the word of disbelief while their hearts were at peace in faith. In the noble hadith: "My community is relieved of error, forgetfulness, and that which they are compelled to do."

History records that Yasir, the father of Ammar, and his wife Sumayya were the first two martyrs in Islam. How did they die as martyrs? They were among the earliest Muslims and suffered much torture, until the disbelievers offered them the utterance of the word in exchange for their release. What did these two martyrs do? They proclaimed the truth and insisted upon faith until they attained martyrdom in the way of God, and they did not take the concession of taqiyya.

Their son Ammar was the first to take it, when he was subjected to the torture of the polytheists.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was informed that Ammar ibn Yasir had disbelieved. He (ﷺ) rejected this and said: "Indeed, Ammar's faith is from the crown of his head to his feet, and faith has mingled with his flesh and blood."

When Ammar came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he was weeping. He then recounted to him the harm he had suffered at the hands of the polytheists, and said: "By God, O Messenger of God, I was freed from their hands only because I spoke of you and mentioned their gods favourably." The Prophet (ﷺ) then wiped Ammar's tears with his blessed hand and said to him: "If they return to you, then say to them what you said."

This concession provoked the anger of some Companions, who questioned the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about it and said: "What about Bilal?" He said: "Ammar has availed himself of a concession, while Bilal proclaimed the truth."

There is no doubt that these are two stations in facing falsehood and its people, and that proclaiming the truth and patience in trial is a higher station and a loftier rank than availing oneself of the concession, because the first believed with his heart and his tongue, while the other believed with his heart only and his tongue uttered disbelief.

Therefore, during the apostasy movement, Musaylima the Liar tried to go around the tribes to extract from them a testimony to the truth of his prophethood. He said to a man: "What do you say about Muhammad?" He said: "The Messenger of God." He said: "And what do you say about me?" The man replied shrewdly: "You too," meaning that he extricated himself from this predicament without openly acknowledging the prophethood of this liar.

Then he met another and asked him: "What do you say about Muhammad?" He said: "The Messenger of God." He said: "And what do you say about me?" The man replied mockingly: "Speak up, for I have become deaf now." He denounced Musaylima's claim, and his reward was execution. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) learned of the two of them he said: "One of them availed himself of the concession, and the other proclaimed the truth."

The scholars have discussed compulsion in the words of the Exalted:

﴿except one who has been compelled while his heart remains firm in faith...﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 16:106).

They have clarified the aspects of compulsion and the ruling for each of them, as follows:

If a person is compelled to do something that is in itself a matter of personal conduct, as when it is said to him: "Drink wine or I will kill you or torture you," they say: he must in this case drink it and save himself, because it is a matter that concerns only him, and there are people who disobey God by drinking it. If it is said to him: "Disbelieve in God or I will kill you or torture you," they say: he is free to choose between availing himself of taqiyya here, using the concession that God has legislated for him, or proclaiming the truth and standing firm.

As for when the compulsion relates to the right of another person, as when it is said to you: "Kill so-and-so or I will kill you," in this case it is not permissible for you to kill him, because if you killed him you would be executed in retaliation (qisas), so what would be the benefit then?

After the Blessed and Exalted Lord has spoken of the ruling concerning one who is compelled while his heart remains firm in faith, He speaks of the other type:

﴿But whoever opens his breast to disbelief...﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 16:106), that is, he utters the word of disbelief content with it, indeed his soul is happy with it and his breast is expanded by it. This type is the one intended in the answer of the conditional clause.

﴿Upon them is wrath from God, and for them is a great punishment﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 16:106).

If the verses have fallen silent about the one who was compelled, and have not made him liable to punishment because he was coerced, they have made clear that whoever opens his breast to disbelief, upon him is wrath from God, that is, in this world, and for them is a great punishment, that is, in the Hereafter.

Just as we have seen in the history of Islam examples of the first type, who was compelled while his heart remained firm in faith, so too we have seen examples of those who opened their breasts to disbelief, namely the hypocrites. Some of them later embraced Islam and their Islam became sound, and among them was Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi al-Sarh from the clan of Amir ibn Lu'ayy.

(ذلك)، i.e., what they deserved of the punishment mentioned earlier.

﴿That is because they preferred the worldly life over the Hereafter.﴾ [16:107]

Istahabba (استحب): i.e., he preferred it and forced himself to love it. For if the sensible person looked at the worldly life in relation to his lifespan within it, he would find it short and too base to be loved for its own sake, and he would find its transient things numerous, changing its people so that no state endures for them. He looks, and behold, conditions change: from wealth to poverty, from health to sickness, from strength to weakness. How then could the worldly life be preferred over the Hereafter?!

The Truth, blessed and exalted, wants us to give each of the worldly life and the Hereafter the love it deserves. So we love the worldly life without excess in loving it; we love it as a field for the Hereafter, for otherwise how would we seek reward and recompense from God? Therefore we say: the worldly life is too important to be forgotten, and too trivial to be an ultimate goal. The Truth, glorified is He, has said:

﴿And do not forget your share of the worldly life.﴾ [28:77]

Some understood the verse as a call to work for the worldly life and take its portions, but whoever reflects on the meaning of the verse finds that the Truth, glorified is He, makes the worldly life a small thing liable to being forgotten and neglected, so He reminds us of it and urges us to take a share of it. For I do not say to you, "Do not forget such-and-such a thing," unless I know it is liable to being forgotten. This is one aspect of the moderation and balance in Islam.

It suffices us that this life is described as "the worldly" (al-dunya), for there is no description lower than this one; its counterpart requires us to say "the higher," which is the Hereafter. Yes, we do not deny the worth of the worldly life, nor do we diminish its due, for in it are life, sensation and movement, in it are righteous deeds and good remembrance... etc.

But despite that, it is subject to cessation and annihilation, whereas the Hereafter is the true, enduring, abiding life that is not touched by cessation nor threatened by death, as the Truth, glorified is He, said:

﴿And indeed the Last Abode is the true life, if they only knew.﴾ [29:64], i.e., the true life that we must strive for and love. Among that is His saying, exalted is He:

﴿O you who have believed, respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life.﴾ [8:24]. And His saying:﴿...over the Hereafter.﴾ [16:107].

One may say: the verse speaks of those who do not believe in the Hereafter, so how is it said of them: ﴿they preferred the worldly life over the Hereafter﴾ [16:107]?

We say: among those who do not believe in the Hereafter are those of whom Allah said: ﴿And they swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that Allah will not raise up one who dies﴾ [16:38].

And also among them are those who said:

﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a destination.﴾ [18:36]

So among these are those who believe in the Hereafter but prefer the worldly life over it. His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And indeed, Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾ [16:107], i.e., He does not guide them with the guidance of help and success. It has been previously said that guidance is of two kinds: guidance of direction (hidayat dalala), in which the believer and the disbeliever are equal, and guidance of help (hidayat ma'ouna), which is specific to the believer.

So: when guidance is negated, the intended meaning is the guidance of help. The non-guidance of Allah has settled upon the disbeliever because he is a disbeliever; it is as if his disbelief preceded his not being guided, or we may say: because he is a disbeliever, Allah has not guided him.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 16, verse 108:

Ṭaba' (ṭabaʿa): that is, He sealed over them. If you reflect on sealing, you will find that its purpose is that what is inside remains inside and does not come out, and what is outside remains outside and does not enter.

There is a difference between human sealing and the sealing of our Lord, glorified is He. The utmost we do is seal important things, such as secret letters for example, or when we wish to close a place we seal it with red wax to make sure it is closed. Nevertheless, we find someone who can circumvent this seal, open it, and perhaps restore it as it was.

But when the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, seals over something, no one can circumvent it, glorified is He. So the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has sealed over their hearts﴾ (Surah an-Nahl) is that the disbelief within them does not leave, and the faith that is outside them does not enter. That is because the heart is the vessel into which the senses pour, and the senses are the means of perception of known things, most importantly hearing and sight. With hearing you hear the revelation and the message from Allah, and with sight you see the signs of Allah's power in His creation and the wondrous craftsmanship that draws your attention to Allah's power and calls you to believe in Him, glorified is He. So when these senses deviate from what Allah intended for them, and instead of supplying the heart with the evidences of faith, their function becomes idle.

Hearing exists as an instrument that hears, but it hears only empty speech; there is no hearing in the meaningful sense. Likewise sight exists as an instrument that sees, but it sees what Allah has forbidden; there is no sight in the meaningful sense. So what, then, will reach the heart through these senses?

As long as the heart does not hear guidance and does not see the signs of Allah's power in His creation, we will find in it nothing but disbelief. If it wishes to believe, we say to it: you must first expel disbelief from your heart, for disbelief and faith cannot gather in one heart. Therefore there is a law found even in material things, which they call (non-interpenetration, ʿadam al-tadakhkhul). You can witness it when you fill an empty bottle with water: you see that the water enters only to the extent that the air leaves. The same is the case in immaterial vessels.

So if you wish to believe, O disbeliever, first expel from your heart the disbelief, and make it free of every desire. Then search with your intellect into the proofs of disbelief and the proofs of faith, and what you reach and are convinced of, admit into your heart. But to search the proofs of faith while disbelief is in your inner being is not valid. The heart must first be emptied, and you must place the two matters on an equal footing.

Therefore the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his body﴾ (Surah al-Ahzab).

And it is reported in a narration: "The love of this world and the love of Allah do not gather in one heart." This is because a human being has one heart, in which two opposites do not gather. Thus did the power of Allah will the heart to be in this form, so do not make it crowded with what is placed in it.

Moreover, the sealing of Allah over the hearts of the disbelievers indicates that the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, gives His servant what he wants, even if what he wants is disbelief. It is as though He, glorified is He, is saying to them: if you want disbelief and love it, and your breasts are expanded toward it, then I will seal over them, so disbelief does not leave them and faith does not enter them. Indeed, I will increase it for you if you love it, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿In their hearts is a disease, so Allah increased their disease﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah). So enjoy your disbelief, and depart, with no regret over you. And His saying: ﴿And those are the heedless﴾ (Surah an-Nahl).

Al-ghafil (the heedless): one who has a matter that he should be alert to, but he neglects it, as if he were waiting for a sign that would alert his intellect to reach the truth.

Then the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Undoubtedly...﴾ (Surah an-Nahl), meaning: truly and certainly, there is no doubt that these people will be losers in the Hereafter, because of what they committed of things that necessitate loss, and because of the grounds (haythiyyat) that brought about the judgment of their loss in the Hereafter. So that has become binding upon them and has been established for them. Whoever follows the preceding verses will find these grounds in them, beginning with their saying about the Messenger of Allah ﷺ:

﴿You are only a fabricator.﴾ (Surah an-Nahl, 16:101)

And their saying: ﴿It is only a human being who teaches him.﴾ (Surah an-Nahl, 16:103)

And their not believing in the signs of Allah, their being liars and fabricators against Allah, their contentment with disbelief, the expansion of their breasts toward it, and their preferring the worldly life over the Hereafter.

All of these are grounds and causes that necessitated for them loss in the Hereafter, on the Day when accounts are settled and the profits and losses are revealed. And how could its outcome not be loss for one who has committed all these crimes?!

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 16, verse 110:

Allah the Exalted says:

﴿Then, after that, those who were tested and then emigrated, struggled and were patient — indeed your Lord, after these things, is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (Surah An-Nahl)

Meaning: they were tried and tortured with painful torment because they had embraced Islam. As for His saying:

﴿Indeed your Lord, after them, is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (Surah An-Nahl)

It is among the mercy of Allah the Exalted that He opens the door of repentance for His servants who have transgressed against themselves. And among His mercy also is that He accepts the repentance of whoever repents, for if Allah did not open the door of repentance to the sinner, he would despair of Allah's mercy, and he would turn into a criminal who causes harm to society, even if he committed only a single sin. He would see before him no glimmer of hope that calls him to righteousness, nor any motive that drives him to give up sin.

But when he sees the door of his Lord open night and day, accepting the repentance of the penitent and forgiving the sin of the wrongdoer, as the noble hadith says: "Indeed Allah extends His hand by night to accept the repentance of the one who sinned by day, and extends His hand by day to accept the repentance of the one who sinned by night, until the sun rises from its west."

Moreover, our Lord, glory be to Him, increases him from His bounty if he repents well and regrets what he did, by replacing his evil deeds with good deeds, as He, glory be to Him, said:

﴿Except for those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds; for those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (Surah Al-Furqan, 70)

If the sinner sees this, it is more likely to reform him and more beneficial in rescuing him from the pit into which he has fallen. Thus, the legislation of repentance from the Truth, glory be to Him, is a mercy, and its acceptance from the sinner is another mercy. Therefore He, glory be to Him, said:

﴿Then He turned to them in forgiveness that they might repent.﴾ (Surah At-Tawbah, 118), meaning: He prescribed repentance for them and guided them to it, so that they might repent. If someone is deceived by the mercy and bounty of Allah and says: "I will commit many evil deeds so that Allah will replace them for me with good deeds," we say to him: And who tells you that the conditions of those whose evil deeds Allah replaces with good deeds do not apply to you? Can you guarantee that your term will be granted until you repent, when you know that death comes suddenly?

This verse may be connected to the preceding verse and related to it, so the meaning would be: ﴿Indeed, your Lord after that is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ [An-Nahl: 110].

This happens:

﴿On the Day when every soul will come pleading for itself...﴾ [An-Nahl: 111].

That is, the Day of Resurrection. Or the meaning may be: Mention, O Muhammad:

﴿The Day when every soul will come pleading for itself﴾ [An-Nahl: 111].

Does a person have more than one soul, so that one soul pleads on behalf of another?

The truth is that a person has one soul, in this world and in the Hereafter, but it differs in this world from how it is on the Day of Resurrection. This is because the Truthful One, glory be to Him, granted it choice in this world and made it free to act or not to act. Thus among souls there are the obedient, the disobedient, the compliant, and the obstinate.

When the soul stands in the position of the Resurrection and confronts the truth it used to oppose, it knows that obstinacy is of no benefit in that situation, and it has no recourse except to plead and defend itself. So it is as if the soul of the Resurrection pleads on behalf of the soul of this world, in a situation in which the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, calls out: ﴿Whose is the dominion today? It is for Allah, the One, the Irresistible﴾ [Ghafir: 16].

The Noble Qur'an has related examples of the soul's pleading on the Day of Resurrection. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [Al-An'am: 23]. ﴿And those who take protectors besides Him, [saying], "We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to Allah in position"...﴾ [Az-Zumar: 3]. ﴿Our Lord, show us those who misled us from among the jinn and mankind; we will put them under our feet...﴾ [Fussilat: 29].

So: it is one soul, pleading on its own behalf, on a Day when no soul will avail another in anything. Each is occupied with his own distress, held accountable for his own sin, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The Day a man will flee from his brother, and his mother and his father, and his wife and his children. For every man that Day, there will be a matter that will occupy him﴾ [Abasa: 34-37].

And His saying:

﴿And every soul will be paid in full for what it did, and they will not be wronged﴾ [An-Nahl: 111].

The Truthful One, glory be to Him, gives us a swift glimpse of the reckoning and recompense on the Day of Resurrection. The scale is a scale of justice and a straight balance that wrongs no one. ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [Az-Zalzalah: 7-8].

His saying, ﴿And every soul will be paid in full...﴾ [An-Nahl: 111],

indicates that the recompense from Allah is complete, with neither deficiency nor injustice. All are servants of Allah, and they are distinguished only by their deeds. If He shows them mercy, it is by His bounty, and if He punishes them, it is by His justice. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves﴾ [An-Nahl: 118].

Then the Truthful One, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And Allah strikes an example...﴾.

Having spoken of faith in God and of belief in the truthfulness of His Messenger in conveying the message, and of receiving God's methodology in the Book and the Sunnah, the Exalted spoke of the opposite of that: disbelief, obstinacy, and stubborn opposition to God, His Messenger, and His method. He, glory be to Him, wanted to give us a tangible reality in life for all of this, so He struck this parable for us.

The meaning of a parable (*mathal*) is that two matters are completely alike in a specific respect, such that you can say: "This is exactly like that."

The purpose of striking parables is to clarify the unknown through the known. If you do not know a person we are speaking about, we may say to you: "He is like so-and-so, whom you know, in height, and like so-and-so in complexion," and so on through the familiar images. After you gather these images, you will have a complete picture of this person whom you did not know.

Therefore, for that which has no like, beware of striking a parable for it, as the Truth, glory be to Him, said:

﴿So do not strike forth comparisons for God.﴾ (Surat al-Nahl, 74), because He, glory be to Him, has no like and no equal, neither in His essence, nor in His attributes, nor in His acts. He, glory be to Him, is the One who strikes the parable for Himself, whereas we strike parables only for the created beings subject to Him. Therefore we find in the Noble Qur'an many parables that clarify for us the unknown through what is known to us, and clarify the abstract matter through the sensible, tangible matter.

Among these is what God struck as a parable concerning spending in the way of God, and that God multiplies the expenditure and replaces it for its owner many times over. Observe how the Qur'an depicted this matter for us:

﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of God is as the likeness of a grain that grows seven ears, in every ear a hundred grains. And God multiplies for whom He wills, and God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾ (Surat al-Baqarah, 261).

Thus the parable clarified for us the unseen, unknown matter through the observed, sensible matter that everyone knows, until this unknown settled in the mind, and indeed became a certain matter standing vividly before us.

The one who reflects on this illustrative parable finds that what the Truth, glory be to Him, has clarified is stronger in giving than that through which He clarified it. For if these manifold multiplications are the yield of the earth, and the earth is a creation of God, Exalted is He, then what of the giving of the Creator, glory be to Him and Exalted?

The word (*daraba*, "to strike"), is taken from "striking the coin" (*darb al-'umlah*). In the past, coins were of gold or silver, and because of the fear of adulteration, since they would mix gold, for example, with copper, the *nuqqad* (assayers, i.e., experts in distinguishing coins) would strike them, meaning they would stamp upon them, so they became accredited, trusted, valid, and fit for circulation. Likewise, when God strikes a parable for an unknown thing through a known thing, it settles in the mind and is accredited.

So He, exalted, said in this parable: ﴿And God struck a parable: a city...﴾ (112).

The purpose of striking this parable is that the Truth, glory be to Him and Exalted, wants to clarify for us that when a person is blessed by God with various kinds of blessings, yet denies them, does not thank Him for them, does not render God's right in them, and uses God's blessing in disobedience to Him, he has exposed it to zawal (disappearance) and has exposed himself to a grievous outcome and an evil end. Therefore, one should bind the blessing by thanking for it and rendering God's right in it. For this reason, the poet said:

*If you are in blessing, then guard it,*
*for sins remove blessings.*
*Preserve it by thanking God,*
*for God is severe in retribution.*

But the city that God struck as a parable here, is it a specific city or is the meaning general? A specific city may be meant, as some said it is Makkah, or other cities. In any case, specifying it is of no benefit and does not affect the purpose of striking the parable with it.

Al-qaryah (the city) is the name of a town where people settle, a place of residence, i.e., a settled place. It is the name of a place, so when one speaks about it, the people dwelling in it are meant, as in His saying:

﴿And ask the city in which we were...﴾ (Surat Yusuf, 82).

So the meaning is: ask the people of the city, because the city as a place cannot be asked. This is what the scholars of tafsir (exegesis) said, on the basis that the verse contains a *majaz mursal* (metonymy, a figurative usage) whose relation is locality (*al-mahalliyyah*). But with the progress of modern knowledge, the Truth, blessed and exalted, gives us a new support, as He, glory be to Him, said:

﴿We shall show them Our signs on the horizons and within themselves...﴾ (Surat Fussilat, 53).

Now discoveries present us with the possibility of capturing images and recording the voices of those who came before. For example, after we leave this place, they can record this sitting of ours in sound and image.

This means that the place is conscious and keeps for us the images and voices for many long years. On this basis, we can say: the city can be asked, and can answer; it has a conscious memory that records and retains what it has recorded. Moreover, they aspire to restore images and voices from the beginning of creation, on the basis that they exist in the atmosphere, deposited in it in the form of waves that have not been lost or perished.

These waves are like the spreading of water when a stone is thrown into it. Asking the city will be more eloquent than asking its people, because its people may lie, whereas it does not know falsehood. With this understanding of the noble verse, there is in it one of the miracles of Qur'anic expression.

And His saying:

﴿It was secure and tranquil...﴾ (112).

*Aminah* (secure): meaning safe from raids on it from outside, and security is among the greatest blessings of God upon lands and their peoples. His saying: ﴿*mutma'innah*⁠ (tranquil)...﴾ (112), meaning it has the means of life within itself, so it does not need anything else. Life in it is stable and comfortable, and a person is not at rest except in a place free of disturbances, where he finds all the means of life. Security and tranquility are the secret of the happiness and stability of life. When God bestowed His favour upon Quraysh, He said:

﴿For the familiarity of Quraysh, their familiarity with the caravan of winter and summer. So let them worship the Lord of this House, who has fed them against hunger and secured them against fear.﴾ (Surat Quraysh, 1–4).

For as long as the stomach is filled and the soul is secure, life settles in a person.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) gives us an ideal picture of worldly life, when he said: "Whoever wakes up healthy in his body, secure in his dwelling, having his food for the day, it is as if the world has been gathered for him in its entirety."

The Truth, glory be to Him, describes this city as:

﴿Its provision comes to it abundantly from every place...﴾ (112).

It is well known that people are the ones who go out to seek provision, but in this city provision comes to it. This supports the view that it is Makkah, because God, Exalted, said of it:

﴿Have We not established for them a secure sanctuary, to which the fruits of everything are brought as provision from Us? But most of them do not know.﴾ (Surat al-Qasas, 57). Whoever finds life made easy for him in Makkah sees there fruits and products from all regions of the world. Thus the blessing was completed for them, and the means of a noble, secure, and serene life were perfected for them. So what did they do? Did they receive it with thanks to God? Did they use the blessing upon them in obeying Him and seeking His pleasure? No… rather:

﴿...but it denied the blessings of God...﴾ (112), meaning they denied these blessings and used them to oppose God's method and law. So the outcome was:

﴿So God made it taste the garment of hunger and fear, because of what they used to do.﴾ (112). It is as if in the verse there is a warning from the Truth, glory be to Him, to every society that disbelieves in God's blessing and uses the blessing to oppose His method, glory be to Him: its end will be like the end of these people.

﴿So God made it taste...﴾ (112). From *dhawq* (taste): we say *dhaqa* and *tadhawwaqa* the food when he places it on his tongue and tastes it. And taste does not go beyond the papillae of the tongue. So *dhawq* is specific to the flavour of things, but God, glory be to Him, did not say "He made them taste the flavour of hunger," rather He said:

﴿...the garment of hunger and fear...﴾ (112).

He made hunger and fear as if they were a garment that a person wears. The one who reflects on the verse perceives the precision of Qur'anic expression, for hunger and fear may transform into a garment worn by the hungry and the fearful. How is that?

Hunger first appears as a sensation in the belly. If the person finds no food, the body draws on its stored fat; when the fat is exhausted, the body feeds on muscle, then begins to wear away the bones. With severe hunger, one notices pallor on the complexion, emaciation and withering of the skin, then it shrivels and dries, and thus hunger turns into an outward form upon the skin, as if it were a garment the hungry person wears.

One can recognize hunger not from the hungry person's belly, but from his appearance, the paleness of his colour and the change of his skin, as God said of the poor who cannot travel in the land:

﴿You recognize them by their mark; they do not ask people persistently.﴾ (Surat al-Baqarah, 273). Likewise fear, although its seat is the heart, also appears on the body: when fear increases, the sinews tremble; when it increases further, the whole body shakes, so fear appears upon it like a garment one wears. Thus the Qur'anic expression has given these inner feelings a physical form that eyes can see, but it placed them under the sense of taste, because it is the strongest of the senses.

In comparing hunger and fear to a garment there is an indication that they cover the whole body, as clothing envelops it. Hunger is not only in the stomach, and fear is not only in the heart. Among what is well known among lovers and those who speak of love is that its seat is the heart, so we see them speak of hearts, as the poet said:

*The remembrances of you find my affection sweet,*
*so I feel from them a stirring in the heart.*

But when love increases and rises high, these feelings ascend, and love moves from the heart and dwells in all the limbs, mingling with every organ, in the words of the poet:

*No limb of mine is without its passion,*
*so it is as if my limbs were created as hearts.*

And His saying: ﴿...because of what they used to do.﴾ (112), meaning the Truth, glory be to Him, did not wrong them nor treat them unjustly. Rather, what befell them was the result of their deeds, their turning away from the path of God, and their disbelief in His blessings, so God withheld them from them. They confronted the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with aversion, denial, and rejection, harmed him and his companions, and plotted to kill him. So he prayed against them, saying: "O God, tighten Your grip upon Mudar, and make it upon them years like the years of Yusuf." So the Truth, glory be to Him, responded to His Prophet and clothed them in the garment of hunger and fear, to the extent that they would eat carrion and mix hair and wool with blood and eat it. They remained in this state for seven years until they cried out, and hardship and distress reached their limit. So they sent a delegation from among them to the Messenger of God, and he said: "This is your doing with the men of Makkah; what is the matter with its children and women?" So he (ﷺ) would send them what they could eat of lawful and good food.

As for the garment of fear, it was represented in the expeditions (*saraya*) that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would dispatch from Madinah to terrify and disturb them, so that they would know that the Muslims had acquired strength and power.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 16, verse 113:

We have seen how complete the blessing was for the people of Makkah, and this blessing was embodied in their being secure and at peace. This is a material blessing, by which God preserves the human frame, but man still needs something that preserves his values and morals.

This is the blessing of blessings, and God bestowed it upon them when He sent among them a messenger from themselves, for what benefit are material blessings in a land whose values are shaken and whose morals are corrupt? So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came to straighten what had become crooked in their conduct and to set right what had been corrupted of their values and principles. And His saying:

﴿from among themselves ... 113﴾ (Surat al-Nahl), that is, of their own kind, not a stranger to them, and not from the Arabs in general, but from Quraysh, the best and most central of the Arabs. God says:

﴿so they denied him ... 113﴾ (Surat al-Nahl). It would have been expected of them to receive him with what they knew of him of qualities of goodness and perfection, and with what was well known among them of truthfulness and trustworthiness. But just as they disbelieved in the material blessings, they also disbelieved in the blessings of values, embodied in the Messenger of God (ﷺ). And His saying:

﴿So the punishment seized them ... 113﴾ (Surat al-Nahl).

Who seized them?

The verse does not say "God seized them with the punishment," but rather "the punishment seized them," as if the punishment itself yearned for them, pounced upon them, and hastened to take them. In the verse there is a personification that suggests the severity of their punishment, as God says in another verse:

﴿On the Day We say to Hell, "Are you filled?" and it says, "Are there any more?" ... 30﴾ (Surat Qaf).

We said: when the situation of the people of Makkah became severe, to the point that they ate carrion, the Messenger (ﷺ) would send them what they could eat of the lawful and wholesome food, out of his (ﷺ) mercy toward them, and would say: ﴿So eat of what Allah has provided for you…﴾ [16:114], meaning: this provision is not from me, but from Allah.

﴿Lawful and wholesome…﴾ [16:114].

That is because previously they were not scrupulous about eating what Allah had forbidden, nor about eating the foul. So He wanted to alert them that Allah's provision for them is lawful, wholesome and pleasant, so that the lawful would replace the forbidden for them, and the wholesome would replace the foul. As for His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And be grateful for the favor of Allah…﴾ [16:114]. Here there is a warning sign to them that they should not fall into what they had fallen into before, namely denying and rejecting the blessing and disbelieving in it. They had already experienced the consequence of that: Allah removed security from them, clothed them in the garment of fear, removed from them satiety and ease of living, and clothed them in the garment of hunger. So take a lesson, then, from what has passed: ﴿if it is Him alone that you worship﴾ [16:114].

Almighty Allah, after saying:

﴿So eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good...﴾ (Surah an-Nahl 16:114)

wished to repeat a meaning that had been mentioned previously in al-Baqarah and al-Ma'idah. He said in al-Baqarah:

﴿He has only forbidden you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that which has been dedicated to other than Allah. But whoever is compelled [by necessity], neither desiring nor transgressing, there is no sin upon him. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah 2:173)

And the Exalted said in Surah al-Ma'idah:

﴿Prohibited to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that which has been dedicated to other than Allah...﴾ (Surah al-Ma'idah 5:3)

These are things you used to eat while they were forbidden to you. Now, since We have rescued you and granted you a spiritual aid from the Messenger of Allah, eat these things as lawful and good. But why was this meaning repeated here?

The repetition here is for two reasons:

The first: He, glory be to Him, does not want to give them a general picture of the ruling, but a specific picture tied to their condition. For they were hungry and wanted something to eat, even if it was carrion. Islam forbids carrion, so He made clear to them that after this they would eat what is lawful and good.

Second: the wording differs. In al-Baqarah:

﴿...and that which has been dedicated to other than Allah...﴾ (2:173)

And here:﴿...and that which has been dedicated to other than Allah...﴾ (16:115).

This is not a matter of stylistic variation; the meaning is entirely different. This is because al-Ihlal (إهلال) is raising the voice at the time of slaughter. They used to raise their voices at slaughter, but, God forbid, they would say: "In the name of al-Lat," or "In the name of al-'Uzza," thus invoking the names of false partners, and they did not mention the name of Allah, the Bestower.

So sometimes it is dedicated "to other than Allah" (bihi, with the preposition before the object), and sometimes it is "dedicated other than Allah by it" (lighayri Allah bihi). How so?

They said: slaughter was of two kinds. Sometimes they slaughtered to draw near to idols, so the basic character of the slaughter was that it was dedicated to other than Allah, meaning to the idols.

And sometimes they slaughtered to eat, without seeking nearness to anyone, so its basic character was that it was dedicated by it to other than Allah. Thus, the repetition of the verse is for a wisdom, and glory be to the One whose speech this is.

As for His saying:﴿...but whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing...﴾ (16:115).

Al-idtirar (الاضطرار) means that you find nothing to eat and nothing that sustains your life.

Here Almighty Allah grants us a concession: when necessity compels us, we may eat of these forbidden things to the extent that preserves life and quells hunger. So the meaning of "neither desiring" (ghayra baghin) is: not exceeding the limit. If you are compelled and have carrion while you also have lawful food, it is not permissible to eat the carrion in the presence of the lawful.

﴿...nor transgressing...﴾ (16:115), i.e., not exceeding the amount permitted, which is only what keeps life and suppresses your hunger, without satiety.

And He says:﴿...indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (16:115)

In al-Baqarah: ﴿...there is no sin upon him.﴾ (2:173)

The meaning is one, but here He mentioned forgiveness and mercy, and there He mentioned their cause. Here there is an allusion to what some of the atheists boast of, who search the Qur'an for a flaw, saying: "Since Allah has forbidden these things, what is their use in the universe?"

We say: Do you think that everything that exists in the universe was created to be eaten? Does it not have another purpose, and behind it another benefit besides eating? If Islam forbids its eating, it has permitted its benefit in another respect. For example, Allah forbade the eating of swine, but created it for another purpose and made for it a role in cleaning the environment, as it devours filth; thus it performs a function in life.

Likewise, we do not eat snakes, yet they have a purpose in life as well: they produce venom in their bodies, and with this venom some diseases and ailments are treated. There are many other examples.

Also, we must know that Almighty Allah has forbidden these things to us only for a wisdom. Man should take from the reality of his material constitution and his experiences what brings closer to him the religious and value meanings. If he looks at the machines that operate around him, such as engines, cars, airplanes and the like, he will find that each has its own fuel, which may not suit others. Even within one type, we see that car fuel, such as petrol, does not suit airplanes, which use the same fuel but at a higher degree of purity.

So: every thing has its suitable fuel. Likewise you, O human, have your suitable fuel, by which you can carry out your movement in life. You are the workmanship of your Lord, glory be to Him, and He is the One who determines for you what you eat and what you do not eat, and He knows what benefits you and what harms you.

A forbidden thing may be forbidden in itself, like carrion because of the harm in it. Or it may be lawful in itself, but forbidden with respect to a particular person, as when a patient is prevented from eating a certain food because it harms his health or delays his recovery; this is a temporary prohibition until its cause is removed.

Another form of prohibition is when a thing is lawful in itself and harmless to consume, yet you forbid it as a punishment, as you do when disciplining a child if he misbehaves, so you deprive him of a piece of candy, for example.

So: prohibition has many causes, and we will see examples of them shortly.

The meaning of (Your tongues describe the lie): it portrays it in its clearest aspects. Their speech is not merely a lie; it describes it. Whoever does not know what lying is should come to know it from the speech of these people. The lie intended here is their saying: ﴿This is lawful and this is unlawful...﴾ [16:116].

This is a lie and a fabrication against Allah, the Exalted, because He alone is the Owner of permitting and forbidding. So beware of making something lawful from your own self, or forbidding something according to your whim, for this is a fabrication against Allah: ﴿...to fabricate lies against Allah.﴾ [16:116].

And the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who fabricate lies against Allah will not succeed.﴾ [16:116].

If their lie passes over some people, and they take from it an immediate benefit, then soon their affair will be exposed, their lie will be uncovered, and their interests among the creation will be cut off.

Meaning: what they gained by their lying and their fabrication against God is a small, fleeting enjoyment. He will deprive them of the abundant, lasting enjoyment about which God said: ﴿What is with you will vanish, and what is with God is lasting﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 16:96).

This is not all. Rather: ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 16:117).

Following the verses on what Allah made lawful and what He made unlawful, and showing that declaring something lawful or unlawful belongs to Allah the Exalted, there comes an example of prohibition not because the thing itself is forbidden, but as a punishment (تحريم عقوبة), like the example we gave earlier of depriving a child of sweets as a punishment for his misbehaviour.

"Those who were Jews" (والذين هادوا): they are the Jews. Allah punished them by forbidding these things, although they are lawful in themselves, and this is a prohibition specific to them as a punishment. The words of the Exalted:

﴿And for those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws; and of cattle and sheep We forbade them their fat, except what their backs or their entrails carry, or what is mixed with bone. That was Our recompense for their rebellion, and indeed We are truthful.﴾ (Surah al-An'am 6:146)

Ma qasasna 'alayka min qabl (ما قصصنا عليك من قبل), in the words "﴿What We have related to you before...﴾" (16:118), refers to what is mentioned in Surah al-An'am in the verse above.

"Every animal with claws" (كل ذي ظفر): the animal whose toes are not split. "Al-hawaya" (الحوايا): the intestines and bowels. We see that all these things mentioned in the verse are lawful in themselves and lawful for non-Jews, but Allah forbade them to the Jews as a punishment for their wrongdoing and rebellion, as He, the Exalted, said:

﴿For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things that had been lawful for them, and for their hindering many from the way of Allah, and their taking usury though they had been forbidden it, and their devouring people's wealth unjustly. We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment.﴾ (Surah an-Nisa' 4:160–161)

That is, because of their wrongdoing We forbade them these good things.

This is because whoever takes a ruling by fabrication against Allah, forbidding what Allah has made lawful or making lawful what Allah has forbidden, must be punished in kind, so that what is lawful for others becomes forbidden for him. The Jews committed wrongdoing because they dared to transgress the limits of Allah and His teachings. The root and the peak of wrongdoing is associating partners with Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, association with Allah is a great wrong﴾ (Surah Luqman 31:13).

Wrongdoing (الظلم) is the taking of a right from its owner and giving it to another.

Among their wrongdoings: what they said to Musa, peace be upon him, after he had brought them across the sea, when they passed by a people devoting themselves to idols of theirs. They said: "O Musa, make for us a god just as they have gods." The Exalted said:

﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea, and they came upon a people devoting themselves to idols of theirs. They said, "O Musa, make for us a god just as they have gods."﴾ (Surah al-A'raf 7:138)

Among their wrongdoings: they worshipped the calf besides Allah. Among their wrongdoings toward Musa, peace be upon him: they did not believe in him, as the Exalted said:

﴿None believed in Musa except a few of his people, out of fear of Pharaoh and their chiefs that he would persecute them.﴾ (Surah Yunus 10:83)

Among their wrongdoings:

﴿and their taking usury though they had been forbidden it, and their devouring people's wealth unjustly﴾ (Surah an-Nisa' 4:161)

So, because of their wrongdoing and their taking what was not their right, Allah forbade them things that had been lawful to them. The Exalted said:

﴿And We did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves.﴾ (Surah an-Nahl 16:118)

They wronged themselves by giving themselves a little fleeting enjoyment, and they deprived themselves of the true and lasting pleasure.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 16, verse 119:

Almighty Allah gives His servant an opportunity, and opens for him the door of repentance (tawbah) and hope. It is part of Allah's mercy toward His servants that He prescribed repentance from sins for them, and also part of His mercy that He accepts it from them and turns to them in forgiveness.
