Had the door of repentance been closed, the sinner, even after a single lapse, would have turned into a criminal running riot in society; but by opening the door of repentance, Allah protects society from this rampage.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explains the status of repentance, saying: "Allah is more pleased with the repentance of His servant when he repents to Him than any one of you who was on his riding-beast in a barren desert, and it ran away from him, carrying his food and drink. He despaired of it, then came to a tree and lay down in its shade, having despaired of his riding-beast. While he was in that state, behold, it was standing right beside him. He took hold of its halter, then said, out of the intensity of joy: 'O Allah, You are my servant and I am Your lord.' He erred from the intensity of joy."

As for His saying at the beginning of the verse: "Then" (thumma), it indicates the abundance of the sins that preceded it; yet Allah forgave them, in order to show you the vast gulf between the mercy of Allah and the persistence of the disobedient in ingratitude toward Allah and in disobedience.

As for His saying: "out of ignorance" (bijahalah), it means with recklessness, folly and foolishness. All of these fall within ignorance (jahl), in the sense that one believes something that is not the case. Ignorance here does not mean lack of knowledge; rather, the ignorant person is one who holds a proposition contrary to reality and clings to it. The meaning is that he looks at a immediate good in his own view and abandons a deferred good in the view of the Shari'ah.

This meaning appears in the saying of the Almighty:

﴿Repentance is only incumbent upon Allah for those who do evil out of ignorance and then repent soon after.﴾ (Surah al-Nisa', 17)

"Out of ignorance" means in a moment of folly and recklessness. The sinner knows the ruling perfectly, but he is heedless of it and lacks foresight regarding the consequences. Had he reflected on the outcome of his affair, he would not have dared to commit the sin.

Therefore we say: the one who commits a sin does not proceed to it except in the absence of reason (ghaybat al-'aql).

This is why the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A fornicator does not commit fornication while he is a believer, a thief does not steal while he is a believer, and a drinker does not drink wine while he is a believer."

Had he kept in mind the severity of the recompense, he would not have undertaken his disobedience; but his folly and recklessness veil the recompense and conceal it from him, and adorn for him the pleasure and immediate enjoyment that awaits him.

Suppose a person is overwhelmed by the sexual instinct, which is the most fierce of human instincts, and he thinks about indecency, Allah forbid; before he falls into this deep abyss, we take him to the fire-stove and remind him of the recompense and punishment for this crime that he had overlooked.

By Allah, what do you think he would do? Would he persist in his crime? No; because he was dazed and heedless, and as soon as he is reminded, he returns. Thus his recklessness and folly diverted him from reflecting on the outcome, distracted him from reacting, and caused him to view matters with a superficial, hasty glance.

As for His saying: "Then they repented after that and made amends" (Surah al-Nahl, 119).

Repentance here is sincere, genuine repentance, in which its doer intends to desist from the sin and not return to it, and resolves upon this at the time of his repentance. When he does so, Allah accepts it from him and turns to him.

This does not preclude that he may return to the sin again if his soul is weakened in resisting it; if he returns, he returns to repentance anew, because Allah, glorified is He, has among His names "the Oft-Returning (al-Tawwab)", i.e., one who turns in repentance very often. Thus He did not say "tā'ib" (one who repents) but "tawwāb", so repentance on the part of the servant is never cut off, no matter how much he sins, and he must renew repentance for every sin.

Moreover, if the servant repents and repents well, and performs righteous deeds in place of evil, Allah bestows upon him that He changes his evil deeds into good deeds; and this is the dealing of a Lord who is Generous, Forgiving and Merciful.

As for His saying, glorified is He: "Indeed your Lord, after it, is Forgiving and Merciful" (Surah al-Nahl, 119).

It contains an indication of the Prophet's (ﷺ) eagerness for us, and that it gratifies him for Allah to forgive us. "Indeed your Lord" (O Muhammad) is Forgiving and Merciful; it is as if He, glorified is He, bestows a favour upon His Prophet (ﷺ) that He will forgive the sinners of his ummah.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 16, verse 120:

After the verses mentioned a portion of the history of the Jews and a portion of the history of the people of Makkah, they turned to Khalil Allah (the Friend of Allah), Ibrahim, peace be upon him and upon our Prophet.

The question is: why Ibrahim specifically, and not the rest of the prophets?

That is because he is the father of the prophets, and he has a great standing among the prophets, and everyone claims affiliation with him. Even the polytheists say: "We are upon the religion of Ibrahim." The Christians said of him that he was a Christian, and the Jews said that he was a Jew. So the noble verse came to clarify the character of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, to explain his attributes, and to refute and nullify their claims about Ibrahim, peace be upon him. Here are his attributes:

﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was a nation (ummah)...﴾ [16:120]

Ummah: In its general meaning, the ummah is a group of people, and the context is what determines its number. We say, for example, "the ummah of poets," meaning a group of poets. The ummah may also be a small group, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when he arrived at the water of Madyan, he found upon it a community (ummah) of people watering [their flocks]...﴾ [28:23].

So a group of shepherds was called an ummah because they had gone out for one purpose, which was to water their animals. The term ummah is also applied to a kind of people in a place, such as the ummah of Persia and the ummah of the Romans, and it may be applied to a group that follows one of the prophets, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them﴾ [35:24].

When we broaden its meaning, we find that in the message of Muhammad (ﷺ) it includes all nations, because he was sent to all of mankind, and he gathered the nations into one ummah, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, this, your ummah, is one ummah﴾ [21:92]. The meaning of "one ummah" is: encompassing all nations.

The meaning, then, is that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, stands in the place of a complete nation, because absolute perfections belong to Allah alone, while the perfections that Allah bestows on His creatures among the messengers are called human perfections bestowed by Allah. As for those other than the messengers, these perfections have been distributed among them, so each person takes one of them: this one takes forbearance, that one courage, another generosity, and so on. Thus perfections are gathered only in the messengers.

When you look at Ibrahim, peace be upon him, you find in him gifts that are found only in a complete nation. Likewise, our Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ), when he defined his position among the messages of Allah on earth, said: "Goodness is in me and in my ummah." This is the human perfection that Allah gave him.

That is: each of them took a part of this perfection, so it is as if his perfection (ﷺ) is scattered throughout his whole ummah. Therefore, when you follow the history of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, you find that each of his stances gives you a trait of goodness and a quality of perfection. When you gather these qualities, you find them present only in an entire nation. He is an imam and an exemplar combining all traits of goodness.

Among the meanings of "ummah" is that he, peace be upon him, stands in the place of a nation in the worship and obedience of Allah. His saying: ﴿devoutly obedient to Allah﴾ [16:120] means: humbly submissive to Allah, the Exalted, in His worship.

﴿Hanifan﴾ [16:120]. Originally, ḥanīf means: inclining. Ibrahim, peace be upon him, came when the world was in corruption and crookedness in the formation of values, so Ibrahim inclined away from this crookedness and turned away from this corruption.

Allah, glorified and exalted, sends messengers only when corruption has overspread, so his inclining away from crookedness and corruption means that he was upright and balanced upon the true religion, turning away from crookedness and deviating from corruption. Then Allah, glorified, concludes the verse with His saying: ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾ [16:120].

This is the fourth attribute of Khalil Allah Ibrahim, after He described him as being an ummah, devoutly obedient to Allah, and ḥanīf, and all of these negate polytheism (shirk) from him. So what is the benefit of negating polytheism from him once again in: ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾ [16:120]?

We must distinguish between the types of shirk. There is the greater shirk (al-shirk al-akbar), which is that you make partners for Allah, and it is the summit of shirk. And there is hidden shirk (al-shirk al-khafi), which is that you attribute to the causes that He created a role in the existence of things. So the verse here, ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾ [16:120], means hidden shirk. The preceding attributes negated from him the greater shirk, so He, glorified, wanted to negate from him the shirk of causes as well, which is subtle and hidden.

Therefore, when he, peace be upon him, was thrown into the fire, he did not turn to the causes, even though they came through the hand of Jibril, peace be upon him. When he was offered help, he said: "As for you, no." So where is the hidden shirk then, if the causes were absent for him from the very beginning?

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 16, verse 121:

The Exalted's saying: ﴿Grateful for His bounties﴾ (Surat an-Nahl).

In it is an allusion to the people of Makkah who denied the blessing of God and disbelieved in it, although their land was secure and tranquil. Such disbelief and ingratitude do not befit you, while you claim that you follow the creed (millah) of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). Ibrahim was not like that; rather, he was thankful to God for His blessings. And His saying: ﴿He chose him﴾ (Surat an-Nahl), i.e., He selected and chose him for prophethood. The choosing (ijtiba') of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was after testing, as the Exalted said: ﴿And when Ibrahim was tried by his Lord with certain words, and he fulfilled them﴾ (Surat al-Baqarah), meaning: He tested him with some obligations, and Ibrahim fulfilled them in the most complete manner. So his Lord said to him: ﴿Indeed, I will make you a leader for mankind﴾ (Surat al-Baqarah).

But out of his love that leadership (imamah) should continue among his offspring, he said: ﴿And of my descendants?﴾ (Surat al-Baqarah). So God corrected this desire for him and set him right, by informing him that among his descendants there would be wrongdoers. So He said: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ (Surat al-Baqarah).

Therefore Ibrahim (peace be upon him) learned from this situation, and he wished to be cautious for himself afterwards. When he wanted to ask his Lord to provide the people of Makkah with fruits, he said: ﴿Make this a secure city and provide its people with fruits, whoever of them believes in God and the Last Day...﴾ (Surat al-Baqarah).

God also corrected this request for him, for this situation differs from the first. The first concerned the leadership of religion and its values, and this is not something a wrongdoer can carry out. As for this one, it concerns provision and the gift of lordship, which encompasses the believer and the disbeliever, the obedient and the disobedient, for all are equal in provision. So the Exalted said: ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾ (Surat al-Baqarah), i.e., I will provide for the disbeliever as well.

Here the greatness of the lordship is manifest, which nurtures the prophets and shapes them under its own eye. All the positions of the prophets gather in the end and give us the essence of human perfection.

The precision of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) in carrying out what was asked of him is shown in his stance in building the House. After God guided him to its place, he began clearing away the traces of floods and uncovering its foundations. It would have sufficed Ibrahim, in executing his Lord's command, to raise the building to the height his hand could reach, but he loved to bring a raised stone and stand upon it to increase the height of the building. So he brought the stone that is the Station of Ibrahim, all while his son was helping him. Therefore, when he brought the stone, he brought one that only two men could lift.

Likewise is his faithful stance and his abandoning of means when he left his wife Hajar and his infant Isma'il in a valley without vegetation, in a place empty of the essentials of life and the means of livelihood.

He did not believe in means; rather, he believed in the One who causes them. As long as He, glorified is He, exists, He will provide for them from the means that preserve their lives. Therefore, when Hajar asked him: "Is this a dwelling that God has sent down for you, or is it from you?"

When she learned that it was from God, she said: "Then He will not abandon us." It was as if Ibrahim's faith overflowed onto his wife and filled her heart with certainty in God, the Exalted. And His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And He guided him to a straight path﴾ (Surat an-Nahl).

How? After all these attributes of faith, the verses say "and He guided him"; is this not all guidance? We say: the meaning is that He increased him in guidance, as the Exalted said: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and gives them their piety﴾ (Surat Muhammad).

The Almighty explains that Abraham's reward in this world, peace be upon him, is great, before the reward of the Hereafter. What is meant by the "good" of this world is that all the people of the religions love him, that there are many prophets among his descendants, a good conduct, and a good remembrance.

Here we are speaking of his attributes and virtues, and we take pride in him and are honored by him. This bounty from God to Abraham in this world is because he was thorough in obeying his Lord and worshipping Him. Abraham, peace be upon him, asked his Lord for this standing, saying: ﴿My Lord, grant me wisdom and join me with the righteous. And grant me a tongue of truthfulness among later generations﴾ (Surah ash-Shu'ara', 26:83-84).

Hukman (wisdom): that is, wisdom by which I place things in their proper places. And lisan sidq (a tongue of truthfulness): it is the good remembrance and the fine praise after I die. And the words of the Exalted: ﴿And indeed, in the Hereafter he is among the righteous﴾ (Surah an-Nahl, 16:122). So if this is his reward in this world, then there is no doubt that the reward of the Hereafter is greater.

Almighty Allah, after mentioning some of the qualities of the Friend (Khalil) Ibrahim, that he was a community (ummah) devoted obedient to Allah, a ḥanīf, and he was not of the polytheists, and that he was grateful for His blessings, and his Lord chose him and guided him... etc., said:

﴿Then We revealed to you﴾ (Surah an-Nahl, 16:123). O Muhammad: ﴿"Follow the religion (millah) of Ibrahim, a ḥanīf"﴾ (Surah an-Nahl, 16:123). It is as if the pinnacle of Ibrahim's virtues and good deeds is that We revealed to you, O Seal of the Messengers, that you should follow his religion. And millat Ibrahim means: the law (sharī'ah) of monotheism (tawḥīd). Then Almighty Allah affirms Ibrahim's innocence of polytheism, saying: ﴿"And he was not of the polytheists"﴾ (Surah an-Nahl, 16:123).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 16, verse 124:

After the Exalted One spoke of Ibrahim, the father of the prophets, and mentioned some of his qualities and virtues, He spoke of the Children of Israel regarding a matter in which they opposed God's command after having requested it themselves. It is as if the Qur'an were saying to them: You claim that Ibrahim was a Jew; here are Ibrahim's qualities, so what about your qualities? And where are you in relation to Ibrahim, peace be upon him?

God, glory be to Him, gives us an example of their opposition to their Lord in what He commands, and that they are not like Ibrahim in following Him. He mentions what they did concerning the matter of the Sabbath. Al-Sabt (the Sabbath) is the well-known Saturday, which follows Friday and precedes Sunday, and "al-sabt" is derived from sabata, yasbutu, sabtan, meaning: he rested and settled. From it is the Exalted saying: ﴿And We made your sleep a rest﴾ (Surah An-Naba', 9).

The Children of Israel sought a day on which they would rest from work and devote themselves to worshipping God. Their prophet Musa, peace be upon him, suggested that it be Friday, the day on which God completed the creation of the universe in six days, and the day chosen by the Friend, Ibrahim. But they rejected Friday and chose Saturday for themselves, saying:

God created the world in six days, beginning with Sunday and finishing on Friday, and He rested on Saturday; so we too want to rest and devote ourselves to worshipping God on Saturday. Thus this was their desire and their choice.

As for the Christians (al-'Isawiyyun), they refused to follow the Jews on Saturday or Ibrahim on Friday, and chose Sunday on the basis that it is the first beginning of creation. As for the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ), God chose for it Friday, the day of completion and the perfection of blessing.

So, the Jews requested Saturday and chose it for resting from work and devoting themselves to worship. This was their demand, and their Lord, glory be to Him and exalted, agreed to it, and commanded them to devote themselves to His worship on this day. He agreed with them in order to show their obstinacy and stubbornness, and that they would not fulfil what they had committed to, even though they had chosen it themselves. He agreed with them in order to cut off their argument, for had He chosen a day for them, they would have objected to it; but here they chose it themselves.

Also, the story of the Sabbath with the Jews came to serve a general doctrinal issue: that the signs which come to confirm the messengers in conveying from God may be from God and by His choice, exalted be He, and may be by the choice of the people addressed themselves. The Children of Israel did deny both kinds, and therefore the Exalted said: ﴿And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except that the former peoples denied them﴾ (Surah Al-Isra', 59), meaning: because they would propose the sign and then deny it; so their situation was denial upon denial. The story of the Sabbath is mentioned in many places, such as the Exalted saying: ﴿And ask them about the town that was by the sea, when they transgressed in the Sabbath, when their fish came to them openly on their Sabbath day, and on the day they did not observe the Sabbath, they did not come to them. Thus did We test them for what they used to defy.﴾ (Surah Al-A'raf, 163).

The Jews broke their covenant with God as is their habit, violated what they had committed to, and went out to fish on the Sabbath. So God outwitted them and enraged them: the fish would come to them floating on the surface of the water like sails, and they gained nothing from them but regret and sorrow. They would say: perhaps they will come tomorrow, but God disappointed their hope: ﴿and on the day they did not observe the Sabbath, they did not come to them...﴾ (Surah Al-A'raf, 163). The Noble Qur'an called this from them transgression (i'tida'), because they transgressed against what God had legislated. The Exalted said: ﴿And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath, so We said to them: Be apes, despised.﴾ (Surah Al-Baqarah, 65).

And the Exalted saying: ﴿Indeed, the Sabbath was only imposed upon those who differed concerning it...﴾ (Surah An-Nahl, 124).

The word (ikhtalafu, "they differed"), suggests the existence of two opposing groups in this matter. The truth, however, is that the disagreement was not among the Jews themselves, but between them and their prophet, who had chosen Friday for them; they opposed him and chose Saturday, so God made the disagreement a burden upon them.

Thus the meaning is: the Sabbath was only made a proof against those who differed concerning it, because it established their transgression against the day of worship. After they proposed it and chose it, it turned into a proof against them and evidence for their condemnation. If we reflect on His saying: ﴿upon those who...﴾ (Surah An-Nahl, 124), we find that the word (ʿala, "upon") indicates superiority, meaning that there is something higher and something lower; it is as if the Sabbath came against their interest, and as if their disagreement with their prophet turned back upon them. Among this is the Exalted saying: ﴿And indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for the people despite their wrongdoing...﴾ (Surah Ar-Ra'd, 6).

Some interpret it to mean (maʿa, "with"), meaning "despite." We say: the meaning is correct, but the sense of being with does not imply elevation. If we said "maʿa zulmihim" (with their wrongdoing), the meaning would be that forgiveness exists alongside wrongdoing merely as companionship. But the Exalted saying: ﴿And indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for the people upon their wrongdoing...﴾ (Surah Ar-Ra'd, 6) means that forgiveness rose above the wrongdoing. Wrongdoing calls for punishment, but God's mercy and forgiveness rose above treating the wrongdoer as he deserves; God's mercy preceded His wrath. The same point is found in the Exalted saying: ﴿Praise be to God, who has granted me, despite old age, Isma'il and Ishaq﴾ (Surah Ibrahim, 39), for old age called for not having children, but God's gift rose above the custom of old age.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 16, verse 125:

After the verses spoke of the highest model of faith in a human being, in the person of the father of the prophets, Ibrahim, and made among his greatest virtues that Allah commanded the Seal of His messengers to follow him, they began to explain the general features of the method of calling to Allah. His saying: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord...﴾ [16:125].

The Truth, blessed and exalted is He, does not direct this command of calling to His Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, except while knowing that he will carry out what he was commanded, and will undertake the task of calling and bear its responsibility. (ud'u, "invite"): meaning, guide people and show them the way.

﴿...the way of your Lord...﴾ [16:125]. The sabil (way) is the path and the method, and al-hikmah (wisdom) is placing a thing in its appropriate position. But why does calling to Allah need wisdom?

Because you do not call to the method of Allah except to one who has deviated from this method, and whoever has deviated from the method of Allah, you find him accustomed to disobedience and habituated to it. So you must be gentle with him in order to bring him out of what he has become used to and set him upon the correct method. Harshness and violence in calling such a person repel him, because you impose on him two hardships: the hardship of the call and its violence, and the hardship of abandoning what he loves and the ways of life he has become used to. So if you take the path of gentleness and kindness with him, and present the call to him well, he will obey you in abandoning what he was upon of opposing the divine method.

It is well known that advice in general is heavy on the soul, especially in matters of religion. So beware lest the one you advise feel that you consider yourself more knowledgeable than him or better than him. Beware of confronting him with his shortcomings, or embarrassing him before others, because all such conduct from the caller produces only the opposite result: this manner stirs up his resentment and may drive him to obstinacy and stubbornness.

This manner of calling is what is meant by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿with wisdom and good admonition...﴾ [16:125].

On this occasion, that is, the occasion of calling to Allah with wisdom and good admonition, there is related a story that passed between al-Hasan and al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both. This story embodies the true model of what the caller should be like.

It is reported that they saw a man who did not perform wudu well, and they wanted to teach him correct wudu without hurting his feelings. So they staged a dispute between themselves: each said to the other, "You do not perform wudu well." Then they referred the matter to this man, asking him to watch each of them perform wudu and then judge which of them was better than the other. Each of them performed wudu and did it well. Afterwards the judgment came from the man, who said: "Each of you has performed it well, and I am the one who has not performed it well."

This is admonition in its highest form, and example in its most wise form.

Another example of calling is set for us by the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, when a young man came to him in the heat of his youth, complaining of his inability to restrain his sexual desire, which, as we have said, is among the fiercest instincts in a human being. The young man came and said: "O Messenger of Allah, permit me to commit fornication."

Thus the young man was bold and did not conceal his ailment; thus he came to the physician seeking medicine openly, and knowing the illness is the first step toward cure. So what did the Messenger of Allah say?

Observe the method of calling, how it is, and how the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, drew out the disease from this young man's soul. He did not scold him, nor rebuke him, nor harm him; rather he took him, patted his shoulder gently and softly, and then said: "Would you like it for your mother?" He said: "No, O Messenger of Allah, may I be ransomed for you." He said: "Likewise people do not like it for their mothers." He said: "Would you like it for your sister?" He said: "No, O Messenger of Allah, may I be ransomed for you." He said: "Likewise people do not like it for their sisters."

And so on, until he mentioned the paternal aunt, the maternal aunt, and the wife. Then the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, placed his noble hand upon the young man's chest and supplicated for him: "O Allah, purify his heart and guard his chastity." So the young man rose, and the thing most hateful to him was to commit fornication, and he would say: "By Allah, my soul never inclined to anything of this kind but that I remembered my mother, my sister and my wife."

Let us reflect on this gentleness in stating the correct ruling. Treating the ailments of society requires understanding, tact, softness and good conduct. We see even the disbelievers, when they prepare a bitter medicine, coat it with a thin, sweet-tasting layer so that the patient accepts it and it becomes easy for him to take. How similar the treatment of bodies is to the treatment of hearts in this matter.

The people of experience in calling to Allah say: "Advice is heavy, so do not send it as a mountain, and do not make it a debate. Truths are bitter, so borrow for them the lightness of expression."

When the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, heard of something that did not please him, of a sin or an indecency in the community of faith in Madinah, he would climb his noble pulpit and say: "What is the matter with people who say such and such?"

He would suffice with general guidance without wounding anyone, in line with their saying in proverbs: "I mean you, but listen, O neighbor."

Among this is what wise people in the countryside would resort to when someone was robbed, or lost something of value. They would announce the loss of the thing that was lost or stolen and say: "On such a night, after the moon has set, we will throw dust." 

The meaning of "throwing dust" is that each of them brings an amount of dust and throws it in front of the house of the owner of the lost thing. In the morning they search through the dust until they find what was lost from them, and reach what they sought without the matter being exposed, and without anyone being embarrassed. Perhaps if they had confronted the thief, he would have denied it and the matter would have become complicated.

His saying, glorified is He:

﴿...and argue with them in the way that is best...﴾ [16:125].

Argument (jidal) is the discussion of proofs concerning one of the issues, and each of the two parties must present his proof in the best manner, that is, in gentleness and softness, without tension or arrogance.

In this situation of argument you must not anger the opponent, for he may cling to a word from you and take it as a pretext to leave the assembly. His saying, glorified is He:

﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way, and He is most knowing of the guided﴾ [16:125].

Some may ask: what is the connection of this concluding phrase of the verse to the subject of calling to Allah?

The Truth, glorified is He, wants to show us the sensitivity of this task, and that it is built on sincerity to Allah in giving counsel. The caller must never deceive in his calling, aiming through it at something else. You may give an admonition while there is arrogance toward the one admonished in yourself, or a feeling that you are better or more knowledgeable than him.

Among people, God forbid, is one who gathers the husks of a subject and thinks he has become a scholar, so he harms people more than he benefits them.

Therefore: if deceit is unacceptable in anything, it is even less acceptable in the field of calling to Allah. So beware of deceiving about Allah in the name of Allah, for He, glorified and exalted, is most knowing of who has strayed from His way and turns people away from the way of Allah, and He is most knowing of the guided.

We note that this meaning occurs in the verse where Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, then transgress against him in the same way as he transgressed against you﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah 2:194).

By comparing the two verses, we see that they both establish equivalence in repelling aggression: ﴿then retaliate with the like of﴾ (Surah al-Nahl 16:126) and ﴿then transgress against him in the same way as﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah 2:194).

So, Allah the Exalted, although He legislated for us the repelling of aggression with its like, made its implementation difficult. Who can determine the equivalence in retaliation, so that it is exactly its like, without transgression and without an increase in the punishment? It is as if the difficulty of determining equivalence points to the recommendation of turning away from it toward what is better than it, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But if you endure patiently, it is indeed better for the patient﴾ (Surah al-Nahl 16:126).

Allah has placed in patience a breadth, and made it better than returning the punishment and bearing the trouble of determining its equivalence. Besides this, patience brings about the reconciliation of hearts and the removal of resentments, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Repel evil with what is better, and then the one between whom and you there is enmity will become as though he were a devoted friend﴾ (Surah Fussilat 41:34).

In this there is a repelling of the harshness of the soul, a closing of the avenues of revenge, and an end to grudges and hatreds. As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is better for the patient﴾ (Surah al-Nahl 16:126), the goodness here has several aspects:

First: In patience and not returning punishment with its like there is an ending of disputes and a comfort for society, so that it is not terrorized by an endless chain of enmity.

Second: Whoever among the creatures is wronged and then patiently endures their wrongdoing, has been guaranteed that Allah is in his protection, because Allah is jealous on behalf of His wronged servant and places him in His companionship and protection. For this reason they said: "If the wrongdoer knew what Allah has prepared for the wronged, he would begrudge them the wrongdoing."

Whoever examines the verses about patience in the Noble Qur'an finds a similarity in the endings of some verses. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And endure patiently what befalls you. Indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination﴾ (Surah Luqman 31:17).

And in another verse: ﴿But whoever endures patiently and forgives, indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination﴾ (Surah al-Shura 42:43).

We must not forget that the speaker is Allah, so the meaning is not one. Every letter here has a meaning, and the circumstances differ, so consider the precision of the Qur'anic expression. The afflictions that befall a person are of two types:

The first type: There are afflictions that reach a person by the decree and predestination of Allah, with no opponent in them, such as one who is afflicted in his health, or struck by a calamity in his wealth, or whose house collapses, etc. In this type of affliction a person feels the pain of loss and the sting of damage, but there is no resentment in it toward anyone.

So, patience regarding these events is easier, because it is a trial and decree and predestination, and the command to be patient here does not need emphasis. This fits His saying: ﴿And endure patiently what befalls you. Indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination﴾ (Surah Luqman 31:17).

As for the other type: it is the afflictions that occur by the act of an agent, such as killing, for example. Alongside the loss, there is an opponent to you who stirs your anger, incites your rage, and calls you to revenge whenever you see him. So patience in this case is harder, and compelling the soul to it requires emphasis, as in the second verse: ﴿But whoever endures patiently and forgives, indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination﴾ (Surah al-Shura 42:43).

Here He used the emphatic lam (لام التوكيد), because patience here is arduous, and the opportunity is open for Satan to stir up hearts and incite grudges and hatreds. We also notice that in the first verse He said (واصبر) ["and endure patiently"]. In the second He said (صبر وغفر) ["endures patiently and forgives"], because there is an opponent before him who calls him to forgive him.

It is related in the stories of the Arabs that there was a Jewish usurer who gave a man money on condition that he repay it by a known term, and stipulated that if he did not fulfill the repayment at the specified time, he would cut a pound of his flesh. The man agreed, but when the time of repayment came, the man could not pay what he owed.

So the Jew brought the matter before the judge and recounted the agreement between them. The judge, who was a man of insight, said: "Indeed, the contract is the law of the contracting parties," and he ordered that a knife be brought to him. He said: "Take a pound from his flesh, but in one stroke. If you exceed the pound or fall short, we will take from your own flesh."

When the Jew saw the hardship of what he was about to undertake, he preferred safety and reconciled with his opponent.

Now the question is: what is the connection of this verse, ﴿And if you retaliate﴾ (Surah al-Nahl 16:126),

to what precedes it: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction﴾ (Surah al-Nahl 16:125)?

Calling to a method that directs the human being, the vicegerent of Allah on His earth, to adhere to the method of Allah by which He appointed him as vicegerent and laid down this method to regulate the movement of his life. The caller faces those who corrupt the earth and achieve their own interests at the expense of others. Whoever achieves his interest at the expense of another must have strength and power, by which he tyrannizes, domineers, and oppresses.

So when the method of Allah the Exalted comes to alter the conduct of these people, to take them out of what they have become accustomed to, and to strip from them the authority of tyranny and oppression, and to deprive them of this whip by which they benefit, they must argue with it, collide with it, and stand against it. For it has combined upon them severe counsel and reform, and severe abandonment of what they had become accustomed to.

So the caller must adorn himself with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in the way that is better. But if their affair exceeds to aggression against the caller, when corruption spreads and the harshness of dispositions prevails, then we will need another method, since the method of wisdom no longer benefits.

We must take the stand demanded by ordinary manhood, to say nothing of faithful manhood, and we must have the ability to respond with the response that Allah the Exalted has legislated for us, without stubbornness in dispute or extravagance in punishment.

Thus came His saying: ﴿And if you retaliate, then retaliate with the like of that with which you were afflicted﴾ (Surah al-Nahl 16:126).

In the verse there is a warning that the response should not exceed its like. In this way the opponents learn that you are subject to a just divine method, before which all are equal. Even if they deviate and commit crimes, retaliation by like does not go beyond it. Perhaps this will draw their attention to the fact that the One who commanded this did not let the harshness of revenge run free, but calmed it and called to pardon and forgiveness, so that this would be more conducive to their guidance.

This divine directive, restricting punishment to its equivalent, was addressed to his nation before it was addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in a particular matter, one that does not concern a believer in general, but a believer who is beloved to the Messenger of Allah and who holds a great station with him: his uncle and companion Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib, Master of the Martyrs, may Allah be pleased with him.

The disbelievers mutilated him at Uhud; Hind split open his belly and chewed his liver. This was grievous to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and affected him deeply, and he faced this situation with two emotions: his faithful emotion, and the emotion of kinship and blood ties, for he was his uncle who supported and aided him and stood by his side. In his agitation over this emotion, he said: "If Allah grants me victory over them, I will mutilate thirty men from among them." But Allah the Exalted, the Just, who sent down the balance of justice and truth among creation, calmed his distress, and set this matter right for him and for his nation after him, so He said: ﴿And if you retaliate, then retaliate with the like of that with which you were afflicted﴾ (Surah al-Nahl 16:126).

Whoever reflects on the Qur'anic style in this verse notices in it a call to tenderness toward the opponent and mercy toward him. The speaker is Allah the Exalted, so every letter has a meaning. Do not take the words in their general sense, but reflect upon them and you will find behind the letter a purpose and a desired aim. Why did Allah the Exalted say (وإن) ["and if"] and not use (إذا) ["when"], for example?

(إن عاقبتم): as if the meaning is: "He would have loved that you not retaliate."

As for (إذا), it indicates certainty and affirmation, while Allah the Exalted wants to soften hearts and to place the return of punishment with its like in the narrowest scope. This is mercy even toward enemies. This mercy makes them fond of Islam and invites them to it, and through it these enemies become soldiers in the ranks of the call to Allah.

Also, His saying (عاقبتم) ["you retaliate"] is evidence that returning punishment requires strength and readiness, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And prepare against them whatever you can of power and of steeds of war, by which you may terrify the enemy of Allah and your enemy and others besides them whom you do not know but whom Allah knows﴾ (Surah al-Anfal 8:60).

It is as if He is saying: be always prepared, and in a state of strength that enables you to respond if you are attacked. Also, the presence of strength and readiness deters and terrifies the enemy, so that he does not dare to attack from the outset. By strength and readiness the balance in society is preserved, for no one thinks of attacking the strong.

This is what we see today among the nations of the world in their furious struggle over arming themselves with deadly weapons.

As for the word ﴿what you were afflicted with﴾ (Surah al-Nahl 16:126):

We note that the response to aggression is called punishment (عقوبة), but why do we also call the first aggression a punishment? They said: this is a manner of expression called al-mushakalah (a figure of speech in which one term is used for another because of their correspondence in wording), meaning that the actions all came in one form.

Among examples of this is His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ (Surah al-Shura 42:40), since the return of an evil is not called an evil.

Someone may raise a question on this issue: since Islam seeks forgiveness in this matter, why did it not establish it from the beginning? And what is the benefit of speaking about retaliation in kind?

We say: because a society is not sound in its formation unless every person in it is secure in his self, his honor, his property, etc. This security is not achieved except by a strength that protects it. Also, society has a balance, and this balance in society is preserved only by a strength that guarantees the performance of rights and duties, and guarantees that a person's movement in society is free of injustice to him.

Also, Allah the Exalted has a lofty wisdom in legislating punishment for crimes. The aim of the Wise Lawgiver is to restrain crime and prevent its occurrence. If the murderer knew that he would be killed, he would not dare to commit his crime. So in the legislation of punishment there is mercy toward society and preservation of its safety and security.

And we see some objecting to the punishment for apostasy, saying: "How can you kill one who apostatizes from your religion? Then where is freedom of belief?"

We say: in legislating the killing of one who apostatizes from Islam there is a narrowing of the avenues of entry into this religion, so that no one enters it except after complete conviction and firm belief. If this ruling is known from the beginning, then a person is free to enter or not to enter; no one forces him. But let him know that if he enters, the ruling on apostasy is known.

Thus: Islam legislated punishment so that it preserves the balance of society, and to act as a deterrent so that crime does not occur from the outset. But if it does occur, recourse is made to another remedy that uproots the roots of rancor, grudges, and hatreds from society.

For this reason we have previously spoken about the custom of blood revenge in Upper Egypt: that it continues in an endless chain of killing and vendetta, terrifying the whole society, even the secure who have no fault, and hatreds and animosity grow between families in this thorny atmosphere. Then, when one of them is emboldened, he takes his shroud in his hands, goes to the guardian of the slain, and throws himself into his hands, saying: "Here I am before you, and my shroud is with me; do with me what you will." At that point their honor and nobility forbid them from taking revenge on him, and so pardon, forgiveness, and tolerance become the end of the endless chain of vengeance.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 16, verse 127:

After the verses had mentioned the virtue of patience (sabr) and the good that lies in it, the preceding verse seems to pave the way for the command here, "And be patient" (wa-isbir), so that everyone may act upon the command of God, after He has presented to them the grounds that make patience a courage and not a weakness, as they say in the proverb: "Part of courage is to be cowardly for an hour."

So when Satan whispers to you, tempts you toward revenge, and your soul is stirred up, then courage is to be patient and not to obey them both. His, the Exalted's, saying:

﴿And be patient, and your patience is not but through God (127)﴾ (Surat an-Nahl).

It is from the wisdom and mercy of God that He made you patient in the face of harm, because in patience there is good for you. God is the One who helps you to be patient, and who keeps from you the whispering of Satan and the evil thoughts that stir up your anger and drag you toward revenge.

The Truth, glorified and exalted, wants His servant to turn toward carrying out His command. So when He knows that this is in his intention, He takes charge of his affair and helps him, as He, the Exalted, said:

﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and gives them their piety (17)﴾ (Surat Muhammad).

Beware lest you believe that patience comes from you yourself. God wants you to turn toward patience merely as a turning and an intention. When you turn toward it, God mobilises for you the good thoughts that help you to it, make it easy for you, and make you content with it, so your patience comes beautiful, with no resentment in it and no objection to it.

Then He, the Exalted, says: ﴿And do not grieve over them... (127)﴾ (Surat an-Nahl).

God bestowed His favour upon the Arab nation, which received the call of God through the tongue of His Messenger (ﷺ), by sending among them a Messenger from themselves and from their best, whose lineage, history, and character they knew. The Messenger (ﷺ) loved his people and was eager for their guidance, as He, the Exalted, said:

﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves; grievous to him is what you suffer; [he is] concerned over you, to the believers [he is] kind and merciful (128)﴾ (Surat at-Tawbah). That is: your hardship is grievous to him, and your distress and fatigue pain him; he is eager for you, wanting to complete for you every kind of good, because the meaning of ḥirṣ (eagerness) is withholding something (ḍann bi-l-shay'), as if he (ﷺ) were stingy with his people.

This meaning has been clarified in the noble hadith: "The likeness of me and of my community is like a man who kindled a fire, and the moths and insects began to fall into it, while I am taking hold of your waistbands and you are plunging into it."

Therefore the Messenger of God (ﷺ) grieved over his people when he saw their disbelief, obstinacy, and arrogance in refusing the truth, while he wanted for them guidance and righteousness. For when you love a person, you love for him the good you see, like someone who went to a market, found it prosperous and profitable, and pointed it out to those among his family and acquaintances whom he loves. Likewise, when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) tasted the sweetness of faith, he loved that his people should share this delight of faith.

The Truth, glorified and exalted, here consoles His Messenger and lightens for him what distressed him regarding his people. He says to him: Do not grieve over them, and do not burden yourself beyond its capacity, for upon you is only the delivery (of the message). His Lord addresses him in another verse: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over their traces, if they do not believe in this discourse (6)﴾ (Surat al-Kahf), that is: do not be one who destroys himself out of sorrow over them. And His saying: ﴿And do not be in distress over what they plot (127)﴾ (Surat an-Nahl).

Ḍayq (distress): it comes with a fatḥah and with a kasrah: ḍīq, ḍayq.

And ḍayq is that a spacious thing diminishes before you from what you had estimated it to be. Distress befalls a person in degrees: his land may become constricting to him, so he moves to another land.

Perhaps the whole world constricts upon him, and in this state his own self may be able to contain him. But if his own self constricts upon him, he has reached the furthest degree of distress, as He, the Exalted, said about the three who stayed behind from the jihad with the Messenger of God: ﴿And [He also forgave] the three who were left behind, until when the earth, for all its vastness, closed in on them and their souls confined them... (118)﴾ (Surat at-Tawbah).

So the Truth, glorified, forbids His Messenger (ﷺ) to be in distress over the plotting of the disbelievers, because the one who is distressed by a matter is the one who does not find in the field of his thought and his alternatives what would bring him out of this distress. Rather, the one who knows that he has a way out and an exit is not in distress.

So the meaning is: Do not be in distress, O Muhammad, for God is with you; He will make for you an exit from distress and will return their plotting upon them: ﴿And they plot, and God plots, and God is the best of plotters (30)﴾ (Surat al-Anfal).

Therefore, he says: "No distress, for you are the Lord." So at the moment when the world, the family, and the loved ones constrict upon you, and your own self constricts upon you, then your Lord will encompass you, and you should be in His company, glorified is He.

This is the question of God's companionship (ma'iyya) with those who have taqwa. Whoever fears God is in His protection and companionship, and if you are in the companionship of your Lord, who would dare to plot against you or scheme against you?

In the journey of the Hijra, the companionship of God, may He be exalted, becomes manifest and embodied for us in the cave, when the disbelievers surrounded it. Abu Bakr (raḍiya Llāhu ʿanhu) said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "If one of them looked down at his feet, he would see us." The Messenger of God (ﷺ), certain of this companionship, answered him: "O Abu Bakr, what do you think of two whose third is God?" So what is the connection between this answer from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and what Abu Bakr said?

The meaning: since God is their third, they are in God's companionship, and God cannot be perceived by sight; so whoever is in His companionship in this way cannot be perceived by sight. And His saying: ﴿Fear God...﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 128).

Taqwa (God-consciousness, guarding oneself against displeasure) in its general sense is obedience to God by following His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. Among its uses we say: "Fear God" and "Guard yourselves against the Fire," and the one who reflects finds that their meanings meet at one point.

The meaning of "Fear God" is: make between yourself and the punishment of God a shield and barrier that protects you, by following His command and avoiding His prohibition; because the Truth, glory be to Him, has attributes of mercy: He is al-Ra'uf, al-Rahim, al-Ghafur; and He has attributes of majesty: He is al-Muntaqim, al-Jabbar, al-ʿAziz. So make for yourself a shield against the attributes of retribution.

And we say: "Guard yourselves against the Fire," i.e., make between yourselves and the Fire a shield; and protection from the Fire is only through obedience to God by following His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. So the meaning is one, but it came once with the necessary consequence and once with the consequence of the consequence. And His saying: ﴿and those who are doers of good (muhsinun)﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 128).

The muhsin (one who does good, excellence in worship) is the one who obliges himself in worship of God beyond what God has obliged him, and of the same kind as what God has obliged him. If the Sharia has enjoined on you five prayers in the day and night, then ihsan is that you add to them whatever voluntary prayers (nawafil) you can manage; and if fasting is the month of Ramadan, then ihsan is that you fast on such-and-such days of the remaining months; and likewise with zakat and other things God has made obligatory.

Thus we find that ihsan is the highest of the ranks of religion, and this is clear in the hadith of Jibril when he asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about Islam, iman and ihsan, and he said: "Ihsan is that you worship God as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you."

The noble verse suggests to us that those who have taqwa have a reward and companionship, and those who are doers of good have a reward and companionship, each according to his rank; because the Truth, glory be to Him, bestows attributes of perfection on His creatures in proportion to their companionship with Him, glory be to Him. So the one who is content with what has been obliged upon him is not equal to one who does good and adds more; the second must have a distinction and a special status.

In Surah al-Dhariyat He, may He be exalted, says:

﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and springs, "15" taking what their Lord has given them. Indeed, they were before that doers of good. "16"﴾

(Surah al-Dhariyat).

He did not say "believers," because the believer brings only what is obligated upon him. But what is the form of their ihsan? He, may He be exalted, says:

﴿They used to sleep but little of the night, "17" and before dawn they would seek forgiveness, "18" and in their wealth there was a right for the beggar and the deprived. "19"﴾ (Surah al-Dhariyat).

All of these are supererogatory matters that exceed what God has obliged upon them. And we must take note here that what is meant by His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿and in their wealth there was a right for the beggar and the deprived "19"﴾ (Surah al-Dhariyat).

is not zakat, rather it is charity (sadaqa); because regarding zakat He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿a known right...﴾ (Surah al-Ma'arij, 24).
